The run-level abort ( RunAbort in lifecycle.py ) fires when an integration hook aborts the run; a throwing audit cancels the in-flight test method; test-method completion stops the audit loop. Suite code must let asyncio.CancelledError propagate — swallowing it breaks the wind-down. - The read-only utils.signal combines the run-level integration halt with the nearest authored audit scope. Audit scope is inherited only by that node's composed suite: an audit failure cancels its own in-flight work and produces Fail without cancelling an independent parallel sibling. If an audit verdict and suite completion occur in the same event-loop turn, the audit verdict wins; evidence is not discarded by timing luck. - Every started descendant cancelled by an audit still seals its result and dispatches its paired after_each . An unsettled descendant carries the audit's TestFailure class-intact; a descendant already dispatching after_each retains the verdict that hook received. Audit cancellation never becomes a run-wide integration halt. - utils.exec threads cancellation to the underlying child process. When a cancellation fires, in-flight shell commands are killed (SIGTERM) immediately — no zombie processes outlive the test. Developer obligation: - Call self.use_audit() in the constructor with both interval and fn — both are required parameters. - Yield to the event loop ( await ) inside any long-running loop in a test method so cancellation can be delivered, and never suppress asyncio.CancelledError . - Use use_audit for active monitoring that can fail the test (e.g. thermal runaway, watchdog). Use use_survey for passive state snapshots at phase boundaries that never affect the verdict. - Raise TestFailure from the audit fn to fail the test. Return data to continue — it is always recorded as evidence.
docs.title: Audit Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: before_each and after_each are optional integration hooks registered at the root run() call. The framework threads them down to every executed descendant and dispatches them around every node's lifecycle. before_each fires immediately before a node's lifecycle begins. after_each fires immediately after a node's lifecycle completes, receiving the node's RunResult . Pair invariant: after_each fires EVEN IF before_each threw. An integrator writing a "started" row in before_each always gets a "finished" row in after_each — no orphan records in the external system. Throw from either hook → framework wraps as ExternalIntegrationFailure → the shared run-abort fires → every in-flight framework→user await across the tree unwinds at its own framework boundary → every in-flight transport is closed via cancel_in_flight() → enclosing node transitions to Aborted. The integrator's own error class arrives intact as the failure's cause. An operator SIGINT/SIGTERM during a live run takes this same halt path, with OperatorInterrupt as the reason. Hooks receive a deliberately narrow context ( BeforeEachContext / AfterEachContext ): node name, ancestor chain, breadcrumbs, scoped logger, env snapshot. NOT exec , get_shell , or capture_artifact . Integration hooks are for external coordination, not for exercising the hardware. Unpaired registration (only before_each or only after_each ) emits a loud warning at run start unless allow_unpaired_hooks=True is passed. The pairing enforces the started/finished symmetry. Developer obligation: Do not register before_each / after_each inside your TestComponent subclasses. These hooks are the integrator's contract with the outside world, not part of the test's own lifecycle. Use use_survey / use_audit for per-test observation; use before_each / after_each only when composing HILT into a larger harness.
docs.title: Integration Hook Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: When the run-level abort fires (an integration hook throws anywhere in the tree, or the operator sends SIGINT/SIGTERM to a live run), every framework-managed transport is closed HARD immediately — not at the next polling boundary. Cancelling the coroutine is not enough; the framework cancels the RESOURCE. The operator-signal handler is installed by run() / main() only while that run is live, on the running loop, and removed on the way out so a library caller never leaks it. The first signal fires RunAbort with an OperatorInterrupt and hard-closes transports; a second signal inside the finalization window exits the process immediately. SshInterface destroys its underlying asyncssh connection, closing every open channel and failing every pending exec stream at the socket level. Recursively propagates through via chains — a jump-host tunnel and everything tunneled through it collapse together. RemoteInterface subclasses expose cancel_in_flight() for any transport type that needs aggressive close semantics. Long-running user operations (firmware flashes, long-polling requests, multi-step SSH scripts) in flight when the abort fires receive a dead resource, causing their own awaitables to fail and settle harmlessly in the event loop. Consequence: A 30-minute firmware flash in progress when before_each throws does NOT continue to mutate the hardware. This is load-bearing for manufacturing test integrity — the halt signal means "stop touching the hardware," and the framework enforces that at the transport layer.
docs.title: In-Flight Termination Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: TestGroup runs its children concurrently under asyncio.TaskGroup , and the child boundary guarantees the TaskGroup semantics are correct: Fail and node-local Aborted are returned by the boundary, never raised — one child's failure cannot escape into the TaskGroup and cancel healthy siblings. Only a harness-level halt propagates, and the TaskGroup then cancelling everything is exactly right, because that is what Aborted means.
docs.title: Group Isolation Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: TestUtils is the single, fully-scoped utility surface passed to every lifecycle method. utils.exec never throws. It returns an ExecResult(stdout, stderr, exit_code, truncated, captured_bytes) — a non-zero exit code is data for the test method to judge, not an exception. Signal-killed, aborted, and closed-transport commands settle as exit_code=-1 . A ConnectionError from RemoteInterface.exec is absorbed here; the protocol stays loud, the author-facing surface stays total. CancelledError still propagates. Stdout and stderr together are bounded by one named output_budget (default 4 MiB), applied identically by the local executor and SshInterface . The budget is configured at the run seed ( TestComponent.run(output_budget=...) / TestUtils(output_budget=...) ) or at LocalExec / SshInterface construction — never as a process-global. Exceeding it terminates the command the same way abort does (SIGTERM the host process group; SIGTERM then close that SSH channel, session stays up) and settles with the bytes actually received, truncated=True , and captured_bytes equal to what was kept. Truncation is evidence, never an exception. The scoped log names it ( exec output truncated: captured N bytes (budget B) ). Streaming reads preserve interrupted output: decode happens only at settlement, with replacement for a cut in the middle of a UTF-8 sequence. Developer obligation: Use only utils.* inside lifecycle methods — never import framework internals directly into test logic.
docs.title: Utils Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: use_shell is the only writer of the node's exec router. get_shell may open extra endpoints and may read inherit to pick a tunnel; it never assigns the router or the propagate flag. Four use_shell shapes: connection ( host + username ), connection with explicit via , policy-only inherit=False (force local), and bare use_shell() (return the active handle). Explicit via always wins. inherit=False on a connection form skips the parent's hop. Declared in configure() , nowhere else. A declaring use_shell ( host , via , inherit=False , propagate=False ) is admitted only while this node's own configure() is running; from a test method, cleanup , a survey, an audit, or a helper they call, it raises ContractViolation before the router is touched. The exec routing: line is written when configure returns and the FT reads it as the truth for the node's whole run; a route moved later would make that line a lie for every command after the move. The bare use_shell() reads the active handle and may be called from any slot. A second declaration. configure() may declare more than once, since no command has yet run under the route being replaced: open a jump host, then route through it. The last declaration is the route; every shell opened on the way stays opened on this node and is not torn down early. Ownership. The node whose configure() opened a shell, through use_shell or get_shell , owns it. The framework closes it at that node's cleanup (after the post-cleanup survey, before the hop it tunnels through), never earlier and never from another node. Hooks and audits observe the route; they do not set it. They read utils.exec_route and exec through what configure() committed to. A survey runs at phases before configure() and after cleanup() , and an audit runs concurrently with the test method, so neither has a moment at which one route could be declared once. get_shell stays open to them: an auxiliary endpoint changes nothing the routing line states. propagate=False on use_shell stops this node's router from flowing to children; they start local. propagate on get_shell is a documented no-op. The parent owns the route. A route is owned by the node whose configure() declared it and is inherited by every node that node composes, down the tree, until a descendant declares inherit=False (or the owner declared propagate=False ). A device class never takes a routing argument: a gateway is a parent whose configure() opens the hop and whose build_suite() composes the devices behind it, and those devices are routed by being its children. The TestComponent constructor has no via= ; the only via is the tunnel argument to use_shell / get_shell , declared inside configure() by the node that owns the route (issue #137). Children inherit the route through run params ( RouterRunParams ), never through ctx. ctx is instance-local domain data, not infrastructure. Routed tunnels are borrowed; the router owns hop lifecycle. Every hop the router resolves — an explicit via= Shell or an inherited route — is already live, so the connector threads it through the transport's borrowed tunnel= channel, never the owned via= one. The opened interface must not disconnect, cancel, or collapse its hop. What a node opened is recorded on the node ( opened ), stays connected through the node's post-cleanup survey, and closes after that survey and before the hop it tunnels through — the parent's hop closes at the same point of the parent's own lifecycle, after every child is done with it (issue #115), so a survey that execs at post-cleanup reads the device, not a closed transport; a hard abort on the hop kills everything tunneled through it at the socket (In-Flight Termination Contract). A dead hop at open time is an error, not something the router silently brings up. Local exec and every SSH session this router opens share the run's output_budget (see the Utils Contract). A fat command is truncated and killed at the resource; it does not take the rest of the rack with it. A transport's address is fixed while it is live. connect(host, port) re-points an addressed transport only through a closed handle; asking a live one for a different address is refused, never silently replaced. After a flash or DHCP churn the flow is disconnect() , reacquire, connect(new_ip) . There is no self-healing: a socket the framework killed stays dead (In-Flight Termination Contract), and an unexpected drop reaches the author as a ConnectionError on the next exec , not as a quiet redial. utils.exec_route states where utils.exec lands at the moment it is read: local for the test host, otherwise the endpoint of the hop the route attaches to (the last name in the exec routing: chain). It is derived from the router, never stored, so it is right in a survey at every phase, including the pre-configure dispatch before use_shell has run and the pre-cleanup dispatch after a configure that failed before it. The router logs what it opens and where every node's exec lands (see the Evidence Contract). A transport that hides its hop hides the topology: endpoint , hop , and route_label on RemoteInterface are how a transport states its place in the chain, and provenance_lines (starting with connect_provenance ) are the lines the router records for it. Developer obligation: Declare in configure() , and only there, where this node's utils.exec lands when it should be somewhere other than the test host; a test method, survey, or audit that needs a different endpoint reads use_shell() or opens one with get_shell . Do not stuff SSH handles into ctx and expect routing to notice.
docs.title: Exec Routing Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: DeviceApiInterface is a contract, not an exec subclass ( HIL ruling 1 ). The guarantees live in the signed Device API design note ; this page does not restate them. DeviceRequest(..., json=value) is the JSON body convenience (issue #155): it serializes once to UTF-8 payload bytes and supplies Content-Type: application/json unless the request already declares a content type, matched case-insensitively. json=None sends JSON null; omitting json leaves the raw-payload API unchanged. Combining json with a non- None payload , even empty bytes, is a ValueError before any transfer. Non-serializable values and non-finite numbers are refused at construction. The request never mutates the caller's headers or retains its JSON object. DeviceResponse.json() decodes the returned bytes. parse(response_type="json") is the format-selecting form; response_type="yaml" uses yaml.safe_load from the optional hilt-core[yaml] extra. Unknown formats raise ValueError , a missing YAML dependency raises ImportError , and parser errors propagate without a fallback. Parsing is explicit, independent of response status and headers; it preserves body and status , makes no request, and supplies no verdict. A malformed body remains a completed transfer for the suite to judge. Body contents never enter attempt logs. A CoAP status is the dotted code ( "2.05" , a CoapCode constant). An HTTP status stays an integer (issue #156). Developer obligation: Implement DeviceApiInterface as that note specifies.
docs.title: Device API Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: Any TestComponent or subclass thereof can be composed indefinitely in any shape the SE deems appropriate. Developer obligation: Leaves must be self-contained — declare their own readiness preconditions in configure() , not in the parent sequence.
docs.title: Composability Contract

docs.text: Floor Technician guide — reading a result without reading source ¶ This is the station page. You opened a run because something stopped the line. You do not need the suite source, a Slack thread, or a software engineer to categorize what happened. You need result.json , the scoped log next to it, and the recovery protocol below. The Inspector TUI is not in this port yet. Until it is, you read the same two records the Inspector will: the structural tree in result.json , and the temporal log at each node's log_path . Every field below is the field in docs/inspector-json.md , explained from this side of the bench. Clock rule. A station whose system clock is not on NTP cannot produce trustworthy evidence. Do not execute tests on it. The log is used as chronology in customer disputes. Where to look ¶ A completed run always writes a timestamped directory under HILT_ARTIFACT_ROOT (or ./artifacts if that variable was not set). Inside that directory: You want File The verdict and the tree result.json at the run-directory root What happened, in order, for a node that node's timeline.jsonl (the Inspector record) and timeline.log (the same events as readable lines) A captured screenshot, dump, or similar the path in an artifact-pointer log line A CI-flavored projection of the same tree the JUnit XML the runner wrote with --junit , if anyone asked for one. It is not a second record. result.json is present for Pass, Fail, and Aborted. Absence of the file means the invocation never reached a run (usage error, exit 3) — there is no hardware story to read. The last entry in the root node's timeline points at result.json with artifact name result and type run-result . You do not have to guess the run directory name from the clock. Sixty-second recovery protocol ¶ Open result.json . Read state at the root, then failure . That pair is the category. Then follow the protocol. A human still makes the final call; the framework's job is to make the call obvious. Root state What failure looks like Category What you do Pass failure is null The claim held Ship. You are done. Fail name is TestFailure (or a suite-authored subclass), bug absent or false Hardware. The unit did not meet a check the suite named. Pull the unit. Follow the station protocol for that failure name. The fail_message is written in your language; expected / received are the comparison when there is one. Fail banner is CONTRACT VIOLATION , or bug is true Author. The suite broke its contract. This is not the unit. Do not scrap the unit on this evidence. Escalate to the suite author. The message names the node and the fix. Fail banner is FRAMEWORK CONTRACT VIOLATION Framework. Should be unreachable. Escalate to the framework maintainers with the full run directory. Not the unit, not the suite author. Aborted name is ExternalIntegrationFailure Integration / harness. The shop-floor DB, the coordinator, the hook around the suite. Fix the harness. Re-run. The unit was not judged. Aborted name is MissingVerdict , or bug is true with state Aborted Author. The test method returned nothing the framework will accept as a verdict. Escalate to the suite author. Do not treat this as a hardware Fail. Aborted name is OperatorInterrupt , operator is true Operator. Someone sent SIGINT or SIGTERM. The rack was stopped on purpose. Not a Fail, not a harness outage. Re-run when the line is ready. signal names which one. Aborted timeout.declared is abort_after Budget. The node's abort clock fired. The framework refused to forge a Fail. Read timeout.clock for which node declared the budget, then decide with the log whether the unit hung or the budget was tight. A TestFailure raised from configure() means the device did not reach a testable state . Hardware vs infrastructure is not knowable from the file . You decide that, using the message, the survey artifacts, and what you can see on the bench. Do not collapse Fail and Aborted. A Fail says check the hardware. An Aborted says no verdict was produced — check the harness, the author, or the operator, not the unit, unless you have other evidence. How to find the node that matters ¶ The root object is one node. The tree of everything that ran is summary_tree . Walk children in declaration order. Use ancestor_names as the node's identity. It is the root-to-this path as an array of names. Names may contain / , so the array is the durable form. Use bread_crumbs only to display that path. It is exactly ancestor_names joined with / . Do not parse it back into names. A node whose summary_tree state is null never ran (a sequence stopped before it). That is not a fourth terminal state. It has no log and no failure. The declared tree is still complete, so you can see what was skipped. Every field, from this side of the bench ¶ The root result ( result.json ) ¶ Field What you do with it format_version Read this first. Version 1 is this page. A number you do not know is not a result you can guess at — refuse it and get a decoder that names the versions it accepts. state The root verdict: Pass , Fail , or Aborted . This is the first word of the recovery protocol. failure Why this node is not Pass, or null . Shape below. timeout null unless a time budget determined or contributed to this state. Shape below. test_case Stable name of this node. The root's name is usually the suite class name. type The node's shape in the suite: suite , test , parallel , or sequence . A test is one claim. A sequence stops at the first failure. A parallel runs children together and keeps the worst state. ancestor_names Identity. Root-to-this, inclusive. bread_crumbs Display path only. summary_tree The whole declared tree, rooted here. This is the structural view. physical_location Station / slot name from PHYSICAL_LOCATION , or unknown if that variable was not in the run environment. env The run environment as the run declared it. Secrets in an unfiltered environment are in this object verbatim — that is an operator obligation, not a framework rewrite. With environment=DEBUG the allow/deny list is ignored and a warning is in the log. run_data Suite-authored evidence snapshot: what configure() provided, minus anything that is not JSON. Version 1 always has a measurements array: the numbers this node recorded with utils.measure , or empty. Other keys are the suite's. The readings a claim took, and the numbers it measured, are on that claim's node in summary_tree , not here. suite_target Which suite produced this run, as hilt run was told it: the file or module, :: , the class. This is what the Inspector's Re-Run tab executes when you press Enter on a node, so the check you run at the bench is the code that ran in production. null means the run was not started by hilt run ; open the Inspector with --suite if you need to re-run from it. A summary-tree node ¶ Field What you do with it name This node's name. Combine with parent names via ancestor_names on the matching RunResult when you have one; in the tree, the path is the walk from the root. type Same discriminator as the root: suite , test , parallel , sequence . state Terminal state, or null if this step did not run. failure Failure for this node, or null . A parent can be Fail because a child is; look at the child that actually failed. timeout Time-budget evidence for this node, or null . log_path POSIX path of this node's timeline.jsonl , relative to the run directory. null means the records rolled up into an ancestor, or the node never ran. Resolve it against the run directory you opened. The root always has one. children Ordered children. Groups keep declaration order after settlement. evidence The readings this claim handed back with its verdict, or null . Read it beside the failure: a Fail with evidence shows you what the unit measured. evidence_declared The readings this claim promised to take on a pass, or null . A name listed here that is missing from evidence is a reading that was not taken : the claim failed, aborted, or never ran before it got there. It is not a reading of zero. measurements The numbers this claim recorded, with their windows, or null if it never ran. An entry with in_limits: false is a reading outside its window. An entry with value: null is a reading the claim tried to take and the device did not give; it is not a reading of zero. Read state beside either: it is not a Fail unless state says Fail. The cases are in docs/measurements.md , "What the Floor Technician reads". The failure object ¶ Failures keep their framework name so you can tell the cases apart. Unknown fields are additive; read what you know. What you see Meaning name The failure class: TestFailure , a suite subclass ( DimmFailure , …), ContractViolation , FrameworkContractViolation , ExternalIntegrationFailure , MissingVerdict , OperatorInterrupt , ArpResolutionFailure . fail_message The sentence you read out loud. Hardware copy for a TestFailure ; a banner plus a fix for a contract break; "operator interrupted…" for a Ctrl-C. state Fail or Aborted , matching the taxonomy. expected / received Present only when the suite supplied a comparison. Omitted, not nulled, when the failure is self-evident. received is what the suite observed. banner CONTRACT VIOLATION (author) or FRAMEWORK CONTRACT VIOLATION (maintainers). bug true means broken software, not broken hardware. node Which node broke the contract. cause Nested failure or a {name, message} for a plain exception. Follow it; do not stop at the wrapper. hook before_each or after_each on an ExternalIntegrationFailure . That is the harness hook that threw. operator true on OperatorInterrupt . The operator stopped the rack. signal SIGINT , SIGTERM , or signal N . returned What a MissingVerdict node actually returned instead of PASS. key / owner On a context contract break: the ctx key that was never published, or that a claim tried to write after configure() , and which configure() owns it. key On an evidence contract break: the reading a PASS did not carry, could not be written as JSON, or that collided with a ctx key. The claim is broken software, not a bad unit. evidence On a TestFailure : the readings the claim took before it failed, when it handed them over. mac / host On ArpResolutionFailure : the MAC that was not in the table, and which host was asked. Live handles (an open SSH session, a dict with a weird key) degrade to a string rather than making the file unreadable. If received looks like <SshInterface host=dut-12> , that is the degraded form, not a missing value. The timeout object ¶ timeout is null when no deadline contributed. Otherwise: Field What you do with it reason Always timeout . This object exists because a clock fired. declared Which clock won: fail_after or abort_after . budget_seconds How long that clock was willing to wait. elapsed_seconds How long the node had actually been active when it fired. clock Root-to-declaring-node path of the winning clock. The budget may have been declared on a parent. fail_after also puts a hardware-facing TestFailure in failure . abort_after may leave failure null — the timeout record is the reason the node is Aborted. Do not report those two the same way. The timeline ( timeline.jsonl ) ¶ One complete JSON object per line. You may read it while a run is still live; keep every complete line after an interrupt. timeline.log is the same events as escaped human lines. Field What you do with it format_version Timeline schema version; currently 1 . Independent of the result's version. timestamp Timezone-aware UTC, ending in Z . This is the chronology. scope Root-to-emitting-node path. Same idea as ancestor_names . level Logging level ( info , warning , error , …). message The line. Newlines stay escaped inside the JSON. artifact_name Present only on pointer lines. The captured artifact's name, or result for the root result. artifact_path Absolute path of that file. Open it. artifact_type What kind of capture, or run-result for result.json . artifact_timestamp When that evidence was taken, UTC. Ordinary log lines omit the four artifact_* fields rather than setting them to null. A pointer line has all four. Pending nodes create no files. Leaves roll their records into the nearest ancestor that owns a log. If a node has a terminal state and log_path is null, read the nearest ancestor that has a log_path . Operator interrupt, in the file ¶ A Ctrl-C or a SIGTERM during a live run is not a Fail and not a harness outage. In result.json : root state is Aborted failure.name is OperatorInterrupt failure.operator is true failure.signal is SIGINT or SIGTERM failure.fail_message contains operator In the timeline: the same story in order, including any artifacts flushed before the signal. The run directory is still the record; result.json is still written. If operator is missing or false, it was not the operator. Do not guess. Two records, two version numbers ¶ result.json and timeline.jsonl each carry their own format_version . They move independently. The tree points at the log through log_path . Within version 1, new fields may appear. Ignore fields you do not know; do not fail the read. A changed meaning, a renamed field, or a moved file would bump the number. From 1.0.0 that bump is a contract change. Before 1.0.0 the record may still change in place under version 1. The published schemas live next to this guide: docs/schema/result-v1.schema.json docs/schema/timeline-v1.schema.json You do not have to validate against them on the station. They exist so a decoder can refuse a version it was not written for, loudly. What this page is not ¶ It is not the authoring guide ( docs/idioms.md , docs/contracts.md ). It is not the runner's exit-code table ( docs/hilt-run.md ) — though exit 0 / 1 / 2 match Pass/Fail/Aborted, and exit 3 means there is no result.json because no run happened. It is not the Inspector TUI; when that lands, it will consume exactly these files.

Shape below. test_case Stable name of this node. The root's name is usually the suite class name. type The node's shape in the suite: suite , test , parallel , or sequence . A test is one claim. A sequence stops at the first failure. A parallel runs children together and keeps the worst state. ancestor_names Identity. Root-to-this, inclusive. bread_crumbs Display path only. summary_tree The whole declared tree, rooted here. This is the structural view. physical_location Station / slot name from PHYSICAL_LOCATION , or unknown if that variable was not in the run environment. env The run environment as the run declared it. Secrets in an unfiltered environment are in this object verbatim — that is an operator obligation, not a framework rewrite. With environment=DEBUG the allow/deny list is ignored and a warning is in the log. run_data Suite-authored evidence snapshot: what configure() provided, minus anything that is not JSON. Version 1 always has a measurements array: the numbers this node recorded with utils.measure , or empty. Other keys are the suite's. The readings a claim took, and the numbers it measured, are on that claim's node in summary_tree , not here. suite_target Which suite produced this run, as hilt run was told it: the file or module, :: , the class. This is what the Inspector's Re-Run tab executes when you press Enter on a node, so the check you run at the bench is the code that ran in production. null means the run was not started by hilt run ; open the Inspector with --suite if you need to re-run from it.
docs.title: The root result (result.json)

docs.text: Field What you do with it name This node's name. Combine with parent names via ancestor_names on the matching RunResult when you have one; in the tree, the path is the walk from the root. type Same discriminator as the root: suite , test , parallel , sequence . state Terminal state, or null if this step did not run. failure Failure for this node, or null . A parent can be Fail because a child is; look at the child that actually failed. timeout Time-budget evidence for this node, or null . log_path POSIX path of this node's timeline.jsonl , relative to the run directory. null means the records rolled up into an ancestor, or the node never ran. Resolve it against the run directory you opened. The root always has one. children Ordered children. Groups keep declaration order after settlement. evidence The readings this claim handed back with its verdict, or null . Read it beside the failure: a Fail with evidence shows you what the unit measured. evidence_declared The readings this claim promised to take on a pass, or null . A name listed here that is missing from evidence is a reading that was not taken : the claim failed, aborted, or never ran before it got there. It is not a reading of zero. measurements The numbers this claim recorded, with their windows, or null if it never ran. An entry with in_limits: false is a reading outside its window. An entry with value: null is a reading the claim tried to take and the device did not give; it is not a reading of zero. Read state beside either: it is not a Fail unless state says Fail. The cases are in docs/measurements.md , "What the Floor Technician reads".
docs.title: A summary-tree node

docs.text: Failures keep their framework name so you can tell the cases apart. Unknown fields are additive; read what you know. What you see Meaning name The failure class: TestFailure , a suite subclass ( DimmFailure , …), ContractViolation , FrameworkContractViolation , ExternalIntegrationFailure , MissingVerdict , OperatorInterrupt , ArpResolutionFailure . fail_message The sentence you read out loud. Hardware copy for a TestFailure ; a banner plus a fix for a contract break; "operator interrupted…" for a Ctrl-C. state Fail or Aborted , matching the taxonomy. expected / received Present only when the suite supplied a comparison. Omitted, not nulled, when the failure is self-evident. received is what the suite observed. banner CONTRACT VIOLATION (author) or FRAMEWORK CONTRACT VIOLATION (maintainers). bug true means broken software, not broken hardware. node Which node broke the contract. cause Nested failure or a {name, message} for a plain exception. Follow it; do not stop at the wrapper. hook before_each or after_each on an ExternalIntegrationFailure . That is the harness hook that threw. operator true on OperatorInterrupt . The operator stopped the rack. signal SIGINT , SIGTERM , or signal N . returned What a MissingVerdict node actually returned instead of PASS. key / owner On a context contract break: the ctx key that was never published, or that a claim tried to write after configure() , and which configure() owns it. key On an evidence contract break: the reading a PASS did not carry, could not be written as JSON, or that collided with a ctx key. The claim is broken software, not a bad unit. evidence On a TestFailure : the readings the claim took before it failed, when it handed them over. mac / host On ArpResolutionFailure : the MAC that was not in the table, and which host was asked. Live handles (an open SSH session, a dict with a weird key) degrade to a string rather than making the file unreadable. If received looks like <SshInterface host=dut-12> , that is the degraded form, not a missing value.
docs.title: The failure object

docs.text: timeout is null when no deadline contributed. Otherwise: Field What you do with it reason Always timeout . This object exists because a clock fired. declared Which clock won: fail_after or abort_after . budget_seconds How long that clock was willing to wait. elapsed_seconds How long the node had actually been active when it fired. clock Root-to-declaring-node path of the winning clock. The budget may have been declared on a parent. fail_after also puts a hardware-facing TestFailure in failure . abort_after may leave failure null — the timeout record is the reason the node is Aborted. Do not report those two the same way.
docs.title: The timeout object

docs.text: One complete JSON object per line. You may read it while a run is still live; keep every complete line after an interrupt. timeline.log is the same events as escaped human lines. Field What you do with it format_version Timeline schema version; currently 1 . Independent of the result's version. timestamp Timezone-aware UTC, ending in Z . This is the chronology. scope Root-to-emitting-node path. Same idea as ancestor_names . level Logging level ( info , warning , error , …). message The line. Newlines stay escaped inside the JSON. artifact_name Present only on pointer lines. The captured artifact's name, or result for the root result. artifact_path Absolute path of that file. Open it. artifact_type What kind of capture, or run-result for result.json . artifact_timestamp When that evidence was taken, UTC. Ordinary log lines omit the four artifact_* fields rather than setting them to null. A pointer line has all four. Pending nodes create no files. Leaves roll their records into the nearest ancestor that owns a log. If a node has a terminal state and log_path is null, read the nearest ancestor that has a log_path .
docs.title: The timeline (timeline.jsonl)

docs.text: A Ctrl-C or a SIGTERM during a live run is not a Fail and not a harness outage. In result.json : root state is Aborted failure.name is OperatorInterrupt failure.operator is true failure.signal is SIGINT or SIGTERM failure.fail_message contains operator In the timeline: the same story in order, including any artifacts flushed before the signal. The run directory is still the record; result.json is still written. If operator is missing or false, it was not the operator. Do not guess.
docs.title: Operator interrupt, in the file

docs.text: result.json and timeline.jsonl each carry their own format_version . They move independently. The tree points at the log through log_path . Within version 1, new fields may appear. Ignore fields you do not know; do not fail the read. A changed meaning, a renamed field, or a moved file would bump the number. From 1.0.0 that bump is a contract change. Before 1.0.0 the record may still change in place under version 1. The published schemas live next to this guide: docs/schema/result-v1.schema.json docs/schema/timeline-v1.schema.json You do not have to validate against them on the station. They exist so a decoder can refuse a version it was not written for, loudly.
docs.title: Two records, two version numbers

docs.text: It is not the authoring guide ( docs/idioms.md , docs/contracts.md ). It is not the runner's exit-code table ( docs/hilt-run.md ) — though exit 0 / 1 / 2 match Pass/Fail/Aborted, and exit 3 means there is no result.json because no run happened. It is not the Inspector TUI; when that lands, it will consume exactly these files.
docs.title: What this page is not

docs.text: Getting started ¶ This page takes you from a fresh clone to a saved run open in the Inspector, then through the examples in the order they teach. For why HILT is shaped the way it is, read the overview ; for the rules your suite is held to, the contracts . Install ¶ HILT needs Python 3.14 and uv . make install # uv sync + git hooks Your first run ¶ uv run hilt run examples/hello_world.py uv run hilt inspect hilt run loads a suite file or module and runs the one TestComponent subclass it defines, or the one named after :: . Its exit status is the verdict: Exit Meaning 0 Pass 1 Fail 2 Aborted 3 The suite could not be run at all hilt inspect [PATH] opens a saved run in the Inspector , the Floor Technician's terminal surface. Without PATH it opens the latest run under artifacts/ . Three flags shape what a run leaves behind ( hilt run ): --artifact-root DIR puts the run's evidence somewhere specific. --json prints the format_version 1 result record to stdout ( Inspector JSON contract ). --junit PATH writes the JUnit XML projection beside it, for CI. Write your own suite ¶ uv run hilt new WidgetSuite hilt new writes a gated- PASS suite and a matching self-test, so a new suite starts in the right shape instead of as a copy of an example ( hilt new ). hilt-check is the optional tier-3 linter over authored suites ( hilt-check ); idioms collects the authoring patterns. Walk the examples ¶ The locally executable examples build from one explicit claim, through composition, to polling, lifecycle hooks, and the evidence surface: uv run hilt run examples/hello_world.py uv run hilt run examples/test_composition.py::SequencedDevice uv run hilt run examples/test_composition.py::ParallelDevice # exits 1 by design uv run hilt run examples/wait_for_patterns.py::ConfigureGatedDevice uv run hilt run examples/wait_for_patterns.py::MainAssertionDevice uv run hilt run examples/hardware_device_lifecycle.py uv run hilt run examples/run_data_evidence.py wait_for_patterns.py shows readiness polling in configure() and verdict polling in a test method. hardware_device_lifecycle.py registers survey and audit hooks around a rail that comes up, is watched, and is dropped in cleanup. run_data_evidence.py shows limits flowing in through ctx and readings travelling out with the verdict. Every example carries comments explaining the reasoning behind its pattern, not only what the code does. Read them as the authoring guide. Examples against real devices ¶ The SSH-backed examples take their target from utils.env in configure() . A missing variable Fails the suite (exit 1): the device did not reach a testable state, and the message names the variable to set. Optional password and port variables ( SSH_PASSWORD / SSH_PORT , JUMP_* / TARGET_* , GATEWAY_* ) default the port to 22 when unset. SSH_HOST=dut.lab SSH_USER=root uv run hilt run examples/remote_device_ssh.py JUMP_HOST=jump.lab JUMP_USER=ops TARGET_HOST=dut.lab TARGET_USER=root uv run hilt run examples/ssh_tunneling.py DUT_MAC=aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff uv run hilt run examples/networked_device.py::DutDevice TARGET_ADDRESS=pihole.lab TARGET_USER=root uv run hilt run examples/pi_hole_server.py networked_device.py defines Gateway and DutDevice ; pick the station suite with ::DutDevice . GATEWAY_HOST and GATEWAY_USER (both required together) resolve ARP through a hop instead of the test host's table. Deploying to a station ¶ Every test host must synchronize its system clock with NTP before HILT runs. The scoped log is the authoritative chronology for a run, including structured pointers to captured artifacts, and may be used to establish event order in customer disputes. A station with an unsynchronized clock cannot produce trustworthy evidence and must not execute tests. Set HILT_ARTIFACT_ROOT to the run-specific evidence directory. Point-in-time evidence is an immutable Artifact value with no public file-writing method; persist it only with await utils.capture_artifact(artifact) , which writes the file and then appends its pointer to the scoped log timeline. The Floor Technician guide is the station page: how to read a result without reading source. Its rendered page, https://gitlab.com/Tyler-Meador/HILT/-/blob/main/docs/floor-technician.md , is the URL that belongs on a station label. Contributing ¶ Read STANDARDS.md before committing. make fix # auto-format + auto-fix lint make check # the gate (there is no CI; the bench run is it): format check, lint, pyright strict, import cycles, pytest under the coverage floors, hilt-check, wheel smoke install, docs, pip-audit make docs # documentation site (strict: a broken cross-reference is red) make docs-release # the same build into docs/site/, committed on a release branch only API stability defines the public surface, semantic versioning from 1.0.0, and the deprecation procedure. CHANGELOG.md at the repository root records every change to that surface. For a release MR, select the Release template ( .gitlab/merge_request_templates/Release.md ): it records the candidate's checks, changelog cut, and the handoff to Zavala for review. Nothing hosts the docs site. The tree is the documentation: GitLab renders every page under https://gitlab.com/Tyler-Meador/HILT/-/tree/main/docs , and each release branch ( release/MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH ) also carries the built site under docs/site/ ( make docs-release ; open docs/site/index.html from a clone, no network needed). The port design lives in the workspace plan ( ../PLAN.md ); the TypeScript original is the ../hilt-test-legacy/ design reference, and its language server is ../hilt-language-server-legacy/ . Both are read-only — parity with them is explicitly not a goal. PLAN.md section 0 maps the workspace.

docs.text: hilt-check — Tier 3 Static Analysis ¶ hilt-check is the third tier of the enforcement stack described in overview.md . It reads authored suite files as Python ASTs and reports departures from the declarative idiom. Skippable by design ¶ Tier Mechanism Guarantees Skippable? 1 Runtime IoC wrapping Verdict contract, failure taxonomy, lifecycle order, immutable-self freeze Never 2 __init_subclass__ at import Structural contract: sealed internals, lifecycle signatures, hook shape Never 3 hilt-check Declarative syntax: pure build_suite , gated PASS , immutable-self idiom, constructor-only hooks, live composition names, ctx provenance, fulfilled evidence, routes declared in configure , measurements named once and recorded where a node runs, one source per configure() value Yes Nothing that protects hardware or verdict integrity lives only here. Every rule below either has a tier-1 or tier-2 counterpart that holds whether or not the linter ever runs, or guards a style alone and says so in its row. A suite that skips hilt-check loses early, readable feedback at edit time; it does not lose a guard. That is the whole reason this tier may be skipped and the other two may not. Usage ¶ uv run hilt-check suites/ # check a directory (recursive) uv run hilt-check suites/blade.py other/ # files and directories mix freely uv run hilt-check --list-rules # the rule catalogue uv run hilt-check --select hilt/gated-pass suites/ uv run hilt-check --ignore hilt/pure-build-suite suites/ uv run hilt-check --format json suites/ # machine-readable report python -m hilt_check suites/ # same command without the script Output is one line per finding, path:line:col: code message , followed by a count. Exit status — the CI contract ¶ Status Meaning 0 Every checked file is clean. 1 At least one rule violation. 2 A file could not be checked (missing path, unreadable, invalid Python), or the invocation was wrong (unknown rule code, no paths). A path that cannot be parsed is an error, never silence: a suite that did not parse was not checked. Unknown rule codes fail the same way so a typo in a CI job cannot quietly disable a rule. make check runs the tool over examples/ , which is the scaffolding suite authors copy from, so the examples always demonstrate the idiom. Rules ¶ Code Idiom Runtime counterpart (the guarantee) hilt/gated-pass Every return PASS sits inside an if branch or match arm; the pass predicate is visible where the PASS is. Tier 1: the child boundary accepts only the PASS identity and refuses to forge a verdict. hilt/pure-build-suite build_suite is one return of composition calls: no other statements, no conditionals, filtered comprehensions, lambdas, await , or walrus inside; an unfiltered comprehension enumerates leaves (one per core, rail, or channel) and is allowed. Tier 2: __init_subclass__ requires build_suite with the right shape; tier 1 refuses anything but a TestComponent from it. hilt/immutable-self self.<attr> is assigned or deleted only in __init__ ; runtime state returns from configure() into utils.ctx . Tier 1: the instance freezes after the most-derived __init__ ; assignment raises AttributeError . hilt/constructor-hooks use_survey and use_audit are called only in __init__ ; hooks are identity, not runtime state. Tier 1: both registrars raise ContractViolation on a frozen instance. hilt/unannotated-interface Functions and methods inside suite classes annotate every explicit parameter and return; methods passed to self.test declare -> Verdict . Tier 1 for the -> Verdict half: the child boundary accepts only the PASS identity and refuses to forge a verdict. The parameter half is authoring clarity only; an annotation guards nothing at runtime. hilt/raise-test-failure A test method raises TestFailure , not a plain ValueError / RuntimeError / Exception . Tier 1: the failure taxonomy classifies any non- TestFailure exception escaping a test method as a developer-bug Fail. hilt/method-reference self.test takes a method reference, not a lambda or nested def. Tier 2: method references passed to test are auto-bound; the wrapper is unnecessary. hilt/retired-names self.case and self.group are gone; compose with self.test , self.sequence , and self.parallel (issue #110). Tier 1: the attributes no longer exist, so build_suite raises AttributeError before any hardware is touched; the rule names the replacement instead. hilt/no-verdict-in-cleanup cleanup does not return PASS or raise TestFailure ; it restores hardware state. Tier 1: cleanup's return is discarded and its exceptions are swallowed. hilt/ctx-provenance Every utils.ctx["k"] read in a test method, hook, configure , or cleanup names a key that configure() returns (its dict literal or TypedDict ), and ctx is never written: no subscript assignment, update , setdefault , pop , or clear anywhere in the suite. A reading travels with the verdict, and .get() is how an optional key is read (issues #112, #118). Tier 1: a [] read of a key configure() did not provide, and any write after configure() returns, raise ContractViolation naming the test and the key; get and in never do. hilt/shell-in-configure utils.use_shell(...) or utils.use_serial(...) with arguments, the call that declares where this node's utils.exec lands, appears only in configure() ; the bare use_shell() / use_serial() read and get_shell / get_serial may appear anywhere (issue #76). Tier 1: a declaring call ( host , via , inherit=False , propagate=False ) from any slot but configure raises ContractViolation before the router is touched, so the exec routing: line written after configure is the route every command of the node ran under. hilt/evidence-fulfilled Every return PASS({...}) in a method decorated @evidence(...) carries every declared key, and such a method never returns bare PASS (issue #118). Tier 1: the child boundary holds every PASS to the declaration; a missing key is a ContractViolation naming the leaf and the key, a developer-bug Fail. hilt/evidence-shadows-ctx No key @evidence declares (a literal, or a same-module TypedDict field) is a key the class's configure() returns (its dict literal, dict(k=...) , a local literal it builds, its return TypedDict , or a same-module base's keys) or the framework-owned measurements slot. Ctx and evidence land on one record, so the reading cannot reuse the name of the limit or target it was judged against; the finding sits on the declaring literal, where the rename happens (bench finding F14, issue #161). A clash with a key only an enclosing suite's ctx provides is out of a single file's reach and left to tier 1. Tier 1: the child boundary refuses a payload key that is in the node's ctx or is measurements as a ContractViolation naming the leaf and the key; nothing is stripped silently. hilt/measurement-name-unique Two measure(...) calls, either spelling, with the same literal name inside one configure or test method; a measurement's series is keyed on its name, so the second call would overwrite or fork it (issue #132). Tier 1: the duplicate-name guard in TestUtils.measure and hilt.measure raises ContractViolation naming the node and the measurement. hilt/measurement-in-node A measure(...) call, either spelling, inside cleanup , a method registered with use_survey / use_audit , a before_each / after_each hook (by name, or passed under either keyword), or outside any function; a reading belongs to the node whose configure() or test method is running (issue #133). Tier 1: the outside-a-node guard raises ContractViolation naming the node and the measurement for hilt.measure with nothing bound and for either spelling from cleanup , a survey, an audit, a hook, or after the node settled. hilt/no-input-fallback Inside configure() , a value is identity from the constructor or discovered through utils , never one with the other as fallback: no self._ip or await utils.get_arp_resolver(...).resolve() , no conditional expression choosing between them, no local name bound from a self attribute by one assignment and from get_arp_resolver / use_shell / get_shell / use_serial / get_serial / get_http / get_coap by another. Identity fed into discovery and identity read from utils.env stay (issues #142, #144, #147). None, by design: a fallback is a style the ruling forbids, not a guard on hardware or a verdict. The runtime records which utility provided a value either way; the rule moves the ruling to the editor. hilt/env-via-utils Suite code reads the environment through utils.env ( utils.env["K"] , .get , .require ), never os.environ or os.getenv , under any import alias; utils.env is the run's recorded, injectable snapshot and os.environ is invisible to the evidence. None can exist: os.environ is the interpreter's. The rule is the only gate, so it stays narrow and names the replacement. hilt/logger-not-print Suite code logs through utils.logger , whose entries land in the run's timeline; a builtin print inside a TestComponent subclass reaches only the process's stdout, which the framework does not capture. None: the framework cannot intercept the builtin without changing what print means everywhere, so the rule is the gate. hilt/model-resolution-failure An awaited .resolve() / .reacquire(...) / .request(...) inside a suite class sits in a try with a handler that raises TestFailure ; ArpResolutionFailure and DeviceApiOperationFailure are not verdicts, and the suite models the miss instead of leaking it. In cleanup , which gives no verdict and must not throw, the handler instead raises nothing and logs the miss, the shape hilt/no-verdict-in-cleanup also accepts (issue #153). Tier 1: the failure taxonomy classifies the escaping exception as a ContractViolation Fail ("CONTRACT VIOLATION IN ..."), which is correct and unhelpful; the rule moves the fix to the editor and names the exception to catch. From cleanup the exception is logged and swallowed, and the rest of the teardown does not run. hilt/no-swallowed-cancel Inside an async method, a try whose body awaits is not guarded by a bare except , except BaseException , or except CancelledError that fails to re-raise with a bare raise ; contextlib.suppress never names either. asyncio.CancelledError is the abort signal, and a handler that swallows it mints a verdict after the harness gave up. Catch Exception for the failure you modeled. Tier 1: the cancellation discipline of issue #38 shields evidence collection and expects suite code to propagate; this rule is the editor-time half. Run hilt-check --list-rules for the catalogue shipped in the installed version. Each rule's module docstring under tools/hilt_check/rules/ states exactly what it flags, what it leaves alone, and why. Adding a rule ¶ The registry is extensible without touching the CLI: Add a module under tools/hilt_check/rules/ . Define a class deriving from hilt_check.Rule with a stable code ( hilt/<kebab-name> ), a one-line summary , and a check(module) method that yields Violation values via module.violation(node, code, message) . Land its tests in tests/ alongside the others, with a seeded fixture under tests/fixtures/hilt_check/ so the CLI is proven end to end. RuleRegistry.discover() imports every module in the package and instantiates every concrete Rule subclass it finds. SuiteModule carries the structural queries a rule needs — enclosing function, method, and class, the methods a class registers by reference ( use_survey , use_audit , test ), and a static answer to "is this class a TestComponent " — so a rule is only its own idiom. A rule's code is a contract with suite authors' --ignore flags; rename it only with a note in the changelog of the MR that does so. Editor — the pylsp adapter ¶ The same registry the CLI runs is a python-lsp-server plugin. Install the extra so the core package stays dependency-light: uv pip install 'hilt-core[pylsp]' # or, from a checkout: uv sync --extra pylsp python-lsp-server discovers the plugin via the pylsp entry point. docs.text: hilt-check is the third tier of the enforcement stack described in overview.md . It reads authored suite files as Python ASTs and reports departures from the declarative idiom.
docs.title: hilt-check — Tier 3 Static Analysis

docs.text: Tier Mechanism Guarantees Skippable? 1 Runtime IoC wrapping Verdict contract, failure taxonomy, lifecycle order, immutable-self freeze Never 2 __init_subclass__ at import Structural contract: sealed internals, lifecycle signatures, hook shape Never 3 hilt-check Declarative syntax: pure build_suite , gated PASS , immutable-self idiom, constructor-only hooks, live composition names, ctx provenance, fulfilled evidence, routes declared in configure , measurements named once and recorded where a node runs, one source per configure() value Yes Nothing that protects hardware or verdict integrity lives only here. Every rule below either has a tier-1 or tier-2 counterpart that holds whether or not the linter ever runs, or guards a style alone and says so in its row. A suite that skips hilt-check loses early, readable feedback at edit time; it does not lose a guard. That is the whole reason this tier may be skipped and the other two may not.

docs.text: uv run hilt-check suites/ # check a directory (recursive) uv run hilt-check suites/blade.py other/ # files and directories mix freely uv run hilt-check --list-rules # the rule catalogue uv run hilt-check --select hilt/gated-pass suites/ uv run hilt-check --ignore hilt/pure-build-suite suites/ uv run hilt-check --format json suites/ # machine-readable report python -m hilt_check suites/ # same command without the script Output is one line per finding, path:line:col: code message , followed by a count.
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: Status Meaning 0 Every checked file is clean. 1 At least one rule violation. 2 A file could not be checked (missing path, unreadable, invalid Python), or the invocation was wrong (unknown rule code, no paths). A path that cannot be parsed is an error, never silence: a suite that did not parse was not checked. Unknown rule codes fail the same way so a typo in a CI job cannot quietly disable a rule. make check runs the tool over examples/ , which is the scaffolding suite authors copy from, so the examples always demonstrate the idiom.

docs.text: Code Idiom Runtime counterpart (the guarantee) hilt/gated-pass Every return PASS sits inside an if branch or match arm; the pass predicate is visible where the PASS is. Tier 1: the child boundary accepts only the PASS identity and refuses to forge a verdict. hilt/pure-build-suite build_suite is one return of composition calls: no other statements, no conditionals, filtered comprehensions, lambdas, await , or walrus inside; an unfiltered comprehension enumerates leaves (one per core, rail, or channel) and is allowed. Tier 2: __init_subclass__ requires build_suite with the right shape; tier 1 refuses anything but a TestComponent from it. hilt/immutable-self self.<attr> is assigned or deleted only in __init__ ; runtime state returns from configure() into utils.ctx . Tier 1: the instance freezes after the most-derived __init__ ; assignment raises AttributeError . hilt/constructor-hooks use_survey and use_audit are called only in __init__ ; hooks are identity, not runtime state. Tier 1: both registrars raise ContractViolation on a frozen instance. hilt/unannotated-interface Functions and methods inside suite classes annotate every explicit parameter and return; methods passed to self.test declare -> Verdict . Tier 1 for the -> Verdict half: the child boundary accepts only the PASS identity and refuses to forge a verdict. The parameter half is authoring clarity only; an annotation guards nothing at runtime. hilt/raise-test-failure A test method raises TestFailure , not a plain ValueError / RuntimeError / Exception . Tier 1: the failure taxonomy classifies any non- TestFailure exception escaping a test method as a developer-bug Fail. hilt/method-reference self.test takes a method reference, not a lambda or nested def. Tier 2: method references passed to test are auto-bound; the wrapper is unnecessary. hilt/retired-names self.case and self.group are gone; compose with self.test , self.sequence , and self.parallel (issue #110). Tier 1: the attributes no longer exist, so build_suite raises AttributeError before any hardware is touched; the rule names the replacement instead. hilt/no-verdict-in-cleanup cleanup does not return PASS or raise TestFailure ; it restores hardware state. Tier 1: cleanup's return is discarded and its exceptions are swallowed. hilt/ctx-provenance Every utils.ctx["k"] read in a test method, hook, configure , or cleanup names a key that configure() returns (its dict literal or TypedDict ), and ctx is never written: no subscript assignment, update , setdefault , pop , or clear anywhere in the suite. A reading travels with the verdict, and .get() is how an optional key is read (issues #112, #118). Tier 1: a [] read of a key configure() did not provide, and any write after configure() returns, raise ContractViolation naming the test and the key; get and in never do. hilt/shell-in-configure utils.use_shell(...) or utils.use_serial(...) with arguments, the call that declares where this node's utils.exec lands, appears only in configure() ; the bare use_shell() / use_serial() read and get_shell / get_serial may appear anywhere (issue #76). Tier 1: a declaring call ( host , via , inherit=False , propagate=False ) from any slot but configure raises ContractViolation before the router is touched, so the exec routing: line written after configure is the route every command of the node ran under. hilt/evidence-fulfilled Every return PASS({...}) in a method decorated @evidence(...) carries every declared key, and such a method never returns bare PASS (issue #118). Tier 1: the child boundary holds every PASS to the declaration; a missing key is a ContractViolation naming the leaf and the key, a developer-bug Fail. hilt/evidence-shadows-ctx No key @evidence declares (a literal, or a same-module TypedDict field) is a key the class's configure() returns (its dict literal, dict(k=...) , a local literal it builds, its return TypedDict , or a same-module base's keys) or the framework-owned measurements slot. Ctx and evidence land on one record, so the reading cannot reuse the name of the limit or target it was judged against; the finding sits on the declaring literal, where the rename happens (bench finding F14, issue #161). A clash with a key only an enclosing suite's ctx provides is out of a single file's reach and left to tier 1. Tier 1: the child boundary refuses a payload key that is in the node's ctx or is measurements as a ContractViolation naming the leaf and the key; nothing is stripped silently. hilt/measurement-name-unique Two measure(...) calls, either spelling, with the same literal name inside one configure or test method; a measurement's series is keyed on its name, so the second call would overwrite or fork it (issue #132). Tier 1: the duplicate-name guard in TestUtils.measure and hilt.measure raises ContractViolation naming the node and the measurement. hilt/measurement-in-node A measure(...) call, either spelling, inside cleanup , a method registered with use_survey / use_audit , a before_each / after_each hook (by name, or passed under either keyword), or outside any function; a reading belongs to the node whose configure() or test method is running (issue #133). Tier 1: the outside-a-node guard raises ContractViolation naming the node and the measurement for hilt.measure with nothing bound and for either spelling from cleanup , a survey, an audit, a hook, or after the node settled. hilt/no-input-fallback Inside configure() , a value is identity from the constructor or discovered through utils , never one with the other as fallback: no self._ip or await utils.get_arp_resolver(...).resolve() , no conditional expression choosing between them, no local name bound from a self attribute by one assignment and from get_arp_resolver / use_shell / get_shell / use_serial / get_serial / get_http / get_coap by another. Identity fed into discovery and identity read from utils.env stay (issues #142, #144, #147). None, by design: a fallback is a style the ruling forbids, not a guard on hardware or a verdict. The runtime records which utility provided a value either way; the rule moves the ruling to the editor. hilt/env-via-utils Suite code reads the environment through utils.env ( utils.env["K"] , .get , .require ), never os.environ or os.getenv , under any import alias; utils.env is the run's recorded, injectable snapshot and os.environ is invisible to the evidence. None can exist: os.environ is the interpreter's. The rule is the only gate, so it stays narrow and names the replacement. hilt/logger-not-print Suite code logs through utils.logger , whose entries land in the run's timeline; a builtin print inside a TestComponent subclass reaches only the process's stdout, which the framework does not capture. None: the framework cannot intercept the builtin without changing what print means everywhere, so the rule is the gate. hilt/model-resolution-failure An awaited .resolve() / .reacquire(...) / .request(...) inside a suite class sits in a try with a handler that raises TestFailure ; ArpResolutionFailure and DeviceApiOperationFailure are not verdicts, and the suite models the miss instead of leaking it. In cleanup , which gives no verdict and must not throw, the handler instead raises nothing and logs the miss, the shape hilt/no-verdict-in-cleanup also accepts (issue #153). Tier 1: the failure taxonomy classifies the escaping exception as a ContractViolation Fail ("CONTRACT VIOLATION IN ..."), which is correct and unhelpful; the rule moves the fix to the editor and names the exception to catch. From cleanup the exception is logged and swallowed, and the rest of the teardown does not run. hilt/no-swallowed-cancel Inside an async method, a try whose body awaits is not guarded by a bare except , except BaseException , or except CancelledError that fails to re-raise with a bare raise ; contextlib.suppress never names either. asyncio.CancelledError is the abort signal, and a handler that swallows it mints a verdict after the harness gave up. Catch Exception for the failure you modeled. Tier 1: the cancellation discipline of issue #38 shields evidence collection and expects suite code to propagate; this rule is the editor-time half. Run hilt-check --list-rules for the catalogue shipped in the installed version. Each rule's module docstring under tools/hilt_check/rules/ states exactly what it flags, what it leaves alone, and why.

docs.text: The registry is extensible without touching the CLI: Add a module under tools/hilt_check/rules/ . Define a class deriving from hilt_check.Rule with a stable code ( hilt/<kebab-name> ), a one-line summary , and a check(module) method that yields Violation values via module.violation(node, code, message) . Land its tests in tests/ alongside the others, with a seeded fixture under tests/fixtures/hilt_check/ so the CLI is proven end to end. docs.text: hilt new — the suite generator ¶ hilt new writes a gated-PASS suite and a matching self-test so the author starts from a shape that is already correct, annotated, and gated. Examples stay the lessons; this is the scaffolding they used to be copied from. uv run hilt new WidgetSuite uv run hilt new PowerRail --directory suites/ uv run hilt new WidgetSuite --force The command writes two files next to each other: File What it is widget_suite.py One TestComponent subclass named WidgetSuite test_widget_suite.py A pytest stub that constructs it from its name and asserts Pass What is public ¶ The command line is public ( docs/api-stability.md ): the class name, the two files, --directory , --force , and the exit status ( 0 wrote the files, 3 usage error). The Python module behind it is not. The shape it writes ¶ The generated suite is the single source for this shape. Every file hilt new emits has: an annotated __init__ whose extra parameters carry defaults, so hilt run can construct the class from its name alone configure returning a narrowed TypedDict ctx a pure build_suite that returns self.test(...) one test method whose return PASS sits inside an explicit pass predicate cleanup A missing target after construction is TestFailure from configure() : "did not reach a testable state". That is the ruled meaning of a failure there ( docs/contracts.md ). The generated files pass hilt-check , ruff, and pyright strict unmodified on the day they are written. Teaching examples in examples/ are verified against the core of this shape (annotated __init__ , build_suite , gated return PASS ) rather than regenerated from it — they carry lessons the template does not. Exit status ¶ Status Meaning 0 Both files were written. 3 Usage error. The name is not a suite class name, the directory does not exist, or the files already exist and --force was not given. Nothing was overwritten. A name must be a Python identifier, not a keyword, and start with an uppercase letter ( WidgetSuite , not widget_suite and not class ). Existing files are refused unless --force is passed, so a second invocation cannot clobber a suite the author has started editing.

docs.text: hilt run — the runner ¶ hilt run is the one command the developer documents and the Floor Technician types. It loads a suite, runs it through the sealed lifecycle, and exits with a code the station script branches on without parsing output. uv run hilt run examples/hello_world.py uv run hilt run examples/test_composition.py::ParallelDevice uv run hilt run station.suites.psu --artifact-root /var/lib/hilt/psu-0042 uv run hilt run suite.py --json > result.json uv run hilt run suite.py --junit report.xml What is public ¶ Two things are promised ( docs/api-stability.md ): the exit status contract below, and the --json record , which is the same format_version 1 result the framework writes as result.json , governed by the policy in docs/inspector-json.md . The Python module behind the command is private. The record names the suite that produced it. hilt run resolves TARGET to an absolute file or module name and the class it selected, and writes that as suite_target , so hilt inspect can offer the same suite on its Re-Run tab without being told again ( docs/inspector.md ). Exit status ¶ Status Meaning 0 The root settled Pass . 1 The root settled Fail . 2 The root settled Aborted . 3 Usage error. The invocation was wrong, or the suite could not be loaded, selected, or constructed. No run took place, no evidence was written. There is no fourth terminal state and no fourth run-related code. A station script treats 0 as ship, 1 as reject, 2 as re-run after the operator looks, and 3 as a suite-authoring or configuration fault that never reached hardware. uv run hilt run suites/psu.py --artifact-root "$RUN_DIR" case $? in 0) echo ship ;; 1) echo reject ;; 2) echo "aborted; see $RUN_DIR" ;; *) echo "suite could not run" >&2 ;; esac Selecting the suite ¶ TARGET is <path-or-module>[::SuiteClass] . A source ending in .py , or naming an existing file, is loaded from disk , standalone. Anything else is imported by dotted name through the normal import path ( examples.hello_world , station.suites.psu ). With ::SuiteClass , the named attribute may be any TestComponent subclass bound in the module, imported or defined. A station module may therefore re-export the suite it runs. Without ::SuiteClass , a module-level __suite__ bound to a TestComponent subclass is the default: a file that holds a gateway and the device behind it ( examples/networked_device.py ) can say __suite__ = Gateway and be run by path alone. ::SuiteClass still overrides it. A __suite__ bound to anything else is a usage error naming what it found. Without either, the module must define exactly one TestComponent subclass. A module that defines none, or more than one, is a usage error whose message lists what it found. The run record always names the class ( <file>::SuiteClass ), whichever rule picked it, so hilt inspect --rerun selects the same suite after another is added beside it. The runner constructs the selected class as SuiteClass(name=SuiteClass.__name__) . Every other __init__ parameter must carry a default; a constructor that needs more is a usage error naming the parameter. A suite that reads its target from the environment does so in configure() through utils.env , where the value is published as evidence in the same motion ( docs/idioms.md , TestUtils Injection). Evidence ¶ --artifact-root DIR sets the evidence root for this run and overrides HILT_ARTIFACT_ROOT . Without it, the variable applies, then ./artifacts . The run directory, the per-node timelines, and result.json land beneath it as docs/inspector-json.md describes. --json prints the format_version 1 result record to stdout and nothing else goes there, so > result.json captures exactly the record. --junit PATH also writes the run as JUnit XML through hilt.junit.JunitXml ( docs/junit-xml.md ). The runner owns the reporter; a harness that imports the module directly does so off the promised surface. A PATH that cannot be written is an error line on stderr; the exit status stays the verdict's, because the run settled and result.json under the artifact root is the record. The verdict line and the run log go to stderr : hilt run: <node>: <state> with the failure class and message when there is one. The log is the scoped logger at INFO , the same lines the per-node timeline.log records, so the person at the station watches the run as it happens. Python warnings, including DeprecationWarning , are routed through the same log. Operator interrupt ¶ SIGINT or SIGTERM during a run is an operator run-abort ( docs/contracts.md , Operator Interrupt): transports close hard, every unsettled node records the operator's name, result.json is still written, and the exit status is 2 .

docs.text: Framework Idioms & Patterns ¶ The Golden Rule ¶ If implementing something feels awkward or "ugly", you are fighting the framework. Seek the idiomatic approach. Treat that friction as a design-review signal, not a style preference and not immediate evidence that the framework needs another feature. Ask: What established HILT idiom is this design fighting, and which problem-domain concept would let composition, lifecycle boundaries, or utils express the intent coherently? Resolve that question before expanding the public API. A new abstraction is warranted only when the existing idioms cannot express a real manufacturing-test concept without obscuring evidence, hardware ownership, or verdict integrity. Convenience alone is not sufficient. The most important application is the React boundary in the port plan's section 1. HILT borrows React's component model—composition, inversion of control, hooks, and local state—not its runtime model. Reconciliation, re-rendering, and reactivity are out of scope because a hardware test executes once and may produce irreversible physical side effects. If a proposal feels awkward because it tries to import that runtime model, the friction identifies a crossed boundary, not a missing HILT feature. Immutable-self Convention ¶ After __init__ runs, self is read-only. What the tests need flows through configure's return value into utils.ctx , and what they observed leaves with the verdict. This eliminates hidden state coupling and makes the data flow explicit. Rules: - __init__ sets read-only config (MAC, credentials, site, etc.) - configure() returns what the tests will read, as a plain dict — the framework merges it into utils.ctx and closes it - test methods, cleanup() , and all child test bodies read from utils.ctx , not from self ; every key they read with [] is one configure() returned, and a key it did not provide is read with .get() or not at all — a missing [] read is a ContractViolation , not a KeyError (issue #112) - cleanup() reads every key with .get() or in , never [] : it also runs when configure() raised before it returned, and then ctx holds nothing configure() would have provided. A [] read there logs a ContractViolation beside the real Fail (issue #152) - No self.field = value after construction, and no write to utils.ctx after configure() — a reading travels with the verdict, PASS({...}) , and a thing that changes mid-run (an address, a connection) is an object in ctx that manages itself (issue #118) Why: Mutable state, on self or in ctx, creates hidden coupling between lifecycle phases. When inputs flow through ctx and readings flow out with the verdict, the data path is explicit and traceable. The Floor Technician benefits because each leaf's record carries exactly what that leaf handed back, beside the limits it judged against. Enforcement: This is a tier-1 runtime guard, not merely a lint convention. TestComponent freezes only after the most-derived __init__ returns, so subclasses may finish declaring their identity after super().__init__() . Ordinary assignment and deletion then raise AttributeError . Framework-owned lifecycle and evidence transitions use object.__setattr__ directly; suite code receives no framework escape-hatch method. The static no-self-mutation rule remains defense in depth. Scope note: ctx is strictly instance-local. A parent's ctx never flows into composed children — composition is the only coupling mechanism, and ctx inheritance would smuggle hidden state across it. One leaf never reads another's reading either: what a sibling observed is on that sibling's record, not in ctx. Evidence Travels With the Verdict ¶ A test method is a function from utils.ctx to a verdict. Its readings leave with the verdict: PASS({...}) on the pass path, TestFailure(..., evidence={...}) on the fail path. @evidence is the method's return signature — it names the keys a pass must carry, beside the code that keeps the promise (issue #118). @evidence("output_voltage_v") async def _check_voltage(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: v = await self._read(utils, utils.ctx["ip"]) reading = {"output_voltage_v": v} if v <= utils.ctx["voltage_high_v"]: return PASS(reading) raise TestFailure(f"{v} V exceeds limit", evidence=reading) The declaration is fixed at class definition and never computed at run time. Pass criteria that vary by SKU or fixture are a leaf argument or a different leaf, decided before build_suite runs. A pass without its declared evidence is not a pass: the child boundary refuses it as a ContractViolation naming the leaf and the key. Extra keys are allowed; the declaration is a floor. A failure is not held to it, since a failure may fire before every reading was taken; it records what it is handed. The payload is validated entry by entry. A value that is not JSON, or a key that shadows a ctx entry or the framework-owned measurements slot, is a ContractViolation naming the key. Nothing is stripped silently. Ctx and evidence are one namespace, because they land on one record. A key configure() returns names the limit or the target ( kernel , domain , voltage_high_v ); a key @evidence declares names the reading judged against it ( kernel_running , queried , output_voltage_v ). The same word cannot do both, so pick the evidence name with the ctx key in view. hilt-check flags the clash on the declaring literal as hilt/evidence-shadows-ctx (bench finding F14, issue #161). A measurement is not evidence. utils.measure records a number beside the verdict (see Measurements below); it does not satisfy an @evidence declaration, so a claim that wants the reading in both records names it in both. An undecorated method may still return PASS(payload) ; the payload is recorded unchecked. Declare when you want to be held to it. The same decorator accepts a TypedDict . With -> Verdict[MyEvidence] on the method, pyright checks the PASS({...}) payload against the shape at write time; at run time the TypedDict 's required keys are the declaration. class VoltageEvidence(TypedDict): output_voltage_v: float @evidence(VoltageEvidence) async def _check_voltage(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict[VoltageEvidence]: ... hilt-check enforces the declaration statically as hilt/evidence-fulfilled , the one namespace as hilt/evidence-shadows-ctx , and the read-only context as part of hilt/ctx-provenance . The Parent Owns the Route ¶ The node that opens a hop owns it, and everything composed under it inherits it. A gateway is a parent node: its configure() calls utils.use_shell(host=..., ...) , and its build_suite() composes the devices behind the hop.
