The framework routes the gateway's own utils.exec through that hop and hands the route to every child, so a device's configure, surveys, tests, and audits all land on the far side without the device saying so. A device class never takes a routing argument; it is written once and reused on every bench. class Gateway(TestComponent): async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> dict[str, Any]: await utils.use_shell(host="10.0.0.1", username="ops") return {} def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return MyDevice(name="target", mac="aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff") MyDevice run on its own reads the test host; composed under Gateway it reads the gateway. Same bytes. A child that must run locally declares use_shell(inherit=False) in its own configure() ; a parent that must not hand its route down declares propagate=False . The hop stays up until the parent's own teardown, after every child has cleaned up — a child that fails or expires loses only the transports it opened itself, never its parent's hop. A gateway that cannot come up Fails in its own configure() , and the children it never composed stay pending: the bench was not ready, so the device was never asked. The only via in the framework is the tunnel argument to use_shell / get_shell (see SSH Tunnel below). That is the parent's tool for reaching through a jump host inside its own configure() ; it is never a child's burden. The Node Names What It Needs; the Framework Decides Where It Comes From ¶ Ruled on issue #142 (2026-09-12). A constructor argument is identity, fixed at composition time: a name, a MAC, the SKU-specific pass criteria. Runtime state comes from utils in configure() , as one call with no fallback: the IP, the shell, the tunnel, the resolver, the device API. When a parent and a child both could provide the same thing, that thing belongs in TestUtils , where the framework inherits it down the tree and records which way it went; it never travels through ctx or the constructor. A fallback in configure() is the smell that says a utility is missing. # Not allowed: two sources of truth for one ctx key, a branch the suite engineer # wrote, and a record that cannot say which path produced the value. ip = self._ip or await utils.get_arp_resolver(mac=self._mac).resolve() The framework already does this twice. The route flows down through use_shell and is inherited by every composed child; the ARP resolver is scoped to the node's current route and its cache is keyed by the routing label, so devices behind one gateway share ARP state without the suite engineer writing anything to arrange it. Identity reaches a root node through utils.env when no parent composed it: the DUT_MAC a bench-run device reads is the same MAC a rack parent passes to the constructor, and the run's environment is published on the record either way (see Environment Variables below). That is the run's declared input, not discovery, and it is what keeps the bench-run device and the composed one the same bytes. run_data — Automatic Structured Evidence ¶ The default run_data returns a detached snapshot of all serializable values from utils.ctx : the ctx view. JSON primitives (with finite numbers), plain dicts with string keys, and lists survive; class instances ( SshInterface , etc.), functions, live handles, non-finite floats, and cycles are stripped automatically. A leaf's RunResult.run_data is that view plus the evidence its verdict carried, flat, so the limit sits beside the reading; the leaf's summary_tree node carries the same evidence and its declaration. A non-leaf node's run_data is the ctx view alone. Stripping is deterministic and all-or-nothing at each top-level ctx entry. If a list or dict contains one invalid nested value, that complete entry is absent from run_data . HILT does not remove only the handle and leave a plausible-looking partial record. A value the claims need but the record must not carry, such as a session credential obtained in configure() , is named in redact_ctx on the suite class (issue #154). Each entry is a ctx key, exact or as a regular expression the key matches whole. The key appears in run_data as <REDACTED> , and the string under it is masked on every record surface, including a log line or a TestFailure the author hands it to. The record shows that the key was held; it never shows what. ctx itself is unchanged: the claims read the real value. class BlocklistRoundTrip(TestComponent): redact_ctx = ("sid", r"api_.*") async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> dict[str, Any]: sid = await self._login(utils) return {"sid": sid, "api_token": await self._token(utils, sid), "domain": "x.test"} # RunResult.run_data => { # "measurements": [], # "sid": "<REDACTED>", # "api_token": "<REDACTED>", # "domain": "x.test", # } # configure returns data — it appears in run_data automatically async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> dict[str, Any]: ip = await self._resolve() return {"ip": ip, "hostname": "switch-01"} # RunResult.run_data => { # "measurements": [], # "ip": "10.0.0.1", # "hostname": "switch-01", # } Override run_data only when you need computed or filtered output from the context. An override sees the ctx view, not the readings, which are merged when the leaf settles: from hilt import JsonObject @property def run_data(self) -> JsonObject: base = super().run_data return {**base, "within_spec": self._check_spec(base)} Note: non-JSON-safe objects ( datetime , sets, arbitrary classes) are stripped by default. Override run_data if you need custom serialization for these types, and return only JSON-safe data from the override. Every snapshot includes run_data["measurements"] , the list utils.measure fills. It is framework-owned: a ctx entry with that key does not populate or replace it, and it is written after any run_data override runs, so an override cannot drop it. Measurements: utils.measure ¶ A reading with a unit and a window that a process engineer will chart belongs in utils.measure , not only in the evidence payload. The call records and returns; the verdict stays whatever the gated PASS says, because a limit is evidence, never a verdict ( docs/measurements.md ): from hilt import PASS, TestComponent, TestFailure, TestUtils, Verdict, evidence class Rail(TestComponent): @evidence("output_voltage_v") async def _output_rail(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: volts = await self._read_rail(utils) rail = utils.measure("output_voltage_v", volts, unit="V", limits=(4.75, 5.25)) if rail.in_limits: return PASS({"output_voltage_v": volts}) raise TestFailure("rail outside window", "4.75-5.25 V", f"{volts} V") The gate reads in plain sight, so hilt/gated-pass sees the predicate and the next reader sees the criterion. Name the quantity once per node, in the unit it will always carry; the consumer keys its series on that name. Record for trend without a window by passing limits=None . Measure from configure() (a bring-up reading) or the test method only; cleanup , surveys, audits, and hooks are refused. from hilt import measure is the same call resolved to the running node when a helper does not have utils in hand. When the reading comes over a shell, parse it to float | None and hand measure the None instead of wrapping the parse in a try : a reading not taken is recorded as such, it is never inside its window, and the same gate fails the claim (issue #159). Keep NaN out of the call; that is a bug in the suite's arithmetic, not a blank from the device, and the framework refuses it. Composition Factories: self.test , self.sequence , self.parallel ¶ TestComponent exposes three instance factories for building the suite. The names are the vocabulary a suite reads aloud in: a leaf is a test , dependent children run in sequence , independent children run in parallel . There is exactly one spelling for each; case and group are retired (issue #110) and hilt/retired-names flags them. self.test(name, fn, *, fail_after=None, abort_after=None) — the leaf: one verdict method, named here at composition time. Defaults to discrete_log_file=False so entries roll up to the parent artifact. self.sequence(name, children, ...) — serial execution, bails on first failure, and owns a discrete timeline by default. self.parallel(name, children, ...) — concurrent execution via asyncio.TaskGroup , collects all failures, and owns a discrete timeline by default. The name says so: nobody misses that two children share a bus. Pass discrete_log_file=False to self.sequence() or self.parallel() when that composition is too small to merit a separate Inspector timeline. Its records then roll into the nearest owning ancestor, just as leaves do. Authored TestComponent subclasses also default to a discrete timeline and may opt into roll-up through super().__init__(..., discrete_log_file=False) . The root always owns a log so every run has an authoritative temporal backbone. Private methods pass as references directly — Python bound methods carry self for free. def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return self.sequence( self.name, [ self.test("check reachable", self._check_reachable), self.test("check firmware", self._check_firmware), ], ) async def _check_reachable(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: # `self` is preserved — bound at attribute access, no wrapping needed result = await utils.exec("true") if result.exit_code == 0: return PASS raise TestFailure("device unreachable", "exit 0", str(result.exit_code)) Every return PASS sits under the predicate that earns it; hilt-check (the hilt/gated-pass rule) flags a bare one, and the examples show the gated shape. Enumerate Leaves at Runtime ¶ A leaf's name is decided where the tree is composed, not where the method is defined. One method, many leaves: pass the value that varies straight to self.test() after the method, and name each leaf in a comprehension. The framework calls fn(utils, *args, **kwargs) ; utils is always first, and the developer's arguments follow. fail_after and abort_after are the leaf's budget, never the method's parameters. The arguments are checked against the method's signature when the tree is built, so a leaf that could never be called fails build_suite with a ContractViolation before any hardware is touched. class Compute(TestComponent): def __init__(self, *, name: str, cpu_count: int) -> None: super().__init__(name=name) self._cpu_count = cpu_count async def _cpu_stress(self, utils: TestUtils, *, cpu: int) -> Verdict: ... def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return self.parallel( "stress", [ self.test(f"cpu{i}_stress", self._cpu_stress, cpu=i, fail_after=120.0) for i in range(self._cpu_count) ], ) The comprehension maps a known population (every core, every rail, every channel) onto leaves; it does not choose among them. A comprehension with an if filter decides at build time which claims exist, and hilt/pure-build-suite flags it. The population is identity, like a hook: it comes in through __init__ , never out of configure() . self.test() or configure() ? ¶ A long operation such as a firmware flash or a provisioning step is a self.test(...) when the Floor Technician should see it in the report with its own verdict and its own budget. When it is preparation the report should not itemize, it belongs in configure() , where a TestFailure means "the device did not reach a testable state" (see overview.md) and the node reads Fail without a phantom leaf. Ask whether the Floor Technician acts differently when this step fails on its own line. If so, it is a leaf. Time Budgets: Name the Meaning of “Too Long” ¶ Declare a budget on the composition line that owns the work. Use fail_after when missing the time limit is a negative hardware verdict, and abort_after when the harness should stop waiting without claiming the hardware failed. def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return self.parallel( "rack claims", [ self.test("BMC ready", self._bmc_ready, fail_after=45.0), self.test("optional telemetry", self._telemetry, abort_after=10.0), ], fail_after=120.0, ) result = await rack.run(abort_after=300.0) The run budget bounds the whole rack. The parallel node and its leaves may tighten that bound; they cannot lengthen it. If the 45-second leaf is reached with only 8 seconds left on the run clock, the run clock fires after those 8 seconds and its abort_after state applies. The resulting timeout evidence names reason="timeout" , the declared budget, active elapsed time, and the root-to-node path of the winning clock. The timed window is configure through the test method or last child. Cleanup retains its separate finalization allowance. Root-owned before_each / after_each hooks are excluded from every time-budget clock, so a slow shop-floor database cannot manufacture a hardware Fail. In a parallel node, however, a sibling still inside its timed window keeps the shared ancestor clock moving; another sibling's hook or cleanup cannot lend it extra time. Do not catch or suppress asyncio.CancelledError around awaited work. A deadline closes only transports opened by the cut node. An inherited route remains the parent's resource; this is what keeps a timed-out DUT from taking down a healthy sibling behind the same gateway. A gateway parent may declare the same budget pair. Its clock begins when it enters configure ; if the hop is not open by then, the Fail or Aborted state and its timeout evidence are the gateway's own, and the devices behind it are never asked. Pass/Fail/Aborted Contract ¶ A test method returning PASS , or PASS(evidence) with its readings → test passes (state Pass ). The check is isinstance(result, Verdict) , and only PASS mints one. The string "PASS" does not pass, and a PASS missing a key its @evidence declared is a contract violation, not a pass. A test method raising TestFailure (or subclass) → test fails with structured data (state Fail ) A test method raising any other exception → ContractViolation Fail (banner CONTRACT VIOLATION , bug: true ): the developer didn't model this failure mode A test method returning anything other than the PASS sentinel (including falling through with None ) → node-local Aborted . No verdict was produced, so the framework refuses to forge one. Siblings are unaffected. An integration hook ( before_each / after_each ) throwing anywhere in the tree → state Aborted on the enclosing node AND every ancestor Aborted is a peer state to Pass and Fail , not a flavor of failure. It signals that no verdict was produced — either the harness around the test broke, or the test method finished without rendering one. The Floor Technician's recovery protocol is "check the integration layer / the test method," not "check the hardware." Constructor-Only Hooks: use_survey and use_audit ¶ Survey and audit hooks are registered in __init__ , not in configure() . They are stackable — multiple calls register multiple independent hooks, each firing on its own schedule. class ComputeBlade(TestComponent): def __init__(self, params: TestParams) -> None: super().__init__(params) # Passive snapshot at every lifecycle phase boundary self.use_survey(self._dmesg_snapshot) # Active monitoring that can fail the test self.use_audit(interval=5.0, fn=self._check_thermals) Why constructor-registration, not configure-registration? Survey and audit are part of the test's identity — stable across runs, visible on the class — not runtime-configured state. Registering them in the constructor makes them discoverable and keeps configure() focused on runtime wiring. Survey errors are swallowed (never affect the verdict). Audit errors are real failures — a throwing audit cancels in-flight test methods immediately and fails the test. Scheduling a survey. A survey fires at all six Phase boundaries unless the constructor says otherwise. A survey that reads the device through utils.exec has no device to read at pre-configure , before use_shell has run; its dispatch there execs on the test host and records the developer's machine as device evidence. Say which boundaries the survey observes, and guard the route: from hilt import TestComponent, Phase, TestUtils class PiHole(TestComponent): def __init__(self, *, name: str) -> None: super().__init__(name=name) self.use_survey( self._ftl_tail, phases=[phase for phase in Phase if phase >= Phase.POST_CONFIGURE], ) async def _ftl_tail(self, utils: TestUtils) -> object: if utils.exec_route == "local": return None # no device on the other end of exec at this boundary return (await utils.exec("tail -n 50 /var/log/pihole/FTL.log")).stdout Both halves are needed. The phase list is the schedule; the route check is the guard. Order is not reach: when configure fails before use_shell returns, the engine skips post-configure , pre-test , and post-test and still fires pre-cleanup and post-cleanup , and at those two utils.exec is on the test host. utils.exec_route answers "local" there and the hop's endpoint ( "10.10.10.10" ) once the route is up, so a survey that compares against it never tails the wrong machine. An empty phases= is a ValueError at registration, not a survey that silently never fires. Survey artifacts are named for the lifecycle dispatch point and hook index. Audit artifacts use the same survey artifact type and add the audit hook and dispatch indexes to the name. Every non- None return is captured, including empty containers. Python cannot distinguish an explicit or delegated None return from fall-through at runtime, so None writes only an informational log entry. A hook that needs to preserve a deliberate null observation calls await utils.capture_artifact(Artifact(..., data=None)) directly. Once a hook produces an observation, framework shutdown waits for its artifact publication within the bounded evidence budget, even under repeated cancellation. Audit intervals must be positive and finite, and the framework stops every audit loop as soon as the authored suite settles. See examples/hardware_device_lifecycle.py for survey and audit around a device with real state transitions — rail up in configure , thermal audit during the claim, rail down in cleanup . Integration Hooks: before_each / after_each on the Run Params ¶ For composing HILT into a larger harness (shop-floor DB, lab coordinator, audit pipeline), pass before_each and after_each to the root run() call: await root.run( before_each=lambda ctx: shopfloor_db.record_started( fn=ctx.bread_crumbs, station=ctx.env.get("STATION_ID"), at=datetime.now(UTC), ), after_each=lambda ctx: shopfloor_db.record_finished( fn=ctx.bread_crumbs, state=ctx.result.state, failure=ctx.result.failure.fail_message if ctx.result.failure else None, at=datetime.now(UTC), ), ) Register once at the root — the framework fires them around every executed test in the tree. The hook context is deliberately narrow (node name, ancestor_names , bread_crumbs , logger , env ) — NOT exec or get_shell . Integration hooks are for external coordination, not for exercising the hardware. Pair invariant: after_each fires even when before_each threw. Register them as a pair or pass allow_unpaired_hooks=True to opt out of the warning. The exception-path behavior is: throw from either hook → run halts → every enclosing node transitions to Aborted → every in-flight SSH session and subprocess is killed immediately. A 30-minute firmware flash mid-abort must NOT continue to mutate the hardware. Configure-Returns-Context Pattern ¶ configure() returns a plain dict; the framework merges it into utils.ctx for test methods, survey hooks, cleanup() , and all descendant leaves, then closes it. No instance fields are needed for configure-phase data. The return value is the contract with the test methods: it names every key they read with [] , and it is all they will ever find there. Seed no placeholders — a reading belongs on the verdict, not in ctx — and nothing writes ctx after configure returns. hilt-check enforces both statically as hilt/ctx-provenance ; at run time a [] read of a missing key, or any later write, is a ContractViolation naming the test and the key, while .get() and in read an optional key (issues #112, #118). The framework annotation is Mapping[str, Any] ; a plain dict[str, Any] return is the default and satisfies it. When a suite benefits from precise key types, define a local TypedDict and use it as the covariant return annotation — pyright strict accepts the override because a TypedDict is a Mapping , which dict[str, Any] as the base annotation would not allow. This is static information only: a TypedDict is still an ordinary mutable dict at runtime, and the framework copies it into utils.ctx . A context dataclass is deliberately out of contract because it would fight dict merge semantics and require special handling in the default run_data path. class DeviceContext(TypedDict): ssh: RemoteInterface token: str async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> DeviceContext: ... Carrying the same type into the test methods ¶ A TypedDict return tells the reader the shape, but utils.ctx still hands the test methods a Mapping[str, Any] , so a misspelled key survives pyright and reaches the floor as a ContextInsufficient contract violation — a Fail under the bug banner, where the author meant to take a reading (issue #112). Naming the type once on the class closes that gap: declare class MySuite(TestComponent[MyCtx]) and annotate the lifecycle methods utils: TestUtils[MyCtx] , and utils.ctx["volts"] is a float to the editor while utils.ctx["volt"] is a type error before it is ever run (issue #75). class PowerCtx(TypedDict): rail: str volts: float class PowerSuite(TestComponent[PowerCtx]): async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils[PowerCtx]) -> PowerCtx: return {"rail": "3v3", "volts": 3.3} def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return self.test("rail", self._rail_is_up) async def _rail_is_up(self, utils: TestUtils[PowerCtx]) -> Verdict: if utils.ctx["volts"] > 3.0: # a float here, not Any return PASS raise TestFailure("rail low", "> 3.0V", f"{utils.ctx['volts']}V") This is sugar, and it is opt-in in both directions. Writing TestComponent and TestUtils bare means what it always did — the parameter defaults to Mapping[str, Any] — so no existing suite has to change, and a suite that adopts the parameter is making a claim to its own reader, not to the framework. Nothing about the run moves: the context object is the framework's RunContext , a dict[str, Any] it owns; a key configure() never provided is still a runtime ContractViolation rather than a static one; and run_data still strips class instances, functions, and live handles value by value. Composition stays unparameterized on purpose. self.test() , self.sequence() , and self.parallel() speak of TestComponent nodes of any context shape, because a rack composes suites that do not share one context — pinning them to a single CtxT would make the parameter contagious rather than opt-in. class MyDevice(TestComponent): # configure ALWAYS returns the context your test provides to its # lifecycle methods and children. This tells future devs exactly what # context your test requires and what it supplies — important, for # example, for ssh chaining, which requires an "ssh" entry in ctx. async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> dict[str, Any]: # utils.env.require raises TestFailure when the variable is unset or # blank: a verdict from configure — the test lands in Fail without the # suite ever running. The verdict means "did not reach a testable # state"; whether the cause is config/infra or DUT is the human's call # from logs and survey artifacts. Model as many failure modes as # possible so they surface as verdicts rather than bugs. utils.env.port # does the same for a port, defaulting to 22 and rejecting a typo. # utils.env.int and utils.env.float do it for a number: unset uses the # default when one was given, and a bad value Fails naming the variable # and the value. username = utils.env.require("TARGET_USER") password = utils.env.require("TARGET_PASSWORD") address = utils.env.require("TARGET_ADDRESS") shell = await utils.use_shell(host=address, username=username, password=password) # use_shell wires utils.exec to route through SSH automatically return {"ssh": shell.ssh, "token": await self._authenticate()} # pass or fail, cleanup is GUARANTEED to run at the end of the lifecycle. # Use it to close any opened connections, put the device into a neutral state, etc. # It runs after a configure Fail too, so read ctx with .get(): "token" may never # have been returned. async def cleanup(self, utils: TestUtils) -> None: pass # ssh auto-disconnected by framework, after the post-cleanup survey def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return self.sequence( self.name, [ self.test("survey", self._capture_survey), self.test("reachable", self._check_reachable), ], ) async def _check_reachable(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: # utils.exec already routed through ssh result = await utils.exec("true") if result.exit_code == 0: return PASS raise TestFailure("device unreachable", "exit 0", str(result.exit_code)) Composability ¶ A device-level test can be dropped into a rack-level test without modification. "Push state up" to higher-level components; trust the framework lifecycle. Environment Variables ¶ Always use utils.env inside test code. Never os.environ directly. The env snapshot is stored in every RunResult for post-run auditing — filtered by the run's env_allow or env_deny list when one was declared, verbatim otherwise (see docs/inspector-json.md ). text , require , and port read a string, a required string, and a TCP port. int and float read a number the same way: a bad value Fails the run naming the variable and the value, and a missing one uses the default when the call passed one. TestUtils Injection ¶ Call await root.run() to execute a suite. The framework constructs TestUtils ; suite authors import it for lifecycle annotations, not as plumbing they must assemble. Every node receives a distinct TestUtils object with a logger scoped to that node's full root-to-leaf path. Leaves, sequences, and parallel nodes built by one authored instance share that instance's utils.ctx dict, while a composed TestComponent subclass starts with a fresh context. The environment snapshot is immutable and shared across the run; the halt signal is read-only from suite code. Logging ¶ utils.logger is scoped per node — never print() , so evidence is captured in artifacts Artifacts captured automatically discrete_log_file=False rolls log entries into the parent logger. discrete_log_file=True (the default on class-based tests) gives the node its own log file. Inline self.test() bodies default to False . Every full run creates a timestamped directory under the configured artifact root. A logging owner streams both timeline.log for humans and versioned timeline.jsonl for the Inspector, flushing both on every entry. Treat TestComponent.log_path as the authoritative path; directory names are not an API. While a durable timeline is attached, utils.logger.isEnabledFor(...) is true at every level so developer-side guards cannot suppress the authoritative chronology. Process logging handlers still apply their own level policy. Point-in-Time Artifacts ¶ Construct an immutable Artifact and pass it to utils.capture_artifact() . The method persists the JSON artifact under HILT_ARTIFACT_ROOT , then emits a structured pointer through the same scoped logger that records the surrounding test events. Artifact deliberately has no write() or write_file() method: a file without its pointer would be absent from the authoritative chronology. from hilt import Artifact snapshot = Artifact( name="pre-flash", type="hardware-survey", data={"firmware": "2.4.1", "healthy": True}, ) artifact_path = await utils.capture_artifact(snapshot) Artifact names and types accept letters, numbers, dashes, and underscores. Payloads must be JSON serializable. Capture is async, never overwrites an existing artifact, and returns the absolute path recorded in the pointer entry. RunResult Navigation — ancestor_names and bread_crumbs ¶ Every RunResult carries the node's position in the tree: ancestor_names: list[str] — canonical form, root-to-this inclusive. Use for programmatic aggregation (DB keys, leaf identity). bread_crumbs: str — "/".join(ancestor_names) precomputed. Use for display, log lines, error messages. summary_tree: SummaryTreeNode — snapshot of this node's subtree at completion. Enables downstream integrators to reconstruct the full Inspector tree from the root's RunResult alone. The versioned payload and recursive node fields are defined in inspector-json.md . A full run() also persists the root payload automatically as result.json in that run's artifact directory. Authored suites should consume the returned RunResult when they need the live value; they never write the canonical Inspector file themselves. Fractal Design: HILT exposes a single class ¶ Need Use Physical hardware component TestComponent Networked device (MAC-based) TestComponent + utils.get_arp_resolver() in configure Device reached over SSH, connection shared across tests TestComponent with configure returning {"ssh": ...} Device behind a jump host or OOB gateway The gateway is a TestComponent whose configure() opens the hop and whose build_suite() composes the device Standalone test procedure TestComponent The Python examples/ tree is the authoring reference. A broken example means the API changed and the docs need updating. self.sequence() vs self.parallel() ¶ self.sequence() — serial, stops on the first failure. Use when later tests depend on earlier ones. The Floor Technician sees exactly where the chain broke and nothing beyond it. self.parallel() — concurrent via asyncio.TaskGroup , collects all failures. Use when tests are fully independent. The Floor Technician sees everything broken at once. One child's Fail never cancels its siblings — Fail is returned, not raised, at the child boundary; only a harness-level abort cancels the parallel node, and then cancelling everything is exactly what Aborted means. Independent claims can still share one resource. A single DeviceApi handle opened in configure() and read from ctx by every leaf serialises their requests: the leaves run concurrently, their requests go out one at a time in call order, and a latency measured around request includes the wait for siblings. That is correct when the claim is about the bytes; when the claim is about the DUT's own latency, give each leaf its own handle. The same holds for a routed console. use_serial(device=...) in configure() binds utils.exec for the node and its descendants to one SerialInterface , and parallel leaves under it take turns on it in call order ( docs/hil/serial.md , Serial Turn Contract). A console costs more to share than a handle does: the leaves share one shell's state, so a cd or an exported variable in one leaf is visible to the next. Claims that need isolation want one console each, via get_serial(device=...) . ArpResolver — MAC to IP ¶ ArpResolver is a composable utility for resolving a device's IP from its MAC. Create one via utils.get_arp_resolver() in configure() , call resolve() , and return both the resolved data and the resolver into ctx. Test methods read the IP and the resolver from utils.ctx . Call arp.ping(utils) for reachability. Call arp.reacquire(utils) after anything that may change the IP (reboot, firmware flash, DHCP churn): it returns the new address and the resolver remembers it, so a later ping dials the address it last resolved while ctx stays as configure() left it. Carry the new address as evidence on the verdict if the Floor Technician should see it. ArpResolutionFailure is not a TestFailure . Catch it in configure and re-raise as TestFailure so a missing ARP entry is a verdict. Uncaught, it is a developer bug — the suite did not model the failure mode. # In configure(): arp = utils.get_arp_resolver(mac=self._mac) try: resolved = await arp.resolve() except ArpResolutionFailure as error: raise TestFailure( f"{error.mac} did not appear on the network", error.mac, error.host, ) from error return {**resolved, "arp": arp} # In build_suite(): self.test("reachability", self._reachability) See examples/networked_device.py . ArpResolver Behind a Gateway ¶ When the test host cannot reach the target network directly, the SE code is identical to the local case. Compose the device under a gateway parent whose configure() opened the hop, and the framework routes the lookup — the SE never touches SSH. # DutDevice.configure() — no SSH awareness, identical to local ArpResolver usage: arp = utils.get_arp_resolver(mac=self._mac) resolved = await arp.resolve() return {**resolved, "arp": arp} # Gateway.build_suite() — the parent names what sits behind its hop: return self.sequence(self.name, [self.test("gateway-up", self._gateway_up), DutDevice(name="dut")]) See examples/networked_device.py . hilt run ...::DutDevice reads the test host's ARP table; hilt run ...::Gateway runs the same DUT class through the hop. SSH Device — Class-Owned Connection ¶ Extend TestComponent when one SSH connection must be shared across all of the device's leaves. Open in configure() via utils.use_shell() and let the framework route utils.exec through it automatically. Returning {"ssh": ...} from configure() also makes the device eligible as a via target. Pass it as via in TestParams — the framework manages the lifecycle and scopes utils.exec automatically. use_shell vs get_shell : use_shell answers "where does utils.exec go" — it rebinds the routing for this test and its descendants. get_shell hands you an additional interface without touching the routing. A console by device path is the same idiom: await utils.use_serial(device="/dev/ttyUSB0") in configure() declares it as the node's exec route and get_serial opens one as an auxiliary endpoint; both hand back a Shell , the framework closes the port after the post-cleanup survey and from the abort sweep, and no transport is imported or carried in ctx. Behind a hop, pass an SSH Shell as via or let the console inherit the parent's use_shell route. The policy-only shapes ( inherit=False , propagate=False ) stay with use_shell . See examples/remote_device_ssh.py . The pi-hole dogfood suite ( examples/pi_hole_server.py ) is the same class-owned hop plus phase-boundary surveys that tail service logs for the Floor Technician. SSH Tunneling ¶ Pass the Shell an earlier utils.get_shell() returned as the via argument to the next utils.get_shell() to tunnel the new connection through it. Both interfaces are framework-managed — no cleanup() override is needed. jump = await utils.get_shell(host=jump_host, username=jump_user) target = await utils.get_shell(host=target_host, username=target_user, via=jump) See examples/ssh_tunneling.py . Device API — CoAP/HTTP ¶ A device API is not exec with a URL. Open a session from configure() with utils.get_http or utils.get_coap , then request a typed DeviceRequest . The response's status is data — HTTP 4xx/5xx is not an exception, and neither is a CoAP 4.xx. On HTTP, status is the integer. On CoAP it is the dotted code ( CoapCode.CONTENT is "2.05" ), which is what the record stores when the claim puts response.status on the verdict. Catch DeviceApiOperationFailure when the transfer itself did not complete (timeout, refused connection) and model it as a TestFailure . Retries default to zero. Each declared attempt is logged. POST refuses retry unless retry_non_idempotent=True . Attempt logs keep header names and withhold every value unless the author lists that name in evidence_headers . Abort closes the session; it does not invent a shutdown PUT. One handle carries one request at a time. Leaves under a parallel that share the handle configure() opened queue on it in call order — nothing collides and nothing is refused — so a round trip timed in the leaf includes the queue. A request still waiting when the handle is cancelled or closed is never sent; it fails with DeviceApiOperationFailure , the same class as any other transfer that did not complete. Measure the DUT alone with one handle per leaf. api = await utils.get_http(base_url="https://dut.local") response = await api.request(DeviceRequest(method="GET", path="/whoami")) if response.status != 200: raise TestFailure("whoami rejected", 200, response.status) return PASS({"status": response.status}) The backends stay off the public surface, the way SshInterface does. For a JSON body, declare json= instead of encoding bytes and setting a header by hand. Read it back with .json() , or select the parser with .parse(response_type="json") / .parse(response_type="yaml") (YAML needs hilt-core[yaml] ). Both leave the original bytes and status available. Parser errors propagate, so model a malformed response as TestFailure when it is a DUT failure mode. Neither the transfer nor the parser chooses a verdict. response = await api.request(DeviceRequest(method="PUT", path="/settings", json={"enabled": True})) if response.status == 200 and response.json().get("enabled") is True: return PASS({"enabled": True}) raise TestFailure("device did not enable", "enabled", response.status) wait_for Patterns ¶ Where wait_for() is called determines what the timeout means , not what gets raised — both raise TestFailure : In configure() — timeout becomes a TestFailure that halts the lifecycle. The test lands in Fail; the suite never runs. The verdict means "the device did not reach a testable state." Whether the cause is hardware or infrastructure is not knowable from code — the human triager makes that call from logs and survey artifacts. In a test method — timeout becomes a TestFailure that is the verdict itself. The device was reachable but failed to reach the expected state. looking_for is required and must be plain language — it becomes the Floor Technician's primary diagnostic string when a wait times out. The call returns the predicate's truthy value ( True stays True ); a claim that needs what was observed returns it from the predicate instead of closing over a list. The runnable examples/wait_for_patterns.py ports both placements from the legacy example. It also shows how polling observations flow through scoped logs, phase-boundary surveys, point-in-time artifacts, run_data , and the root summary_tree without adding another evidence API.
docs.title: Idioms

docs.text: If implementing something feels awkward or "ugly", you are fighting the framework. Seek the idiomatic approach. Treat that friction as a design-review signal, not a style preference and not immediate evidence that the framework needs another feature. Ask: What established HILT idiom is this design fighting, and which problem-domain concept would let composition, lifecycle boundaries, or utils express the intent coherently? Resolve that question before expanding the public API. A new abstraction is warranted only when the existing idioms cannot express a real manufacturing-test concept without obscuring evidence, hardware ownership, or verdict integrity. Convenience alone is not sufficient. The most important application is the React boundary in the port plan's section 1. HILT borrows React's component model—composition, inversion of control, hooks, and local state—not its runtime model. Reconciliation, re-rendering, and reactivity are out of scope because a hardware test executes once and may produce irreversible physical side effects. If a proposal feels awkward because it tries to import that runtime model, the friction identifies a crossed boundary, not a missing HILT feature.
docs.title: The Golden Rule

docs.text: After __init__ runs, self is read-only. What the tests need flows through configure's return value into utils.ctx , and what they observed leaves with the verdict. This eliminates hidden state coupling and makes the data flow explicit. Rules: - __init__ sets read-only config (MAC, credentials, site, etc.) - configure() returns what the tests will read, as a plain dict — the framework merges it into utils.ctx and closes it - test methods, cleanup() , and all child test bodies read from utils.ctx , not from self ; every key they read with [] is one configure() returned, and a key it did not provide is read with .get() or not at all — a missing [] read is a ContractViolation , not a KeyError (issue #112) - cleanup() reads every key with .get() or in , never [] : it also runs when configure() raised before it returned, and then ctx holds nothing configure() would have provided. A [] read there logs a ContractViolation beside the real Fail (issue #152) - No self.field = value after construction, and no write to utils.ctx after configure() — a reading travels with the verdict, PASS({...}) , and a thing that changes mid-run (an address, a connection) is an object in ctx that manages itself (issue #118) Why: Mutable state, on self or in ctx, creates hidden coupling between lifecycle phases. When inputs flow through ctx and readings flow out with the verdict, the data path is explicit and traceable. The Floor Technician benefits because each leaf's record carries exactly what that leaf handed back, beside the limits it judged against. Enforcement: This is a tier-1 runtime guard, not merely a lint convention. TestComponent freezes only after the most-derived __init__ returns, so subclasses may finish declaring their identity after super().__init__() . Ordinary assignment and deletion then raise AttributeError . Framework-owned lifecycle and evidence transitions use object.__setattr__ directly; suite code receives no framework escape-hatch method. The static no-self-mutation rule remains defense in depth. Scope note: ctx is strictly instance-local. A parent's ctx never flows into composed children — composition is the only coupling mechanism, and ctx inheritance would smuggle hidden state across it. One leaf never reads another's reading either: what a sibling observed is on that sibling's record, not in ctx.
docs.title: Immutable-self Convention

docs.text: A test method is a function from utils.ctx to a verdict. Its readings leave with the verdict: PASS({...}) on the pass path, TestFailure(..., evidence={...}) on the fail path. @evidence is the method's return signature — it names the keys a pass must carry, beside the code that keeps the promise (issue #118). @evidence("output_voltage_v") async def _check_voltage(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: v = await self._read(utils, utils.ctx["ip"]) reading = {"output_voltage_v": v} if v <= utils.ctx["voltage_high_v"]: return PASS(reading) raise TestFailure(f"{v} V exceeds limit", evidence=reading) The declaration is fixed at class definition and never computed at run time. Pass criteria that vary by SKU or fixture are a leaf argument or a different leaf, decided before build_suite runs. A pass without its declared evidence is not a pass: the child boundary refuses it as a ContractViolation naming the leaf and the key. Extra keys are allowed; the declaration is a floor. A failure is not held to it, since a failure may fire before every reading was taken; it records what it is handed. The payload is validated entry by entry. A value that is not JSON, or a key that shadows a ctx entry or the framework-owned measurements slot, is a ContractViolation naming the key. Nothing is stripped silently. Ctx and evidence are one namespace, because they land on one record. A key configure() returns names the limit or the target ( kernel , domain , voltage_high_v ); a key @evidence declares names the reading judged against it ( kernel_running , queried , output_voltage_v ). The same word cannot do both, so pick the evidence name with the ctx key in view. hilt-check flags the clash on the declaring literal as hilt/evidence-shadows-ctx (bench finding F14, issue #161). A measurement is not evidence. utils.measure records a number beside the verdict (see Measurements below); it does not satisfy an @evidence declaration, so a claim that wants the reading in both records names it in both. An undecorated method may still return PASS(payload) ; the payload is recorded unchecked. Declare when you want to be held to it. The same decorator accepts a TypedDict . With -> Verdict[MyEvidence] on the method, pyright checks the PASS({...}) payload against the shape at write time; at run time the TypedDict 's required keys are the declaration. class VoltageEvidence(TypedDict): output_voltage_v: float @evidence(VoltageEvidence) async def _check_voltage(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict[VoltageEvidence]: ... hilt-check enforces the declaration statically as hilt/evidence-fulfilled , the one namespace as hilt/evidence-shadows-ctx , and the read-only context as part of hilt/ctx-provenance .
docs.title: Evidence Travels With the Verdict

docs.text: The node that opens a hop owns it, and everything composed under it inherits it. A gateway is a parent node: its configure() calls utils.use_shell(host=..., ...) , and its build_suite() composes the devices behind the hop. The framework routes the gateway's own utils.exec through that hop and hands the route to every child, so a device's configure, surveys, tests, and audits all land on the far side without the device saying so. A device class never takes a routing argument; it is written once and reused on every bench. class Gateway(TestComponent): async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> dict[str, Any]: await utils.use_shell(host="10.0.0.1", username="ops") return {} def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return MyDevice(name="target", mac="aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff") MyDevice run on its own reads the test host; composed under Gateway it reads the gateway. Same bytes. A child that must run locally declares use_shell(inherit=False) in its own configure() ; a parent that must not hand its route down declares propagate=False . The hop stays up until the parent's own teardown, after every child has cleaned up — a child that fails or expires loses only the transports it opened itself, never its parent's hop. A gateway that cannot come up Fails in its own configure() , and the children it never composed stay pending: the bench was not ready, so the device was never asked. The only via in the framework is the tunnel argument to use_shell / get_shell (see SSH Tunnel below). That is the parent's tool for reaching through a jump host inside its own configure() ; it is never a child's burden.
docs.title: The Parent Owns the Route

docs.text: Ruled on issue #142 (2026-09-12). A constructor argument is identity, fixed at composition time: a name, a MAC, the SKU-specific pass criteria. Runtime state comes from utils in configure() , as one call with no fallback: the IP, the shell, the tunnel, the resolver, the device API. When a parent and a child both could provide the same thing, that thing belongs in TestUtils , where the framework inherits it down the tree and records which way it went; it never travels through ctx or the constructor. A fallback in configure() is the smell that says a utility is missing. # Not allowed: two sources of truth for one ctx key, a branch the suite engineer # wrote, and a record that cannot say which path produced the value. ip = self._ip or await utils.get_arp_resolver(mac=self._mac).resolve() The framework already does this twice. The route flows down through use_shell and is inherited by every composed child; the ARP resolver is scoped to the node's current route and its cache is keyed by the routing label, so devices behind one gateway share ARP state without the suite engineer writing anything to arrange it. Identity reaches a root node through utils.env when no parent composed it: the DUT_MAC a bench-run device reads is the same MAC a rack parent passes to the constructor, and the run's environment is published on the record either way (see Environment Variables below). That is the run's declared input, not discovery, and it is what keeps the bench-run device and the composed one the same bytes.
docs.title: The Node Names What It Needs; the Framework Decides Where It Comes From

docs.text: The default run_data returns a detached snapshot of all serializable values from utils.ctx : the ctx view. JSON primitives (with finite numbers), plain dicts with string keys, and lists survive; class instances ( SshInterface , etc.), functions, live handles, non-finite floats, and cycles are stripped automatically. A leaf's RunResult.run_data is that view plus the evidence its verdict carried, flat, so the limit sits beside the reading; the leaf's summary_tree node carries the same evidence and its declaration. A non-leaf node's run_data is the ctx view alone. Stripping is deterministic and all-or-nothing at each top-level ctx entry. If a list or dict contains one invalid nested value, that complete entry is absent from run_data . HILT does not remove only the handle and leave a plausible-looking partial record. A value the claims need but the record must not carry, such as a session credential obtained in configure() , is named in redact_ctx on the suite class (issue #154). Each entry is a ctx key, exact or as a regular expression the key matches whole. The key appears in run_data as <REDACTED> , and the string under it is masked on every record surface, including a log line or a TestFailure the author hands it to. The record shows that the key was held; it never shows what. ctx itself is unchanged: the claims read the real value. class BlocklistRoundTrip(TestComponent): redact_ctx = ("sid", r"api_.*") async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> dict[str, Any]: sid = await self._login(utils) return {"sid": sid, "api_token": await self._token(utils, sid), "domain": "x.test"} # RunResult.run_data => { # "measurements": [], # "sid": "<REDACTED>", # "api_token": "<REDACTED>", # "domain": "x.test", # } # configure returns data — it appears in run_data automatically async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> dict[str, Any]: ip = await self._resolve() return {"ip": ip, "hostname": "switch-01"} # RunResult.run_data => { # "measurements": [], # "ip": "10.0.0.1", # "hostname": "switch-01", # } Override run_data only when you need computed or filtered output from the context. An override sees the ctx view, not the readings, which are merged when the leaf settles: from hilt import JsonObject @property def run_data(self) -> JsonObject: base = super().run_data return {**base, "within_spec": self._check_spec(base)} Note: non-JSON-safe objects ( datetime , sets, arbitrary classes) are stripped by default. Override run_data if you need custom serialization for these types, and return only JSON-safe data from the override. Every snapshot includes run_data["measurements"] , the list utils.measure fills. It is framework-owned: a ctx entry with that key does not populate or replace it, and it is written after any run_data override runs, so an override cannot drop it.
docs.title: run_data — Automatic Structured Evidence

docs.text: A reading with a unit and a window that a process engineer will chart belongs in utils.measure , not only in the evidence payload. The call records and returns; the verdict stays whatever the gated PASS says, because a limit is evidence, never a verdict ( docs/measurements.md ): from hilt import PASS, TestComponent, TestFailure, TestUtils, Verdict, evidence class Rail(TestComponent): @evidence("output_voltage_v") async def _output_rail(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: volts = await self._read_rail(utils) rail = utils.measure("output_voltage_v", volts, unit="V", limits=(4.75, 5.25)) if rail.in_limits: return PASS({"output_voltage_v": volts}) raise TestFailure("rail outside window", "4.75-5.25 V", f"{volts} V") The gate reads in plain sight, so hilt/gated-pass sees the predicate and the next reader sees the criterion. Name the quantity once per node, in the unit it will always carry; the consumer keys its series on that name. Record for trend without a window by passing limits=None . Measure from configure() (a bring-up reading) or the test method only; cleanup , surveys, audits, and hooks are refused. from hilt import measure is the same call resolved to the running node when a helper does not have utils in hand. When the reading comes over a shell, parse it to float | None and hand measure the None instead of wrapping the parse in a try : a reading not taken is recorded as such, it is never inside its window, and the same gate fails the claim (issue #159). Keep NaN out of the call; that is a bug in the suite's arithmetic, not a blank from the device, and the framework refuses it.
docs.title: Measurements: utils.measure

docs.text: TestComponent exposes three instance factories for building the suite. The names are the vocabulary a suite reads aloud in: a leaf is a test , dependent children run in sequence , independent children run in parallel . There is exactly one spelling for each; case and group are retired (issue #110) and hilt/retired-names flags them. self.test(name, fn, *, fail_after=None, abort_after=None) — the leaf: one verdict method, named here at composition time. Defaults to discrete_log_file=False so entries roll up to the parent artifact. self.sequence(name, children, ...) — serial execution, bails on first failure, and owns a discrete timeline by default. self.parallel(name, children, ...) — concurrent execution via asyncio.TaskGroup , collects all failures, and owns a discrete timeline by default. The name says so: nobody misses that two children share a bus. Pass discrete_log_file=False to self.sequence() or self.parallel() when that composition is too small to merit a separate Inspector timeline. Its records then roll into the nearest owning ancestor, just as leaves do. Authored TestComponent subclasses also default to a discrete timeline and may opt into roll-up through super().__init__(..., discrete_log_file=False) . The root always owns a log so every run has an authoritative temporal backbone. Private methods pass as references directly — Python bound methods carry self for free. def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return self.sequence( self.name, [ self.test("check reachable", self._check_reachable), self.test("check firmware", self._check_firmware), ], ) async def _check_reachable(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: # `self` is preserved — bound at attribute access, no wrapping needed result = await utils.exec("true") if result.exit_code == 0: return PASS raise TestFailure("device unreachable", "exit 0", str(result.exit_code)) Every return PASS sits under the predicate that earns it; hilt-check (the hilt/gated-pass rule) flags a bare one, and the examples show the gated shape.
docs.title: Composition Factories: self.test, self.sequence, self.parallel

docs.text: A leaf's name is decided where the tree is composed, not where the method is defined. One method, many leaves: pass the value that varies straight to self.test() after the method, and name each leaf in a comprehension. The framework calls fn(utils, *args, **kwargs) ; utils is always first, and the developer's arguments follow. fail_after and abort_after are the leaf's budget, never the method's parameters. The arguments are checked against the method's signature when the tree is built, so a leaf that could never be called fails build_suite with a ContractViolation before any hardware is touched. class Compute(TestComponent): def __init__(self, *, name: str, cpu_count: int) -> None: super().__init__(name=name) self._cpu_count = cpu_count async def _cpu_stress(self, utils: TestUtils, *, cpu: int) -> Verdict: ... def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return self.parallel( "stress", [ self.test(f"cpu{i}_stress", self._cpu_stress, cpu=i, fail_after=120.0) for i in range(self._cpu_count) ], ) The comprehension maps a known population (every core, every rail, every channel) onto leaves; it does not choose among them. A comprehension with an if filter decides at build time which claims exist, and hilt/pure-build-suite flags it. The population is identity, like a hook: it comes in through __init__ , never out of configure() .
docs.title: Enumerate Leaves at Runtime

docs.text: A long operation such as a firmware flash or a provisioning step is a self.test(...) when the Floor Technician should see it in the report with its own verdict and its own budget. When it is preparation the report should not itemize, it belongs in configure() , where a TestFailure means "the device did not reach a testable state" (see overview.md) and the node reads Fail without a phantom leaf. Ask whether the Floor Technician acts differently when this step fails on its own line. If so, it is a leaf.
docs.title: self.test() or configure()?

docs.text: Declare a budget on the composition line that owns the work. Use fail_after when missing the time limit is a negative hardware verdict, and abort_after when the harness should stop waiting without claiming the hardware failed. def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return self.parallel( "rack claims", [ self.test("BMC ready", self._bmc_ready, fail_after=45.0), self.test("optional telemetry", self._telemetry, abort_after=10.0), ], fail_after=120.0, ) result = await rack.run(abort_after=300.0) The run budget bounds the whole rack. The parallel node and its leaves may tighten that bound; they cannot lengthen it. If the 45-second leaf is reached with only 8 seconds left on the run clock, the run clock fires after those 8 seconds and its abort_after state applies. The resulting timeout evidence names reason="timeout" , the declared budget, active elapsed time, and the root-to-node path of the winning clock. The timed window is configure through the test method or last child. Cleanup retains its separate finalization allowance. Root-owned before_each / after_each hooks are excluded from every time-budget clock, so a slow shop-floor database cannot manufacture a hardware Fail. In a parallel node, however, a sibling still inside its timed window keeps the shared ancestor clock moving; another sibling's hook or cleanup cannot lend it extra time. Do not catch or suppress asyncio.CancelledError around awaited work. A deadline closes only transports opened by the cut node. An inherited route remains the parent's resource; this is what keeps a timed-out DUT from taking down a healthy sibling behind the same gateway. A gateway parent may declare the same budget pair. Its clock begins when it enters configure ; if the hop is not open by then, the Fail or Aborted state and its timeout evidence are the gateway's own, and the devices behind it are never asked.
docs.title: Time Budgets: Name the Meaning of “Too Long”

docs.text: A test method returning PASS , or PASS(evidence) with its readings → test passes (state Pass ). The check is isinstance(result, Verdict) , and only PASS mints one. The string "PASS" does not pass, and a PASS missing a key its @evidence declared is a contract violation, not a pass. A test method raising TestFailure (or subclass) → test fails with structured data (state Fail ) A test method raising any other exception → ContractViolation Fail (banner CONTRACT VIOLATION , bug: true ): the developer didn't model this failure mode A test method returning anything other than the PASS sentinel (including falling through with None ) → node-local Aborted . No verdict was produced, so the framework refuses to forge one. Siblings are unaffected. An integration hook ( before_each / after_each ) throwing anywhere in the tree → state Aborted on the enclosing node AND every ancestor Aborted is a peer state to Pass and Fail , not a flavor of failure. It signals that no verdict was produced — either the harness around the test broke, or the test method finished without rendering one. The Floor Technician's recovery protocol is "check the integration layer / the test method," not "check the hardware."
docs.title: Pass/Fail/Aborted Contract

docs.text: Survey and audit hooks are registered in __init__ , not in configure() . They are stackable — multiple calls register multiple independent hooks, each firing on its own schedule. class ComputeBlade(TestComponent): def __init__(self, params: TestParams) -> None: super().__init__(params) # Passive snapshot at every lifecycle phase boundary self.use_survey(self._dmesg_snapshot) # Active monitoring that can fail the test self.use_audit(interval=5.0, fn=self._check_thermals) Why constructor-registration, not configure-registration? Survey and audit are part of the test's identity — stable across runs, visible on the class — not runtime-configured state. Registering them in the constructor makes them discoverable and keeps configure() focused on runtime wiring. Survey errors are swallowed (never affect the verdict). Audit errors are real failures — a throwing audit cancels in-flight test methods immediately and fails the test. Scheduling a survey. A survey fires at all six Phase boundaries unless the constructor says otherwise. A survey that reads the device through utils.exec has no device to read at pre-configure , before use_shell has run; its dispatch there execs on the test host and records the developer's machine as device evidence. Say which boundaries the survey observes, and guard the route: from hilt import TestComponent, Phase, TestUtils class PiHole(TestComponent): def __init__(self, *, name: str) -> None: super().__init__(name=name) self.use_survey( self._ftl_tail, phases=[phase for phase in Phase if phase >= Phase.POST_CONFIGURE], ) async def _ftl_tail(self, utils: TestUtils) -> object: if utils.exec_route == "local": return None # no device on the other end of exec at this boundary return (await utils.exec("tail -n 50 /var/log/pihole/FTL.log")).stdout Both halves are needed. The phase list is the schedule; the route check is the guard. Order is not reach: when configure fails before use_shell returns, the engine skips post-configure , pre-test , and post-test and still fires pre-cleanup and post-cleanup , and at those two utils.exec is on the test host. utils.exec_route answers "local" there and the hop's endpoint ( "10.10.10.10" ) once the route is up, so a survey that compares against it never tails the wrong machine. An empty phases= is a ValueError at registration, not a survey that silently never fires. Survey artifacts are named for the lifecycle dispatch point and hook index. Audit artifacts use the same survey artifact type and add the audit hook and dispatch indexes to the name. Every non- None return is captured, including empty containers. Python cannot distinguish an explicit or delegated None return from fall-through at runtime, so None writes only an informational log entry. A hook that needs to preserve a deliberate null observation calls await utils.capture_artifact(Artifact(..., data=None)) directly. Once a hook produces an observation, framework shutdown waits for its artifact publication within the bounded evidence budget, even under repeated cancellation. Audit intervals must be positive and finite, and the framework stops every audit loop as soon as the authored suite settles. See examples/hardware_device_lifecycle.py for survey and audit around a device with real state transitions — rail up in configure , thermal audit during the claim, rail down in cleanup .
docs.title: Constructor-Only Hooks: use_survey and use_audit

docs.text: For composing HILT into a larger harness (shop-floor DB, lab coordinator, audit pipeline), pass before_each and after_each to the root run() call: await root.run( before_each=lambda ctx: shopfloor_db.record_started( fn=ctx.bread_crumbs, station=ctx.env.get("STATION_ID"), at=datetime.now(UTC), ), after_each=lambda ctx: shopfloor_db.record_finished( fn=ctx.bread_crumbs, state=ctx.result.state, failure=ctx.result.failure.fail_message if ctx.result.failure else None, at=datetime.now(UTC), ), ) Register once at the root — the framework fires them around every executed test in the tree. The hook context is deliberately narrow (node name, ancestor_names , bread_crumbs , logger , env ) — NOT exec or get_shell . Integration hooks are for external coordination, not for exercising the hardware. Pair invariant: after_each fires even when before_each threw. Register them as a pair or pass allow_unpaired_hooks=True to opt out of the warning. The exception-path behavior is: throw from either hook → run halts → every enclosing node transitions to Aborted → every in-flight SSH session and subprocess is killed immediately. A 30-minute firmware flash mid-abort must NOT continue to mutate the hardware.
docs.title: Integration Hooks: before_each / after_each on the Run Params

docs.text: configure() returns a plain dict; the framework merges it into utils.ctx for test methods, survey hooks, cleanup() , and all descendant leaves, then closes it. No instance fields are needed for configure-phase data. The return value is the contract with the test methods: it names every key they read with [] , and it is all they will ever find there. Seed no placeholders — a reading belongs on the verdict, not in ctx — and nothing writes ctx after configure returns. hilt-check enforces both statically as hilt/ctx-provenance ; at run time a [] read of a missing key, or any later write, is a ContractViolation naming the test and the key, while .get() and in read an optional key (issues #112, #118). The framework annotation is Mapping[str, Any] ; a plain dict[str, Any] return is the default and satisfies it. When a suite benefits from precise key types, define a local TypedDict and use it as the covariant return annotation — pyright strict accepts the override because a TypedDict is a Mapping , which dict[str, Any] as the base annotation would not allow. This is static information only: a TypedDict is still an ordinary mutable dict at runtime, and the framework copies it into utils.ctx . A context dataclass is deliberately out of contract because it would fight dict merge semantics and require special handling in the default run_data path. class DeviceContext(TypedDict): ssh: RemoteInterface token: str async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> DeviceContext: ...
docs.title: Configure-Returns-Context Pattern

docs.text: A TypedDict return tells the reader the shape, but utils.ctx still hands the test methods a Mapping[str, Any] , so a misspelled key survives pyright and reaches the floor as a ContextInsufficient contract violation — a Fail under the bug banner, where the author meant to take a reading (issue #112). Naming the type once on the class closes that gap: declare class MySuite(TestComponent[MyCtx]) and annotate the lifecycle methods utils: TestUtils[MyCtx] , and utils.ctx["volts"] is a float to the editor while utils.ctx["volt"] is a type error before it is ever run (issue #75). class PowerCtx(TypedDict): rail: str volts: float class PowerSuite(TestComponent[PowerCtx]): async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils[PowerCtx]) -> PowerCtx: return {"rail": "3v3", "volts": 3.3} def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return self.test("rail", self._rail_is_up) async def _rail_is_up(self, utils: TestUtils[PowerCtx]) -> Verdict: if utils.ctx["volts"] > 3.0: # a float here, not Any return PASS raise TestFailure("rail low", "> 3.0V", f"{utils.ctx['volts']}V") This is sugar, and it is opt-in in both directions. Writing TestComponent and TestUtils bare means what it always did — the parameter defaults to Mapping[str, Any] — so no existing suite has to change, and a suite that adopts the parameter is making a claim to its own reader, not to the framework. Nothing about the run moves: the context object is the framework's RunContext , a dict[str, Any] it owns; a key configure() never provided is still a runtime ContractViolation rather than a static one; and run_data still strips class instances, functions, and live handles value by value. Composition stays unparameterized on purpose. self.test() , self.sequence() , and self.parallel() speak of TestComponent nodes of any context shape, because a rack composes suites that do not share one context — pinning them to a single CtxT would make the parameter contagious rather than opt-in. class MyDevice(TestComponent): # configure ALWAYS returns the context your test provides to its # lifecycle methods and children. This tells future devs exactly what # context your test requires and what it supplies — important, for # example, for ssh chaining, which requires an "ssh" entry in ctx. async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> dict[str, Any]: # utils.env.require raises TestFailure when the variable is unset or # blank: a verdict from configure — the test lands in Fail without the # suite ever running. The verdict means "did not reach a testable # state"; whether the cause is config/infra or DUT is the human's call # from logs and survey artifacts. Model as many failure modes as # possible so they surface as verdicts rather than bugs. utils.env.port # does the same for a port, defaulting to 22 and rejecting a typo. # utils.env.int and utils.env.float do it for a number: unset uses the # default when one was given, and a bad value Fails naming the variable # and the value. username = utils.env.require("TARGET_USER") password = utils.env.require("TARGET_PASSWORD") address = utils.env.require("TARGET_ADDRESS") shell = await utils.use_shell(host=address, username=username, password=password) # use_shell wires utils.exec to route through SSH automatically return {"ssh": shell.ssh, "token": await self._authenticate()} # pass or fail, cleanup is GUARANTEED to run at the end of the lifecycle. # Use it to close any opened connections, put the device into a neutral state, etc. # It runs after a configure Fail too, so read ctx with .get(): "token" may never # have been returned. async def cleanup(self, utils: TestUtils) -> None: pass # ssh auto-disconnected by framework, after the post-cleanup survey def build_suite(self) -> TestComponent: return self.sequence( self.name, [ self.test("survey", self._capture_survey), self.test("reachable", self._check_reachable), ], ) async def _check_reachable(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: # utils.exec already routed through ssh result = await utils.exec("true") if result.exit_code == 0: return PASS raise TestFailure("device unreachable", "exit 0", str(result.exit_code))
docs.title: Carrying the same type into the test methods

docs.text: A device-level test can be dropped into a rack-level test without modification. "Push state up" to higher-level components; trust the framework lifecycle.
docs.title: Composability

docs.text: Always use utils.env inside test code. Never os.environ directly. The env snapshot is stored in every RunResult for post-run auditing — filtered by the run's env_allow or env_deny list when one was declared, verbatim otherwise (see docs/inspector-json.md ). text , require , and port read a string, a required string, and a TCP port. int and float read a number the same way: a bad value Fails the run naming the variable and the value, and a missing one uses the default when the call passed one.
docs.title: Environment Variables

docs.text: Call await root.run() to execute a suite. The framework constructs TestUtils ; suite authors import it for lifecycle annotations, not as plumbing they must assemble. Every node receives a distinct TestUtils object with a logger scoped to that node's full root-to-leaf path. Leaves, sequences, and parallel nodes built by one authored instance share that instance's utils.ctx dict, while a composed TestComponent subclass starts with a fresh context. The environment snapshot is immutable and shared across the run; the halt signal is read-only from suite code.
docs.title: TestUtils Injection

docs.text: utils.logger is scoped per node — never print() , so evidence is captured in artifacts Artifacts captured automatically discrete_log_file=False rolls log entries into the parent logger. discrete_log_file=True (the default on class-based tests) gives the node its own log file. Inline self.test() bodies default to False . Every full run creates a timestamped directory under the configured artifact root. A logging owner streams both timeline.log for humans and versioned timeline.jsonl for the Inspector, flushing both on every entry. Treat TestComponent.log_path as the authoritative path; directory names are not an API. While a durable timeline is attached, utils.logger.isEnabledFor(...) is true at every level so developer-side guards cannot suppress the authoritative chronology. Process logging handlers still apply their own level policy.
docs.title: Logging

docs.text: Construct an immutable Artifact and pass it to utils.capture_artifact() . The method persists the JSON artifact under HILT_ARTIFACT_ROOT , then emits a structured pointer through the same scoped logger that records the surrounding test events. Artifact deliberately has no write() or write_file() method: a file without its pointer would be absent from the authoritative chronology. from hilt import Artifact snapshot = Artifact( name="pre-flash", type="hardware-survey", data={"firmware": "2.4.1", "healthy": True}, ) artifact_path = await utils.capture_artifact(snapshot) Artifact names and types accept letters, numbers, dashes, and underscores. Payloads must be JSON serializable. Capture is async, never overwrites an existing artifact, and returns the absolute path recorded in the pointer entry.
docs.title: Point-in-Time Artifacts

docs.text: Every RunResult carries the node's position in the tree: ancestor_names: list[str] — canonical form, root-to-this inclusive. Use for programmatic aggregation (DB keys, leaf identity). bread_crumbs: str — "/".join(ancestor_names) precomputed. Use for display, log lines, error messages. summary_tree: SummaryTreeNode — snapshot of this node's subtree at completion. Enables downstream integrators to reconstruct the full Inspector tree from the root's RunResult alone. The versioned payload and recursive node fields are defined in inspector-json.md . A full run() also persists the root payload automatically as result.json in that run's artifact directory. Authored suites should consume the returned RunResult when they need the live value; they never write the canonical Inspector file themselves.
docs.title: RunResult Navigation — ancestor_names and bread_crumbs

docs.text: Need Use Physical hardware component TestComponent Networked device (MAC-based) TestComponent + utils.get_arp_resolver() in configure Device reached over SSH, connection shared across tests TestComponent with configure returning {"ssh": ...} Device behind a jump host or OOB gateway The gateway is a TestComponent whose configure() opens the hop and whose build_suite() composes the device Standalone test procedure TestComponent The Python examples/ tree is the authoring reference. A broken example means the API changed and the docs need updating.
docs.title: Fractal Design: HILT exposes a single class

docs.text: self.sequence() — serial, stops on the first failure. Use when later tests depend on earlier ones. The Floor Technician sees exactly where the chain broke and nothing beyond it. self.parallel() — concurrent via asyncio.TaskGroup , collects all failures. Use when tests are fully independent. The Floor Technician sees everything broken at once. One child's Fail never cancels its siblings — Fail is returned, not raised, at the child boundary; only a harness-level abort cancels the parallel node, and then cancelling everything is exactly what Aborted means. Independent claims can still share one resource. A single DeviceApi handle opened in configure() and read from ctx by every leaf serialises their requests: the leaves run concurrently, their requests go out one at a time in call order, and a latency measured around request includes the wait for siblings. That is correct when the claim is about the bytes; when the claim is about the DUT's own latency, give each leaf its own handle. The same holds for a routed console. use_serial(device=...) in configure() binds utils.exec for the node and its descendants to one SerialInterface , and parallel leaves under it take turns on it in call order ( docs/hil/serial.md , Serial Turn Contract). A console costs more to share than a handle does: the leaves share one shell's state, so a cd or an exported variable in one leaf is visible to the next. Claims that need isolation want one console each, via get_serial(device=...) .
docs.title: self.sequence() vs self.parallel()

docs.text: ArpResolver is a composable utility for resolving a device's IP from its MAC. Create one via utils.get_arp_resolver() in configure() , call resolve() , and return both the resolved data and the resolver into ctx. Test methods read the IP and the resolver from utils.ctx . Call arp.ping(utils) for reachability. Call arp.reacquire(utils) after anything that may change the IP (reboot, firmware flash, DHCP churn): it returns the new address and the resolver remembers it, so a later ping dials the address it last resolved while ctx stays as configure() left it. Carry the new address as evidence on the verdict if the Floor Technician should see it. ArpResolutionFailure is not a TestFailure . Catch it in configure and re-raise as TestFailure so a missing ARP entry is a verdict. Uncaught, it is a developer bug — the suite did not model the failure mode. # In configure(): arp = utils.get_arp_resolver(mac=self._mac) try: resolved = await arp.resolve() except ArpResolutionFailure as error: raise TestFailure( f"{error.mac} did not appear on the network", error.mac, error.host, ) from error return {**resolved, "arp": arp} # In build_suite(): self.test("reachability", self._reachability) See examples/networked_device.py .
docs.title: ArpResolver — MAC to IP

docs.text: When the test host cannot reach the target network directly, the SE code is identical to the local case. Compose the device under a gateway parent whose configure() opened the hop, and the framework routes the lookup — the SE never touches SSH. # DutDevice.configure() — no SSH awareness, identical to local ArpResolver usage: arp = utils.get_arp_resolver(mac=self._mac) resolved = await arp.resolve() return {**resolved, "arp": arp} # Gateway.build_suite() — the parent names what sits behind its hop: return self.sequence(self.name, [self.test("gateway-up", self._gateway_up), DutDevice(name="dut")]) See examples/networked_device.py . hilt run ...::DutDevice reads the test host's ARP table; hilt run ...::Gateway runs the same DUT class through the hop.
docs.title: ArpResolver Behind a Gateway

docs.text: Extend TestComponent when one SSH connection must be shared across all of the device's leaves. Open in configure() via utils.use_shell() and let the framework route utils.exec through it automatically. Returning {"ssh": ...} from configure() also makes the device eligible as a via target. Pass it as via in TestParams — the framework manages the lifecycle and scopes utils.exec automatically. use_shell vs get_shell : use_shell answers "where does utils.exec go" — it rebinds the routing for this test and its descendants. get_shell hands you an additional interface without touching the routing. A console by device path is the same idiom: await utils.use_serial(device="/dev/ttyUSB0") in configure() declares it as the node's exec route and get_serial opens one as an auxiliary endpoint; both hand back a Shell , the framework closes the port after the post-cleanup survey and from the abort sweep, and no transport is imported or carried in ctx. Behind a hop, pass an SSH Shell as via or let the console inherit the parent's use_shell route. The policy-only shapes ( inherit=False , propagate=False ) stay with use_shell . See examples/remote_device_ssh.py . The pi-hole dogfood suite ( examples/pi_hole_server.py ) is the same class-owned hop plus phase-boundary surveys that tail service logs for the Floor Technician.
docs.title: SSH Device — Class-Owned Connection

docs.text: Pass the Shell an earlier utils.get_shell() returned as the via argument to the next utils.get_shell() to tunnel the new connection through it.
