docs.text: This is the first deliverable of #89 . It carries the legacy Floor Technician guide into the Python port, adjusted for the signed decisions on #88 , #106 , and #107 . It specifies the terminal UI, which hilt inspect now opens. The Floor Technician guide remains the station page for reading the evidence by hand. The review rulings on !119 set the implementation order: Inspect first, Run as a separate increment behind its own decision. Ty ruled on that increment on 2026-09-10: the Re-Run tab ships, the Failures list is folded into Inspect as a key that hides passing rows, and the cut between the two tabs is the one the legacy tool drew. Inspect is the archive of the production run and executes nothing. Re-Run is the bench, where a node is executed again with the code that ran in production and nothing it produces persists. The internal timeline reader ( hilt.inspector_timeline.TimelineReader ) is implemented as a foundation for the log pane. It asynchronously reads a selected timeline path, validates each version-1 object against the packaged published schema, and returns records and line-numbered diagnostics in physical order. Additive fields and recorded scopes and pointers survive unchanged. A complete final JSON object is readable without a trailing newline; an unfinished final object or UTF-8 sequence produces a truncation diagnostic. Malformed complete records, duplicate keys, non-finite numbers, and unsupported versions are explicit diagnostics, and later valid records remain readable. Missing or unreadable logs produce a file-level unavailable diagnostic. These are reader observations, never test verdicts. The timeline reader does not open artifact pointers or resolve tree ownership. Its read_reference(run_root, reference) boundary opens a recorded POSIX log_path only beneath the selected run directory, preserving the complete relative path after a move. Empty, absolute, traversing, missing, non-file, and symlink-escaping references produce unavailable diagnostics. The read retains the recorded reference and the resolved source path; a reference that cannot resolve has no source path. It never searches another directory for a matching basename. Timeline and capture readers share one checked, cached loader for the packaged schemas; evidence is read afresh on every call. The operator's selected run directory may itself use symlinks or .. ; the reader resolves that directory before containing recorded links. The internal capture reader ( hilt.inspector_artifacts.ArtifactReader ) now reads absolute pointers beneath an opened run root. An explicit, established original root enables relocation while preserving the full relative tail; without that mapping a pointer outside the opened root is unavailable. The reader checks resolved containment, refuses non-file targets, and never falls back to the original run or a basename match. It validates the artifact envelope or root result against its packaged version-1 schema, retaining additive fields and explicit null observations. Missing files, malformed JSON, and unsupported versions are diagnostics that retain the recorded reference. JSON parsing is shared with the timeline reader, so duplicate keys and non-finite values are refused consistently. The original-root mapping remains an input to this internal component; the saved-run loader establishes it from publication evidence. The internal tree reader ( hilt.inspector_tree.TreeReader ) now opens a selected result through that validated result boundary. It resolves the operator's selection before deriving the run root, so a symlink such as latest/result.json or a path with .. opens the same saved evidence as its direct path. References inside saved records still obey the capture reader's traversal and containment checks. read_selected() retains the resolved run directory alongside the validated tree; read() returns just that tree through the same selection boundary. Unresolvable operator paths produce unavailable diagnostics in either form. Its InspectorTree preserves every recorded node in declaration preorder, including pending descendants, and keeps full name components rather than splitting display breadcrumbs. Stable row indices keep duplicate names distinct. Inspect selection and the Failures projection share the same rows: previous/next failure includes Fail and Aborted, skips Pass and pending, and does not wrap. The model retains failure causes, timeout fields, and additive evidence; declared readings absent from evidence are exposed by name, while null and zero remain present observations. For an executed selection, the model identifies its own or nearest ancestor's recorded timeline link. A pending selection has no owner and must render not run . An owner identifies a recorded link, not proof the file is available: the model opens no timeline, and its caller must still enforce run-root containment and report unavailable files. The internal selection model ( hilt.inspector_selection.InspectorSelection ) joins that tree to contained timeline loading for both Inspect and Failures. Its caller supplies the validated tree and the opened directory containing that same result, then navigates through the selection model. Selection clears the previous chronology before I/O, keeps the claim and its recorded owner together, and reads only through read_reference . Every request has its own identity: a delayed load cannot overwrite a later selection, even if the cursor returned to the same row. Pending rows render not run ; executed rows with no owner or an unreadable file render log unavailable . Complete records, their scopes, partial reads, and decoding diagnostics remain intact. Reselection reads evidence afresh. Cancellation and reader defects propagate to the caller and return only the affected current load to idle; they never restore an earlier log or become verdicts. The internal saved-run loader ( hilt.inspector_run.SavedRunReader ) now opens a validated result, its contained root timeline, and a capture reader for that same run. It uses TreeReader.read_selected() so selection errors and the resolved run boundary have one owner. The tree's chronology ownership also governs this opening: a pending root supplies no timeline or relocation origin, even if a damaged record gives it a link. It establishes the original root only from one final root-scoped pointer with artifact_type="run-result" , artifact_name="result" , and an absolute, non-traversing path to result.json . The result's ancestor names must agree with its tree root; full name components are compared without splitting breadcrumbs, and a disagreement names the result defect instead of directing the technician to the log. A missing, damaged, ambiguous, or misplaced publication leaves the original root explicitly unavailable while preserving the saved tree and timeline diagnostics. Complete records without a trailing newline remain readable. The loader never guesses from a basename or timestamp, reads the original station, or edits saved pointers. Reopening reads the evidence afresh. Without a mapping, captures already beneath the opened root remain readable, but pointers outside it cannot relocate. The internal timeline presentation model ( hilt.inspector_timeline_view.TimelineView ) pages a completed selection's chronology without changing its recorded data. It opens at the tail with filtering off; toggling errors returns to the first page. The filter retains Python error and critical records (case-insensitively) and every reader diagnostic. Custom levels have no inferred severity and remain in the full view. Each page retains physical line numbers, scopes, timestamps, and additive fields. Resizing changes the number of records per page and clamps the current page; an empty projection has one empty page. The terminal supplies that size after reserving its header and controls. This model counts records, not wrapped terminal lines. Structured pointers receive one-based numbers across the complete loaded chronology, before paging or filtering. Lookup keeps the same target even when its row is hidden; message text never supplies a path. An empty recorded path remains numbered so the capture reader can diagnose it. All numbers remain addressable, including those above the 1 – 9 direct shortcuts. The returned record supplies the pointer fields to the saved run's capture reader, including the distinct run-result decoding kind. A new completed selection read gets a fresh presentation model; selection/load state remains owned by InspectorSelection . The moved 70-DUT test exercises this composition without executing suite code or changing saved bytes. The internal artifact navigation model ( hilt.inspector_artifact_navigation.ArtifactNavigation ) now groups the complete timeline's numbered pointers by recorded type. Types follow first appearance; captures within a type retain chronology order. Opening selects exactly the requested number, including one above nine or hidden by a filter; an invalid number is rejected instead of opening another capture. Single-view type navigation wraps and selects the new type's first capture, while capture navigation clamps at either end. Diff selection requires at least two captures of the same type. It starts with the single-view capture on the left and the first other capture on the right. The bracket actions cycle the left target and the arrow actions cycle the right target within that type. When a move reaches the other target, the two sides swap; they never collapse onto one capture. Leaving diff restores the original single-view selection. Targets retain their timeline number, full pointer record, recorded reference, and decoding kind for the existing contained capture reader. Empty paths remain selectable and produce that reader's unavailable diagnostic. A moved 70-DUT test opens null and named captures and the root result without suite execution or saved-byte changes. The internal artifact modal model ( hilt.inspector_artifact_view.ArtifactModal ) joins that selection to the saved run's capture reader and pages what it reads. A capture is printed in its recorded key order, so two captures of one type line up; an unavailable or undecodable capture shows the reader's diagnostic with the recorded reference and is never replaced by another file. In diff mode the two captures are aligned row by row and one page cursor moves both sides together, as the artifact table above specifies; a singleton type stays single without a reload, and every change of selection returns to the first page because a capture is read from its top. A delayed read never replaces a newer selection, in the pattern of the selection model. The shared 70-DUT recording in tests/inspector_rack.py proves the composition without suite execution or saved-byte changes. The main view ( hilt.inspector_app.InspectorApp ) is the first terminal screen, built on Textual by Ty's ruling of 2026-09-09. It renders the tab row, the tree, and the chronology pane from the models above and forwards the quick-reference keys, one model call per key: Inspect and Re-Run share one cursor, the chronology loads on cursor movement without Enter and names its owner when the node's records rolled up, the owner's row carries the cyan arrow, arrows jump between Fail and Aborted rows without wrapping, h hides passing rows, n / p page, and f filters to errors while a truncation marker stays in place. Tree depth is drawn with the legacy glyphs ( ├─ , └─ , │ ), computed over the rows on screen so a hidden branch still closes on its last visible child. The plain text of every redraw is kept on the app so the self-tests drive it against the recorded runs in tests/inspector_rack.py and a screenshot can be read back against this guide. The re-run session ( hilt.inspector_rerun.RerunSession ) is the adapter behind the Re-Run tab. It receives a suite factory from the command line, never a suite derived from evidence; loads it on the tab's first opening, off the event loop; refuses a suite whose declared tree differs from the saved one, naming the first row that differs; executes the pressed node through TestComponent.run(subtree=...) , the sealed lifecycle with every leaf outside that subtree left pending; reads the result back through the same saved-run reader the archive uses, so the tab shows a re-run's states and chronology with the same code paths; and keeps that evidence under a scratch directory emptied per node on each re-run and removed when the Inspector closes. Interrupting a live re-run raises the operator signal, so the framework's own termination contract settles the node Aborted with bounded cleanup. The artifact modal screen ( hilt.inspector_app.ArtifactScreen ) opens from a digit in the log pane over the capture carrying that number and owns the artifact keys until b closes it: [ and ] move between types or the left side of a comparison, the arrows between captures of the type or the right side, n and p page both sides together, d enters and leaves the comparison. It renders the modal model only: one capture as its lines, a comparison as two aligned columns with differing rows highlighted, a diagnostic as the reader's words with the recorded reference. The entry point is hilt inspect [PATH] ( hilt.cli ): PATH is a run directory or its result.json ; without PATH the most recently modified result.json under the artifact root opens ( HILT_ARTIFACT_ROOT , default artifacts/ ; --artifact-root DIR overrides), the legacy discovery rule carried over. Nothing under the root, or a selection that is not a saved version-1 run, is refused with the reader's diagnostic on stderr and exit status 3. Opening runs no suite code. --suite TARGET names the suite the Re-Run tab executes, in the form hilt run accepts, and is loaded at the prompt so a wrong target is exit 3 there; without it the tab uses the suite_target the run recorded, loaded only when the tab is first opened. The Inspector serves the person at the station when a test stops the line. Its test of success is concrete: find what happened, categorize it, and begin the station's recovery protocol within sixty seconds, without opening suite source.

docs.text: Inspect mode replays saved evidence. Moving the cursor, paging a log, opening an artifact, or comparing two captures never touches the DUT and never executes suite code. The input is a run directory containing result.json , its per-node timeline.jsonl files, and the point-in-time artifacts referenced by those timelines. The structural tree comes entirely from summary_tree ; the temporal view comes entirely from the linked JSON Lines records. A saved 70-DUT rack must be inspectable without live TestComponent objects, source discovery, an SSH connection, or the test station that produced it. The Inspector JSON contract owns the field definitions and version policy. This page owns their presentation. It introduces no new result fields or verdict rules. The result and each timeline record have independent format_version values; select and validate each decoder separately, accept additive fields, and report unsupported versions explicitly rather than guessing their meaning.
docs.title: What the Inspector reads

docs.text: hilt inspect PATH opens a selected result.json , or the result.json inside a selected run directory, and treats its containing directory as the run root. hilt inspect alone opens the most recently modified result.json under the artifact root ( HILT_ARTIFACT_ROOT , default artifacts/ ; --artifact-root DIR overrides), the legacy convenience carried over by Ty's ruling of 2026-09-09 on #89. The legacy npm run inspect command and summary-tree.artifact input are not Python interfaces. If no result is available, explain that there is no saved tree to inspect. Do not start a test to manufacture one: hilt inspect with nothing under the root exits 3 saying so, and a selection that is not a saved version-1 run exits 3 with the reader's diagnostic, never another file opened in its place. Absence of result.json is not a verdict: an invocation may have failed before a run, or a process may have ended before result publication. Preserve any surviving timeline evidence for diagnosis.

Depth is drawn with the legacy glyphs: ├─ for a child with siblings below it, └─ for the last child, │ continuing a branch that has more children further down. docs.text: Display every declared node, with its recorded state and failure message. Color and symbols help scanning, but the state must remain legible as text. State Presentation and meaning Pass Green success mark. The framework accepted an explicit verdict and any required evidence. A string "PASS" is not a passing verdict. Fail Red failure mark. Read the failure object: this can be a modeled TestFailure or a software contract violation. Aborted Distinct, named state. No verdict was produced; the cause may be integration, operator interrupt, missing verdict, or an abort budget. null Dim Pending / unreached row. This declared step never ran; it is not a fourth terminal state. Left and right arrows move backward and forward through nodes needing attention, skipping Pass and pending rows. Preserve the legacy implementation's inclusion of both Fail and Aborted in that navigation, while keeping their labels and recovery meanings distinct. At either end, leave the cursor where it is; do not wrap unexpectedly. h hides every Pass row and shows them again. This replaces the legacy Failures list (Ty, 2026-09-10): the same recorded tree with the passing branches folded away, so a failure buried inside a large rack is found without leaving the tree or losing its place in it. Pending rows stay visible; they are not passes. If the cursor was on a row that just disappeared, it lands on the nearest visible row above it. When every node passed, the pane says so rather than showing nothing. Show the selected leaf's evidence beside its claim and failure. For every name in evidence_declared absent from evidence , show not taken by name. An absent reading is neither zero nor a successful measurement. Do not present the reserved empty run_data["measurements"] slot as an implemented measurement or SPC feature.
docs.title: Inspect — the default

docs.text: The same tree, unhydrated: every row reads not re-run until the technician executes it. Move to any node and press Enter to execute that node and everything beneath it with the code that ran in production. Switching tabs or highlighting a node never runs anything; Enter on the Inspect tab does nothing. The purpose is the floor's quick check: the ping failed, the cable is reseated, the one claim is re-run with the production code, and only then is the whole suite restarted through the station's normal procedure. What executes is the sealed lifecycle, confined to one subtree. TestComponent.run takes subtree= , the child positions from the root to the pressed node. Every node on the path to it runs its own configure and cleanup, because that is their lifecycle and the only way the pressed node meets the hop its ancestors own; every leaf outside the subtree is left pending, never executed. The framework continues to own configure and cleanup. This is not the legacy ↑ctx ancestor-configure replay, which stays prohibited: no parent's configure is replayed outside the lifecycle to make a device runnable, and the instance-local context idiom is untouched. The suite is supplied, never derived. hilt run records the loader target it used in result.json as suite_target (absolute file or module name, :: , class), and hilt inspect loads that suite the first time the tab is opened; --suite TARGET names another, and is loaded at the prompt. Nothing is reconstructed from result.json , artifact contents, or source found beside the run directory. Before any node runs, the supplied suite's declared tree is compared with the saved one, name and type in preorder; a difference is refused by path, and the pane says which suite to name instead. A run that recorded no target, one started from a developer's own harness, leaves the tab unavailable with that reason until --suite is given. Nothing the bench produces persists. Each re-run writes its evidence under a scratch directory, in a subdirectory per pressed node. Re-running the same node empties that subdirectory first, so the ninth re-run leaves nothing of the eighth. The whole scratch directory is removed when the Inspector closes. After a re-run the pressed node and its descendants that ran show their fresh states; rows the re-run never reached keep whatever an earlier re-run left, or not re-run . The log pane shows the highlighted node's re-run chronology, read by the same reader as the archive, with the same owner arrow; a node no re-run reached says so instead of borrowing the archive's log. A node above the pressed one reads partly re-run, never a verdict. Its lifecycle ran and its chronology is worth reading, but the state it rolled up covers only the child the bench was pointed at: every sibling was left pending and contributed nothing to it. Drawn as a verdict, that rollup turns a group whose other child failed in production into a Pass and carries the Pass to the root, which is the one reading the floor must never be given (issue #141). The bench answers for the branch it ran; the verdict on the whole node belongs to the archive on the Inspect tab, or to a re-run of that node, which runs every claim beneath it and so reads as a verdict again. The run's recorded environment seeds the re-run, so the station's variables travel with the record; the live environment overrides it, so a technician can change one deliberately before pressing Enter. A live re-run is live hardware. Tab is held while a node runs, as in the legacy UI, and Enter starts nothing else. q during a re-run is the operator interrupt: it takes the framework's termination contract , the node settles Aborted with bounded cleanup, and only then does the Inspector exit. A second q during that cleanup exits immediately, as a second signal does at the station. The legacy promise that Ctrl-C always exits immediately with nothing at stake applies to the archive, not to the bench.
docs.title: Re-Run — the bench

docs.text: Find the node needing attention. Use right/left to move forward/backward without scrolling through passed leaves. Read the recorded state before choosing a recovery. Read the failure message and comparison. Show fail_message , and expected / received when present. Preserve bug banners, nested causes, hook names, and operator signals; a plain-language message alone does not establish hardware fault. Read the timeline already below the tree. n advances a page, p returns a page, and f toggles the errors-only filter. Log severity does not replace the verdict. Open a referenced artifact. Press its displayed digit, 1 – 9 . Survey captures can show whether the device's reported health agrees with what actually happened. Choose the recovery protocol. Read the failure's cause and the available evidence. The human makes the final determination; uncertainty is a reason to escalate. The five categories follow the current Failure Taxonomy Contract , which supersedes the legacy guide's separate, automatically assigned infrastructure category: Category Evidence to read Recovery direction DUT failed a check Modeled TestFailure , comparisons, and captured readings. A configure failure means the device did not reach a testable state; hardware versus infrastructure remains a human determination. Follow the station protocol for the established cause. Hardware lying Survey evidence contradicts a claimed healthy state or the apparent verdict. Preserve the discrepancy and seek deeper inspection, even after Pass. Test method bug Contract-violation banner, bug , or MissingVerdict . The latter is Aborted; thrown bugs are Fail. A framework-contract banner identifies the framework maintainer as the owner. Escalate the software defect; do not condemn the unit from this signal. External integration failure ExternalIntegrationFailure , its hook, and its cause. Restore the harness or coordination service before retrying. Operator interrupt OperatorInterrupt , operator: true , and its signal. The rack was stopped deliberately; resume only under the station's procedure. Time-budget evidence supplements this taxonomy. Display the winning timeout.clock , declaration, budget, and elapsed time. fail_after produces Fail; abort_after produces Aborted and may have no failure object at all. Do not relabel the latter as a hook failure just because both are Aborted. The station recovery table gives the full reading procedure.
docs.title: The main workflow: diagnosing a failure

docs.text: Resolve a node's non-null log_path relative to the selected run directory. A terminal node with a null link rolled its records into the nearest ancestor with a link; indicate that ancestor with the legacy cyan owner arrow. Keep each entry's scope visible so sibling records in the shared timeline cannot be mistaken for this leaf's readings. A pending node has no chronology anywhere. Show not run , not its parent's timeline as though the pending node produced evidence. A missing file for a node that did run is a separate, explicit log unavailable condition. Neither condition changes state. Read JSON Lines incrementally, preserving file order and every complete valid record. For an interrupted final line, display the complete preceding records and a visible truncation marker; do not fill in the unfinished object. Report malformed complete records or unsupported versions as decoding errors rather than silently dropping them. An errors-only filter must not hide these reader diagnostics.
docs.title: The timeline and its owner

docs.text: Number structured artifact-pointer entries in the loaded timeline and show [N] on the corresponding row. Digits 1 – 9 open the matching numbered capture in a modal. Take the link from the pointer fields, not from a path-looking substring in message . Retain numbering when paging or filtering so a digit never silently changes its target. The modal groups captures by artifact_type and labels each with its name and timestamp. Show the persisted content, including an explicit null observation; nothing in the viewer recomputes a verdict. The root run-result pointer opens result.json , whose shape differs from a point-in-time artifact envelope. The capture reader checks the envelope's own version and published schema as required by the JSON version policy . An unavailable or unreadable capture produces a visible diagnostic containing the reference, while the log and tree remain usable. The saved files are never edited. Version 1 stores absolute artifact_path pointers, whereas tree log links are relative. The reader resolves captures under the selected run root. For a moved run, try re-anchoring the recorded path's run-root-relative tail beneath the opened run root before declaring the capture unavailable. Preserve that full relative path: two nodes may capture different evidence with the same filename. Never search for or substitute a file merely because its basename matches. Re-anchoring requires an established original run root. If the reader cannot establish that mapping, or the mapped capture cannot be read under the opened root, show artifact unavailable with the recorded reference; do not guess a root or silently fall back to another run's evidence. The reader implementation must demonstrate that mapping and its unavailable cases in tests before claiming moved-run support. This is a reader rule. Saved pointers remain unchanged and absolute at version 1. Changing their stored representation to relative paths is a record-contract change under the version policy , requiring Ty's decision before an implementation MR.
docs.title: Artifacts — the evidence behind the verdict

docs.text: Key Single-artifact view Diff view [ / ] Previous / next artifact type. Change the left artifact within the current type. ← / → Previous / next artifact within the current type. Change the right artifact within the current type. n / p Next / previous content page. Page both sides together. d Enter diff when the type has at least two artifacts. Return to the single-artifact view. b Close the modal and return to the log. Close the modal and return to the log. Diff shows two captures of the same type side by side, highlighting changed lines and dimming unchanged lines. Preserve the legacy guide's intended swap when the two selected indices collide, so a two-capture comparison can reverse sides. This is a display of recorded differences, not an automatic diagnosis of hardware truth.
docs.title: Reading and comparing artifacts

docs.text: Context Key Action Saved inspection, including a modal q / Ctrl-C Quit without changing evidence or touching hardware. Live re-run q / Ctrl-C Operator interrupt: the node settles Aborted through bounded cleanup, then the Inspector exits. A second press during cleanup exits at once. Main view Tab Switch Inspect / Re-Run. Held during a live re-run. Either tree ↑ / ↓ Move through the rows on screen; hidden passes are stepped over. Either tree ← / → Previous / next Fail or Aborted node of the saved run; skip passed and pending rows. Inspect tree h Hide passing rows, or show them again. Re-Run tree Enter Execute the highlighted node and everything beneath it; nothing else runs anything. Log pane, no modal n / p Next / previous page. Log pane, no modal f Toggle errors-only filtering. Log pane, no modal 1 – 9 Open the artifact carrying that number. Artifact modal b , [ , ] , ← , → , n , p , d Use the artifact controls above; the modal owns these keys until it closes.
docs.title: Key bindings quick reference

docs.text: An ancestor owns the log. The owner arrow explains roll-up; it says nothing about context inheritance. The legacy ↑ctx ancestor-configure replay is prohibited. An error appears in a passing test. Survey errors are logged but do not decide the verdict. Read the state and the surrounding capture, not just the line's color. Many nodes are Aborted. An integration halt or operator interruption can affect the whole in-flight tree. A missing verdict or an abort budget is node-local. Read the cause instead of inferring a rack-wide hardware failure from repeated labels. The record ends abruptly. Retain the accepted chronology and mark the missing tail. Neither incomplete evidence nor missing declared readings may become Pass.
docs.title: Things that need careful reading

docs.text: The screen implementation ( hilt.inspector_app ) and the entry point ( hilt inspect ) follow this document. The view model is testable independently of the terminal and driven by a recorded 70-DUT rack: Reconstruct tree order, peer states, pending descendants, failure causes, timeout evidence, and missing declared readings from version-1 records alone. Navigate failures and load the selected node's own or rolled-up timeline immediately, with correct owner and scope; never show stale content after a cursor change. Open numbered pointers, group artifacts by type, and compare captures using the specified keys, including the two-artifact index collision. Preserve complete lines under truncation and distinguish unavailable evidence, malformed records, unsupported versions, and nodes that never ran. Make Inspect usable from saved evidence without source or hardware, hidden passes included; it never waits for a suite. The saved-view command and discovery rule are the ones under "Opening a run". Verify moved-run resolution preserves the complete run-relative path and remains under the opened root. Exercise captures with identical basenames in different nodes, an unestablished root mapping, and unavailable files; preserve the recorded reference in every unavailable diagnostic and never substitute another capture. Hold Re-Run to its ruling. Its adapter accepts only an operator-supplied suite through the command line ( suite_target or --suite ), never reconstruction from evidence or neighboring source, and refuses a suite whose declared tree differs from the saved one. Execution is TestComponent.run(subtree=...) : ancestors' own lifecycle, the pressed subtree, every other leaf pending. Ancestor-configure replay stays prohibited. A node above the pressed one shows partly re-run , never the state it rolled up over the one child the bench ran. Scratch evidence is replaced per node and removed on close. A live re-run holds Tab, and quitting it goes through the operator-interrupt path to Aborted with bounded cleanup before the Inspector exits. If the message, chronology, and captures do not establish a recovery category, keep the run directory and escalate with the selected node's path. The Inspector must make that uncertainty visible. Evidence earns a conclusion; the screen cannot supply one for it.
docs.title: Implementation acceptance

docs.text: The behavioral reference is the read-only hilt-test-legacy/docs/inspector.md , with navigation checked against src/inspector/InspectTab.mts , RunTab.mts , TreePanel.mts , DebugView.mts , and ArtifactModal.mts in that repository. The guide's workflow, split panes, Run tab, tree glyphs, owner arrow, failure navigation, modal, and diff controls are retained; the Failures list became the h key. Python record names, the five current categories, instance-local ctx, explicit evidence, and interruption semantics follow this port's contracts. No TypeScript runtime or language-server behavior is required to specify this saved-evidence viewer.
docs.title: Migration references

docs.text: JUnit XML reporter ¶ Every CI system reads JUnit XML. hilt.junit.JunitXml maps a RunResult summary tree onto that schema so a hilt run shows up beside every other suite with no adapter. The Floor Technician's taxonomy survives the mapping: a red build says hardware, harness, or bug — not just red. The runner calls JunitXml.write : hilt run --junit PATH writes the report beside the run's evidence ( docs/hilt-run.md ). A harness adapter that imports hilt.junit directly does so off the promised surface ( docs/api-stability.md ). This is a projection of the Inspector JSON contract, not a second source of truth. RunResult.to_json() remains the evidence record. JUnit is what CI already knows how to paint. Mapping of the three terminal states ¶ There is no fourth terminal state. A declared node that did not run ( state is null on the summary tree — a later step in a failed sequence) is skipped , which is a JUnit status, not a HILT state. HILT JUnit element What the FT still sees Pass testcase with neither failure nor error A green row. Fail failure Taxonomy class on @type , fail_message on @message , full to_json() payload in the body. bug: true means broken code, not broken hardware. Aborted error Same payload shape. Aborted is not a flavor of Fail; CI must not count it as failures . unreached ( state null) skipped The node was declared and never ran. @type is the taxonomy class name ( TestFailure , ContractViolation , MissingVerdict , ExternalIntegrationFailure , OperatorInterrupt ). The body is the same JSON object RunResult.to_json() already publishes under failure , so a CI log and the Inspector agree. Tree → testcases ¶ Every leaf (a summary-tree node with no children) is one testcase . Groups, sequences, and suites become classname : the root-to-parent path, joined with / . ancestor_names is still the durable identity in the Inspector JSON; classname is display. A composite that settled before any child ran (configure failed, abort during bring-up) is itself a testcase . Otherwise CI would paint skip — or nothing — for a Fail. Declared children that exist on the tree and never ran are skipped . Counts on testsuites / testsuite ( tests , failures , errors , skipped ) are the counts of emitted testcases, not of composite nodes. Artifacts ¶ Point-in-time evidence stays in the run directory. JUnit gets pointers, not copies: system-out contains timeline: <log_path> when the node (or the nearest ancestor that owns a log) has a timeline.jsonl relative to the run directory. A timeout that determined the state adds a timeout: … line with the same fields as the Inspector timeout object. Consumers resolve log_path against the run directory that holds result.json . Document shape ¶ Jenkins-compatible JUnit (the schema GitLab CI, Jenkins, and pytest-junit share): <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <testsuites name="rack" children="3" failures="1" errors="1" skipped="1"> <testsuite name="rack" children="3" failures="1" errors="1" skipped="1"> <testcase name="identity" classname="rack/claims"/> <testcase name="firmware" classname="rack/claims"> <failure type="TestFailure" message="gate remained closed">{taxonomy JSON}</failure> <system-out>timeline: rack/timeline.jsonl</system-out> </testcase> <testcase name="never reached" classname="rack/ordered claims"> <skipped/> </testcase> </testsuite> </testsuites> No time attribute is emitted: RunResult does not carry per-node duration, and inventing 0 would lie.

docs.text: Parametric Measurements ¶ Design note for #85, signed off by Ty on the issue 2026-09-05 and implemented under 86. This page owns the protocol; docs/inspector-json.md owns the record's place in ¶ result.json . A test method already hands its readings back with the verdict ( PASS(evidence) , docs/idioms.md ). That record answers the Floor Technician's question: did the unit meet the claim. It does not answer the process engineer's question: where inside the window did this unit land, and where are the last five hundred landing. That question needs a number with a unit and limits, in a shape a statistical consumer can read without the suite source. utils.measure records that number, in one call, without touching the verdict. The rule this note is built on: a limit is evidence, never a verdict. A measurement outside its limits is recorded as such, beside the verdict; the verdict stays whatever the gated PASS says. A Pass keeps meaning exactly what it has always meant, and the framework forges nothing. The call ¶ utils.measure is the documented home. It is a method on TestUtils , the scoped service object every lifecycle method already receives, so a measurement is scoped to its node the way a log line is. def measure( self, name: str, value: int | float | None, *, unit: str | None = None, limits: tuple[float | None, float | None] | None = None, ) -> Measurement: ... It is synchronous. It records and returns; it performs no I/O, so there is nothing to await and no place for a cancellation to land between the reading and the record. name — a non-empty str , unique within the node. The name is the identity the downstream consumer keys on, together with the node path (see The export contract ): for the life of the suite it names the same quantity in the same unit. Use the same spelling discipline as evidence keys ( output_voltage_v , boot_time_s ). Recording the same name twice in one node is a ContractViolation naming the node and the name; the second reading is not silently appended, because a consumer that sees two output_voltage_v rows for one node cannot tell a retry from a bug. value — an int or a finite float , or None for a reading the suite tried to take and could not. bool is refused (it is an int to Python and a category to a process engineer), as are NaN and the infinities, for the same reason run_data refuses them: a JSON consumer cannot carry them. A textual observation ( ftl_state: "running" ) is evidence on the verdict, not a measurement; SPC and Cpk are defined on numbers, and this protocol does not pretend otherwise. None and NaN are kept apart on purpose (issue #159, bench finding F10). A blank answer over a shell is a fact about the device, and the record is where the Floor Technician should find it; a NaN can only come from arithmetic in the suite, and that is a bug the ContractViolation names. Before #159 every reading parsed from a shell needed its own try to turn the blank into a failure; now the parse hands measure the None and the gate below does the rest. unit — a free string the developer chooses ( "V" , "ms" , "°C" ), or None for a dimensionless count. The framework validates nothing about it and never converts; it is a label the consumer reads back. That is why the name must not change meaning: a name that was volts in one release and millivolts in the next breaks every chart built on it. limits — None , or a (low, high) tuple, inclusive at both ends, with None for an open side: (4.75, 5.25) , (None, 250.0) , (0, None) . A tuple is enough: it reads as the window it is, and it puts no new type into a public signature. Both sides None , a bound that is not a finite number, or low > high is a ContractViolation at the call — a limit that bounds nothing is a bug in the suite, not a wide window. With limits=None the measurement is recorded for trend and in_limits is null . The return is a frozen Measurement record: name , value , unit , limits , in_limits , timestamp , exactly what was recorded. It exists so the developer can gate on it in plain sight: @evidence("output_voltage_v") async def _check_rail(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: v = await self._read_rail(utils, utils.ctx["ip"]) rail = utils.measure("output_voltage_v", v, unit="V", limits=(4.75, 5.25)) if rail.in_limits: return PASS({"output_voltage_v": v}) raise TestFailure( "5V rail out of window", "4.75..5.25 V", f"{v} V", evidence={"output_voltage_v": v} ) The framework evaluated the limit once, the developer chose what to do about it, and hilt/gated-pass can see the predicate beside the PASS . Whether an out-of-window reading is a TestFailure , a warning to trend, or a reason to re-seat the probe and read again is the suite author's decision, taken in the suite. A reading not taken ¶ measure(name, None, ...) records that the suite tried and the device gave nothing. The verdict rule for it follows from the one above and adds nothing to it: A missing reading is never inside its window. With limits , in_limits is false , so the gate in the example fails the claim however it is spelled ( if rail.in_limits: or if rail.in_limits is False: ). The claim then says what the hole means, usually a TestFailure naming the command that answered blank. Without limits , in_limits is null , as for any trend reading. The framework still changes nothing. A limit is evidence, never a verdict, and a hole is no different: a claim that gates on the reading fails through its own gate; a trend-only reading leaves the verdict where the claim put it. A Pass beside a value: null means the claim did not gate on that reading, and that is the claim author's decision, visible in the record. The record keeps the entry. The reading sits in measurements in call order with value: null , so the consumer sees a hole in the series where there was one, and the Floor Technician sees the name of what was not taken rather than a shorter array. @evidence("root_used_pct") async def _root_filesystem(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: result = await utils.exec("df --output=pcent / | tail -n 1") used = _number(result.stdout.rstrip().rstrip("%")) # float | None; no try here reading = utils.measure("root_used_pct", used, unit="%", limits=(None, 90)) if reading.value is None: raise TestFailure("df gave no percentage", "N%", result.stdout.strip()) if reading.in_limits: return PASS({"root_used_pct": reading.value}) raise TestFailure("root filesystem too full", "<= 90 %", f"{reading.value:g} %") Where it may be called ¶ configure and the test method. Those are the two slots that produce the node's record: configure provides ctx, the test method produces the verdict, and both receive the node's own TestUtils . A bring-up reading (ambient at start, supply voltage before the DUT is powered) belongs to configure ; a reading under test belongs to the test method. A composite node ( sequence , parallel ) has a configure and may measure there. Not from cleanup , which restores state and produces no evidence ( hilt/no-verdict-in-cleanup is the same rule from the verdict's side). Not from surveys or audits: they already have an artifact channel for what they observe, and an audit's samples are a time series with its own semantics, which this protocol does not define. Not from integration hooks, which are deliberately denied utils . A call from any of those, or after the node has settled, is a ContractViolation naming the node, in the pattern of ContextImmutable : the record is sealed at the same moment run_data is snapshotted, and nothing writes into a sealed record. The package-root alias ¶ Ty's condition on the approval: from hilt import measure and hilt.measure(...) must both work. They do, with the same signature and the same rules, and utils.measure remains the home the documentation teaches. The alias is convenience, not a second mechanism. The alias has to find the current node's TestUtils without a global, because a parallel node runs its children concurrently in one process and a global would hand one child's reading to another. The mechanism is a contextvars.ContextVar that the framework binds around each slot that admits measurements, at the seam in src/hilt/base.py where the child boundary is handed fn(utils) for configure and the test method: set before the boundary runs the slot, reset in finally . A ContextVar is task-local, and asyncio copies the context into every task it creates, so each child of a parallel node sees its own binding and a gateway parent sees its own inside its own slots. hilt.measure reads the variable and delegates to that TestUtils.measure ; when nothing is bound — module scope, a hook, cleanup , a helper called from outside a run — it raises ContractViolation saying that measure was called outside a running node and naming utils.measure inside configure or a test method as the fix. The self-tests hold the alias to the method: every guard above fires identically through either spelling. A TestUtils is not otherwise reachable from the package root; the variable is private to the framework, is never exported, and is read by nothing else. The recorded shape ¶ Each call appends one object to the node's measurements array, in call order: { "name": "output_voltage_v", "value": 5.02, "unit": "V", "limits": { "low": 4.75, "high": 5.25 }, "in_limits": true, "timestamp": "2026-09-06T21:14:03.118402Z" } Field JSON type Meaning name string The measurement's identity within the node; unique in the array. value number or null The reading, exactly as passed; null when the suite tried to take it and could not. A consumer charting the series skips null: it is a hole, not a zero. unit string or null The developer's label. Never converted. limits object or null { "low": number or null, "high": number or null } , inclusive; null when the call declared none. in_limits boolean or null low <= value <= high with an open side always satisfied; false when value is null and limits is not; null when limits is null. Evidence, not a verdict. timestamp string When the reading was recorded, UTC ending in Z , the same form the timeline uses. The node path, the run, and the station are not repeated in every entry. They are properties of the node and the run directory the array sits in, and repeating them would invite a consumer to trust the copy over the tree. In two lines: measurements is an array, one object per measure call in call order, each {name, value: number | null, unit, limits: {low, high} | null, in_limits: bool | null, timestamp} . It appears on the node's run_data and on the node's summary_tree entry; node path comes from the tree, run id from the run directory. It does not raise, does not change state , does not add a failure, and does not warn the boundary. The consumer reads them beside state and decides what an Aborted node's numbers are worth to a capability index. Feeding them in blind is the consumer's mistake, not a gap in the record. An entry with in_limits: false is a reading outside its window. Read state beside it: it is not a Fail unless state says Fail. state in_limits on an entry What it means What you do Fail false The claim named that window in its check and the unit missed it. evidence on the same node usually carries the same reading. Hardware. Follow the station protocol for the failure name; the entry tells you by how much. Pass false The claim recorded the number for trend and did not gate on it, or the window is not yet a pass criterion. Ship on the verdict. Do not scrap the unit on this line alone; route the reading to the process engineer. Pass or Fail null Recorded without a window. Trend only. Nothing to act on here. any false or null , with value: null The claim tried to take this reading and the device gave nothing. Not a reading of zero. Read state and failure beside it: a Fail names what answered blank. A Pass means the claim did not gate on it; route the hole to the process engineer, not to scrap. Aborted anything The number was taken before the run stopped; no verdict exists. Follow the Aborted protocol for the failure. The measurement is context, not a category. In the timeline, every call writes one scoped line so the chronology carries the number next to what the suite was doing when it took it: measurement: output_voltage_v = 5.02 V limits=[4.75, 5.25] in_limits=true measurement: output_voltage_v = 5.31 V limits=[4.75, 5.25] in_limits=false measurement: output_voltage_v not taken limits=[4.75, 5.25] in_limits=false An in-window or unlimited reading logs at info ; an out-of-window reading, or one not taken, logs at warning , so it stands out in timeline.log without the FT filtering for it. The not-taken line says so in words rather than printing = null V , which reads as a number missing its digits. The line is a log entry and nothing more: it is not the record (the array is), and it does not change the node's state. The two records answer different questions, are validated by different contracts, and live in different fields: evidence is what the verdict carried, validated at the child boundary against the @evidence declaration and the reserved keys, and null when there was no verdict. The one interaction that exists is the reserved name. measurements is not a legal evidence key and not a ctx key that reaches run_data ; both guards predate this note and stay. The export contract ¶ The downstream consumer is an SPC or Cpk tool reading a directory of run directories, or the after-each integrator forwarding each RunResult to a database. What it needs, and where each part lives in the record, is fixed here so the consumer can be written against this page and the schema alone: The consumer needs Where it is Stability A stable name measurements[].name , unique within the node The developer's promise; a rename is a new series. A unit measurements[].unit A label, never converted. Changing it under a name breaks the series. Names may contain / ; do not parse bread_crumbs . The station physical_location on the root PHYSICAL_LOCATION , or unknown . The node's verdict state on the same tree node The consumer keys on it before it aggregates. A series is (station, node path, name) . Everything the consumer aggregates over is in result.json or in the directory name; it never needs the suite source, the live objects, or the timeline, though the timeline carries the same numbers in order for a human. Tiers ¶ The tier-1 guards live in the framework, in TestUtils.measure and the package-root alias, and every one of them is a ContractViolation (developer bug, bug: true , banner: CONTRACT VIOLATION ) naming the node and, where there is one, the measurement: Guard Fires when Duplicate name The node already recorded that name. Not numeric value is a bool , a str , NaN , an infinity, or anything that is not int / float . None is not refused: it is the reading not taken (#159). docs.text: result.json . A test method already hands its readings back with the verdict ( PASS(evidence) , docs/idioms.md ). That record answers the Floor Technician's question: did the unit meet the claim. It does not answer the process engineer's question: where inside the window did this unit land, and where are the last five hundred landing. That question needs a number with a unit and limits, in a shape a statistical consumer can read without the suite source. utils.measure records that number, in one call, without touching the verdict. The rule this note is built on: a limit is evidence, never a verdict. A measurement outside its limits is recorded as such, beside the verdict; the verdict stays whatever the gated PASS says. A Pass keeps meaning exactly what it has always meant, and the framework forges nothing.
docs.title: 86. This page owns the protocol; docs/inspector-json.md owns the record's place in

docs.text: utils.measure is the documented home. It is a method on TestUtils , the scoped service object every lifecycle method already receives, so a measurement is scoped to its node the way a log line is. def measure( self, name: str, value: int | float | None, *, unit: str | None = None, limits: tuple[float | None, float | None] | None = None, ) -> Measurement: ... It is synchronous. It records and returns; it performs no I/O, so there is nothing to await and no place for a cancellation to land between the reading and the record. name — a non-empty str , unique within the node. The name is the identity the downstream consumer keys on, together with the node path (see The export contract ): for the life of the suite it names the same quantity in the same unit. Use the same spelling discipline as evidence keys ( output_voltage_v , boot_time_s ). Recording the same name twice in one node is a ContractViolation naming the node and the name; the second reading is not silently appended, because a consumer that sees two output_voltage_v rows for one node cannot tell a retry from a bug. value — an int or a finite float , or None for a reading the suite tried to take and could not. bool is refused (it is an int to Python and a category to a process engineer), as are NaN and the infinities, for the same reason run_data refuses them: a JSON consumer cannot carry them. A textual observation ( ftl_state: "running" ) is evidence on the verdict, not a measurement; SPC and Cpk are defined on numbers, and this protocol does not pretend otherwise. None and NaN are kept apart on purpose (issue #159, bench finding F10). A blank answer over a shell is a fact about the device, and the record is where the Floor Technician should find it; a NaN can only come from arithmetic in the suite, and that is a bug the ContractViolation names. Before #159 every reading parsed from a shell needed its own try to turn the blank into a failure; now the parse hands measure the None and the gate below does the rest. unit — a free string the developer chooses ( "V" , "ms" , "°C" ), or None for a dimensionless count. The framework validates nothing about it and never converts; it is a label the consumer reads back. That is why the name must not change meaning: a name that was volts in one release and millivolts in the next breaks every chart built on it. limits — None , or a (low, high) tuple, inclusive at both ends, with None for an open side: (4.75, 5.25) , (None, 250.0) , (0, None) . A tuple is enough: it reads as the window it is, and it puts no new type into a public signature. Both sides None , a bound that is not a finite number, or low > high is a ContractViolation at the call — a limit that bounds nothing is a bug in the suite, not a wide window. With limits=None the measurement is recorded for trend and in_limits is null . The return is a frozen Measurement record: name , value , unit , limits , in_limits , timestamp , exactly what was recorded. It exists so the developer can gate on it in plain sight: @evidence("output_voltage_v") async def _check_rail(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: v = await self._read_rail(utils, utils.ctx["ip"]) rail = utils.measure("output_voltage_v", v, unit="V", limits=(4.75, 5.25)) if rail.in_limits: return PASS({"output_voltage_v": v}) raise TestFailure( "5V rail out of window", "4.75..5.25 V", f"{v} V", evidence={"output_voltage_v": v} ) The framework evaluated the limit once, the developer chose what to do about it, and hilt/gated-pass can see the predicate beside the PASS . Whether an out-of-window reading is a TestFailure , a warning to trend, or a reason to re-seat the probe and read again is the suite author's decision, taken in the suite.
docs.title: The call

docs.text: measure(name, None, ...) records that the suite tried and the device gave nothing. The verdict rule for it follows from the one above and adds nothing to it: A missing reading is never inside its window. With limits , in_limits is false , so the gate in the example fails the claim however it is spelled ( if rail.in_limits: or if rail.in_limits is False: ). The claim then says what the hole means, usually a TestFailure naming the command that answered blank. Without limits , in_limits is null , as for any trend reading. The framework still changes nothing. A limit is evidence, never a verdict, and a hole is no different: a claim that gates on the reading fails through its own gate; a trend-only reading leaves the verdict where the claim put it. A Pass beside a value: null means the claim did not gate on that reading, and that is the claim author's decision, visible in the record. The record keeps the entry. The reading sits in measurements in call order with value: null , so the consumer sees a hole in the series where there was one, and the Floor Technician sees the name of what was not taken rather than a shorter array. @evidence("root_used_pct") async def _root_filesystem(self, utils: TestUtils) -> Verdict: result = await utils.exec("df --output=pcent / | tail -n 1") used = _number(result.stdout.rstrip().rstrip("%")) # float | None; no try here reading = utils.measure("root_used_pct", used, unit="%", limits=(None, 90)) if reading.value is None: raise TestFailure("df gave no percentage", "N%", result.stdout.strip()) if reading.in_limits: return PASS({"root_used_pct": reading.value}) raise TestFailure("root filesystem too full", "<= 90 %", f"{reading.value:g} %")

docs.text: configure and the test method. Those are the two slots that produce the node's record: configure provides ctx, the test method produces the verdict, and both receive the node's own TestUtils . A bring-up reading (ambient at start, supply voltage before the DUT is powered) belongs to configure ; a reading under test belongs to the test method. A composite node ( sequence , parallel ) has a configure and may measure there. Not from cleanup , which restores state and produces no evidence ( hilt/no-verdict-in-cleanup is the same rule from the verdict's side). Not from surveys or audits: they already have an artifact channel for what they observe, and an audit's samples are a time series with its own semantics, which this protocol does not define. Not from integration hooks, which are deliberately denied utils . A call from any of those, or after the node has settled, is a ContractViolation naming the node, in the pattern of ContextImmutable : the record is sealed at the same moment run_data is snapshotted, and nothing writes into a sealed record.
docs.title: Where it may be called

docs.text: Ty's condition on the approval: from hilt import measure and hilt.measure(...) must both work. They do, with the same signature and the same rules, and utils.measure remains the home the documentation teaches. The alias is convenience, not a second mechanism. The alias has to find the current node's TestUtils without a global, because a parallel node runs its children concurrently in one process and a global would hand one child's reading to another. The mechanism is a contextvars.ContextVar that the framework binds around each slot that admits measurements, at the seam in src/hilt/base.py where the child boundary is handed fn(utils) for configure and the test method: set before the boundary runs the slot, reset in finally . A ContextVar is task-local, and asyncio copies the context into every task it creates, so each child of a parallel node sees its own binding and a gateway parent sees its own inside its own slots. hilt.measure reads the variable and delegates to that TestUtils.measure ; when nothing is bound — module scope, a hook, cleanup , a helper called from outside a run — it raises ContractViolation saying that measure was called outside a running node and naming utils.measure inside configure or a test method as the fix. The self-tests hold the alias to the method: every guard above fires identically through either spelling. A TestUtils is not otherwise reachable from the package root; the variable is private to the framework, is never exported, and is read by nothing else.

A consumer charting the series skips null: it is a hole, not a zero. unit string or null The developer's label. Never converted. limits object or null { "low": number or null, "high": number or null } , inclusive; null when the call declared none. in_limits boolean or null low <= value <= high with an open side always satisfied; false when value is null and limits is not; null when limits is null. It appears on the node's run_data and on the node's summary_tree entry; node path comes from the tree, run id from the run directory.

docs.text: A measurement is not an evidence key. The two records answer different questions, are validated by different contracts, and live in different fields: evidence is what the verdict carried, validated at the child boundary against the @evidence declaration and the reserved keys, and null when there was no verdict. Its shape is the developer's mapping. measurements is what the node recorded, validated at each call, sealed with the node whatever its state. Its shape is fixed by this note. Recording a measurement therefore does not satisfy an @evidence declaration, and a declared key absent from PASS is still EvidenceViolation.not_carried no matter how many measurements share its name. A developer who wants a reading held to the declaration names it in both places, as the rail example above does: utils.measure for the process engineer, PASS({...}) for the claim. That is one extra name in a dict literal, and it keeps each record honest on its own terms. The alternative — merging measurements into evidence automatically — was considered and rejected: it would make the boundary's evidence check depend on calls made earlier in configure , would let a measurement shadow a ctx key by another route, and would give the SPC consumer two shapes for one number. The one interaction that exists is the reserved name. measurements is not a legal evidence key and not a ctx key that reaches run_data ; both guards predate this note and stay.
docs.title: Relationship to @evidence and PASS(evidence)

docs.text: The downstream consumer is an SPC or Cpk tool reading a directory of run directories, or the after-each integrator forwarding each RunResult to a database. What it needs, and where each part lives in the record, is fixed here so the consumer can be written against this page and the schema alone: The consumer needs Where it is Stability A stable name measurements[].name , unique within the node The developer's promise; a rename is a new series. A unit measurements[].unit A label, never converted. Changing it under a name breaks the series. A numeric value measurements[].value A JSON number, or null when the reading was not taken (#159); never a string, boolean, or non-finite. The consumer skips null in a series: a hole, not a zero. The limits it was judged against measurements[].limits.low / .high , or null Inclusive; an open side is null. Whether it was inside measurements[].in_limits Evidence; the consumer does not recompute the verdict from it. A timestamp measurements[].timestamp UTC, Z -terminated, same form as the timeline. Depends on the station clock rule in docs/floor-technician.md . The node path The walk from the root of summary_tree to the node; ancestor_names on a per-node RunResult Durable identity. Names may contain / ; do not parse bread_crumbs . The run id The run directory name, HILT_ARTIFACT_ROOT/<timestamp>[.n] , published by the root timeline's result pointer as the directory of artifact_path One directory per run() , collision-safe; result.json does not repeat it because a consumer has already opened the directory to read the file. The station physical_location on the root PHYSICAL_LOCATION , or unknown . The node's verdict state on the same tree node The consumer keys on it before it aggregates. A series is (station, node path, name) . Everything the consumer aggregates over is in result.json or in the directory name; it never needs the suite source, the live objects, or the timeline, though the timeline carries the same numbers in order for a human.

docs.text: The tier-1 guards live in the framework, in TestUtils.measure and the package-root alias, and every one of them is a ContractViolation (developer bug, bug: true , banner: CONTRACT VIOLATION ) naming the node and, where there is one, the measurement: Guard Fires when Duplicate name The node already recorded that name. Not numeric value is a bool , a str , NaN , an infinity, or anything that is not int / float . None is not refused: it is the reading not taken (#159). Invalid limits Both sides None , a non-finite bound, or low > high . Outside a node hilt.measure with nothing bound, or either spelling from cleanup , a survey, an audit, a hook, or after the node settled. They are raised by a ContractViolation subclass in src/hilt/errors.py that is not exported, on the precedent of ContextInsufficient and ContextImmutable : the FT reads the banner, node , and a measurement field naming the reading; the developer follows the class name from the log. Nothing protecting the record lives only in tier 3. Tier-3 rules for hilt-check , each mirroring a guard above so the finding reaches the developer's CI before it reaches a station log: Rule Flags Mirrors Status hilt/measurement-name-unique Two measure(...) calls with the same literal name inside one configure or test method. Tier 1: duplicate name. Shipped (#132). hilt/measurement-in-node A measure(...) call, either spelling, inside cleanup , a survey or audit function, a before_each / after_each , or at module scope. Tier 1: outside a node. Shipped (#133). Neither was part of #86; each was raised as its own issue per docs/hilt-check.md ( Adding a rule ) and both now ship. The -> Verdict and hilt/gated-pass rules already cover the gate a developer writes on .in_limits .
