docs.text: HILT — Project Overview ¶ Philosophy: "The act of running a HILT Test is the act of producing irrefutable evidence." "Happy path" scripts work 99% of the time but cause 100% of the line stoppages because they fail ambiguously. HILT forces the SE to handle the "Sad Path" (Infra vs. Hardware vs. Integration) at design time. What It Is ¶ An opinionated manufacturing test framework built in Python (asyncio). It seeks to implement empathetic architecture by addressing SE → tech communication issues upstream via a pit-of-success model. This is the Python port of the TypeScript original ( ../hilt-test-legacy/ , read-only reference). Parity with the original is explicitly not a goal; the contracts are carried forward, the enforcement is stronger. How it does that ¶ HILT gives the SEs a framework that allows them to focus on getting the test right and logging meaningful evidence. It does this by reducing cognitive load on the SE as much as it possibly can. The SE declares their intent and HILT collects and organizes structured evidence. Much like a real hilt test, the act of executing the test is the act of producing evidence. full stop. The SEs capture meaningful information, and the hilt inspector guarantees that a tech is able to turn that data into information at 2am. The HILT Success Metric ¶ A Floor Technician (the "FT" of the source docstrings) can accurately categorize a failure and initiate the correct recovery protocol within 60 seconds of opening the Inspector, without needing to Slack the Software Engineer. The Core Purpose ¶ "We are giving developers the tools they need to give floor operators the tools THEY need, and doing so without additional cognitive load on the developer." Two-level service contract: 1. Framework → Developer : lifecycle guarantees, automatic evidence collection, structured failure signals — developer focuses on test logic, not plumbing. 2. Developer → Floor Technician : clear names, hardware-domain failure messages, scoped artifacts in the inspector tree — tech makes confident judgment calls without escalating to a software engineer. The Primary Beneficiary: Floor Technician ¶ "Floor technicians simultaneously have the biggest impact on the success of our business, and the least control over how it operates" ¶ Typically early-career technology enthusiast. Passionate, capable, but may be operating at the edge of their knowledge. They are the first person to see failures and to make failure category judgment calls. They are the experts on how to handle any given failure mode. The inspector is their primary tool — and also a containment layer preventing them from going places they shouldn't. The station page is docs/floor-technician.md ( Floor Technician guide ): how to read result.json and what to do next, without opening the suite source. The Atom ¶ TestComponent is the irreducible unit of the manufacturing test problem domain. Does not know or care what the DUT is Does not know what stage it's running at Does not know what surrounds it in the composition Only knows: configure → build_suite → cleanup A rack-level L11 test is not a different kind of thing — it is more atoms composed together. Leaves, sequences, parallel nodes, and full hardware devices are all instances of TestComponent ; the framework is fractal. A TestComponent is simultaneously a claim about hardware and a procedure for verifying that claim: evidence at scale N−1 becomes a verdict at scale N. The DUT tree and the test tree are one structure. The Chemistry Mental Model ¶ Level Framework Construct Atom TestComponent (leaf via self.test() ) Molecule self.sequence() (ordered, bails on failure), self.parallel() (concurrent, collects all) Organelle TestComponent subclass (encapsulates state + lifecycle, produces atoms via build_suite() ) Organism Full rack/system-level suite Emulsion L10+JBOG/JBOD — two molecules behaving as unified system under test Key property : No level needs to know about the levels above it. Composition is the only coupling mechanism and the framework is contractually obligated to provide it. The Three Terminal States ¶ Every run of a TestComponent resolves to one of three peer states — no silent exits, no hidden fourth category: Pass — the test method returned PASS explicitly, bare or as PASS(evidence) carrying its readings. Cannot accidentally pass: the framework checks isinstance(result, Verdict) , and a Verdict is only obtained by importing PASS or calling it, so a string, a truthy value, or a parsed config cannot forge it. A method that declares its evidence with @evidence(...) cannot pass without carrying it. Fail — the test method raised a TestFailure . Structured articulation of what the hardware did wrong, or (for a plain exception) a loud contract violation signal that the developer didn't model this failure mode. Aborted — no verdict was produced. Two causes: Harness-level: an external integration hook ( before_each / after_each on the run params) threw, halting the run before a verdict could be reached. Node-local: the test method returned anything other than the PASS sentinel — a None fall-through or an explicit wrong value (the string "PASS" included). No verdict exists, so the framework refuses to forge Fail (or Pass) on its behalf. Siblings are unaffected. Peer state to Pass/Fail, NOT a flavor of failure. The node-local Aborted cause is a deliberate deviation from the TypeScript original, which folded a missing verdict into the contract violation/Fail path. The port's position: a contract violation that threw produced information (Fail + violation signal); a method that returned wrong produced nothing, and reporting nothing as a verdict would itself be a quiet lie. The tech's recovery protocol differs for each. A Fail says "check the hardware." An Aborted says "check the harness — the shop-floor DB, the coordinator, the integration layer — or the test method that produced no verdict — not the unit." Collapsing these into one category is exactly what the framework refuses to do. A two-layer bug-guard exists alongside the three terminal states: - ContractViolation — developer contract violation, raised at the lifecycle layer - FrameworkContractViolation — framework internal contract violated (should be unreachable, indicates a bug in the framework itself) Failure Taxonomy ¶ Root causes the framework must make obvious: 1. DUT failed a check — TestFailure from a test method or from configure() → state Fail . A TestFailure from configure() means "the device did not reach a testable state"; whether hardware or infrastructure is the cause is not knowable from code — the human triager decides. 2. Hardware lying — survey artifacts expose mismatch (claimed success vs actual state) 3. Test method contract violation — plain exception from a test method or from configure() → violation signal 4. Integration failure — ExternalIntegrationFailure from before_each / after_each aborts the run. The test may be fine; the harness around it broke (e.g. shopfloor DB unreachable, network congestion). 5. Operator interrupt — OperatorInterrupt from SIGINT/SIGTERM during a live run. The Floor Technician reads that the operator stopped the rack, not that the harness or the DUT failed. A human must always make the final determination. The framework presents evidence clearly enough that the tech can make the call without a software engineer's help. The Temporal Backbone ¶ The log artifact is the authoritative chronological record of a test run. Two complementary views: - Structural (inspector tree): what ran, what passed, what failed, how tests compose - Temporal (log backbone): what happened, in what order, what state at each moment await utils.capture_artifact(artifact) stitches artifacts onto the timeline via structured pointer log entries. The public Artifact value has no file-writing method, so the framework cannot persist evidence without also recording that pointer. Every full run creates one timestamped directory beneath the configured artifact root. Logging nodes stream a human timeline.log and a versioned Inspector timeline.jsonl ; leaves roll into their nearest owning ancestor. Both views are flushed entry by entry, preserving the accepted chronology through interruption. When the root reaches Pass, Fail, or Aborted, the framework atomically writes its versioned RunResult to result.json at that run-directory root. The root timeline's final entry points to the file, so the structural and temporal views remain joined. Timestamp integrity is a system requirement. NTP sync on the test host is not optional. The log backbone is used as a legal instrument in customer disputes ("did failures start before your 2pm firmware push?"). Integration Hooks: The External-World Contract ¶ before_each and after_each on the run params are how HILT composes with the world outside the test framework — shop-floor databases, lab coordinators, audit pipelines, any system that needs a "started" signal before each test and a "finished" signal after. Registered once at the root run() call, fire around every executed test in the tree (fractal dispatch) Throw from either hook → run halts → enclosing node transitions to Aborted Pair invariant : after_each fires even when before_each threw, so "started" and "finished" records stay balanced in the external system. No orphan rows. Hooks receive a narrow context (node name, ancestor chain, scoped logger, env snapshot) — NOT utils.exec or get_shell . The interface encodes "integration hooks don't touch the hardware." When a hook throws, the required end state is for the framework to close every in-flight transport across the whole tree immediately (SSH connections destroyed, subprocesses killed). A 30-minute firmware flash in flight when the integration layer halts must NOT continue to mutate the hardware. This is load-bearing for manufacturing test integrity. The Pit of Success Model ¶ The correct pattern must be the path of least resistance — enforced by API shape, not documentation. HILT is deliberately designed so that the right way to write a test is also the easiest way. The framework uses runtime enforcement, import-time structural checks, sensible defaults, and loud signals to guide developers toward honest, evidence-rich tests without requiring them to constantly consult the docs. Here are some of the ways HILT implements this: No pass by default — test methods must explicitly return PASS , or PASS(evidence) with the readings that prove it. Reaching the end of the method without doing so is a missing verdict (node-local Aborted); raising a plain exception is a developer contract violation. A method that declares its evidence with @evidence(...) cannot pass without carrying it. Even internal implementations like TestSequence explicitly model the passing condition as (all tests ran AND all tests passed) — it does not silently pass if nothing threw. Setup is constrained to configure() — All infrastructure wiring, readiness checks, and context creation must happen in configure() . The framework merges the return value into utils.ctx for the rest of the lifecycle and all descendants, and ctx is read-only from then on: inputs come in through configure, readings go out with the verdict. This prevents hidden state coupling and makes the data flow explicit. Unmodeled failure modes are loud — Raising anything other than a TestFailure (or subclass) from a test method produces a clear "CONTRACT VIOLATION" message. The framework refuses to let an unhandled error silently become a pass. use_shell() auto-wires execution routing — Calling utils.use_shell() in configure() automatically rebinds utils.exec to route through the SSH connection. Child tests and descendants inherit the routing with zero extra code. The SE never has to manually thread SSH interfaces. Composition takes bound methods directly — self.test("name", self._my_method) works with a plain bound method reference. No wrapping, no binding ceremony. Sensible defaults reduce boilerplate — self.test("name", self._my_method) defaults to discrete_log_file=False , so its logs automatically roll up into the parent. This gives you one log per logical abstraction instead of one log per screw . Survey and audit hooks belong in the constructor — Registering them only in __init__ makes them part of the test's stable identity (visible on the class and consistent across runs). wait_for() requires intent — The looking_for parameter is mandatory and becomes the primary diagnostic string when a timeout occurs. This nudges developers to write human-readable failure messages. Import-time structural enforcement — a tier the TypeScript original never had. __init_subclass__ on TestComponent verifies at class definition (import time, before any hardware is touched) that the subclass is structurally sound: required lifecycle methods present and async, sealed internals ( main , run , _run_lifecycle , the _safe_* family) not overridden. A malformed test refuses to import; it can never reach the floor. These constraints are not restrictions — they are guardrails that make it difficult to write ambiguous or incomplete tests while making the correct patterns feel natural. Why HILT Rejects "Pass by Default" ¶ Most test frameworks treat "the test reached the end without throwing an error" as a passing result. This is the default mental model the industry has used for decades. HILT rejects it outright. The Quiet Lie ¶ When a test passes by default, it has only proven one thing: It did not encounter any of the failure modes the author happened to think of and write explicit checks for. That is not evidence that the system works. It is a quiet lie — one that accumulates silently until it causes a line stoppage. HILT provides the guardrails that make it difficult to accidentally ship a test that only appears complete. The same conviction governs what a pass carries: a pass without its declared evidence is not a pass. Cases Where Explicit Pass Modeling Feels Awkward ¶ Here are the situations where forcing an explicit PASS can feel clunky if you are coming from a pass-by-default mentality. In every case below, the job is the same: make the pass condition a readable check the next developer can find and understand. return PASS on its own is syntax, not modeling — the conditional that gates it is where your intent lives, and where hilt-check (the static-analysis tier) will insist it goes. Situation Why It Feels Awkward How to Model the Pass Condition Long-running / soak tests Success = "it didn't crash for 8 hours" Track error count or health samples across the run. if errors == 0 and samples_collected >= expected: return PASS — the conditional names what "healthy for 8 hours" actually means. Event-driven / callback tests Success depends on receiving a callback within time if await wait_for(lambda: callback_fired, looking_for=...): return PASS — the wait returning truthy IS the success condition, gated explicitly. Performance / load tests Success = "p99 latency < 50ms and throughput > 10k req/s" Collect metrics, then: if metrics.p99 < 50 and metrics.throughput > 10_000: return PASS — both thresholds named in code, not just in your head. Fuzzing / property-based tests Success is probabilistic ("no counterexample found in 10,000 runs") if iterations_completed == 10_000 and not counterexamples: return PASS — both halves matter : you ran the full budget AND found nothing. Best-effort / smoke tests "It's okay if some optional checks fail" Define the threshold as a variable then if critical_checks_passed: return PASS . The next reader sees the threshold immediately. Non-deterministic external systems Success depends on flaky third-party behavior After retries: if last_attempt_succeeded: return PASS . The retry loop models the flake tolerance; the final conditional models the verdict. Why This Matters to Floor Technicians ¶ Floor Technicians are the primary consumers of everything you produce. They are the ones who will open the Inspector at 2am when a station is down. They need to answer three questions in under 60 seconds: What actually happened? Is this a hardware problem, a test problem, or an infrastructure problem? What should I do next? Pass-by-default tests make all three questions harder. The tech is left guessing at your intent, debugging ambiguous results, and sometimes having to escalate because the evidence is unclear. HILT is built so that the evidence a tech needs is produced automatically and presented clearly — without requiring them to read your source code or understand your design intent. What HILT Demands ¶ The three-tier enforcement stack ¶ HILT does not merely prefer explicit passes — it rejects implicit ones at every tier of the enforcement stack: Tier Mechanism Enforces 1 Runtime IoC wrapping (the child-boundary in lifecycle.py ) Verdict contract, failure taxonomy, lifecycle order — can never be bypassed 2 Import-time structural checks ( __init_subclass__ ) Subclass shape, sealed internals — fires before hardware is touched 3 Static analysis ( hilt-check ) Declarative syntax: pure build_suite , gated PASS , immutable-self idiom Rule: nothing that protects hardware or verdict integrity may live only in tier 3. In the runtime contract: test methods must return the PASS sentinel explicitly. Reaching the end without doing so produces no verdict — the node renders Aborted, never Pass. In internal implementations: even when all conditions are met (as in TestSequence ), the framework still performs an explicit check and refuses to silently pass. At the static-analysis level: returning PASS outside of an if condition is surfaced as a lint error — the framework wants you to model your success condition deliberately. This is more work up front. It forces you to think about what "success" actually looks like with the same rigor you apply to failure modes. In return, you get tests that mean what they say, clear failure categorization, and automatic structured evidence that a floor technician can trust. Where things live ¶ The concepts above are carried by the modules under src/hilt . Each line says what the module is for, not what it contains; the contracts themselves are stated once, in contracts.md and the pages linked from it. Module What it is for __init__.py The public surface: hilt.__all__ is the documented API ( api.md ); every other name in the package is internal. base.py The atom: TestComponent , the one node every suite is composed from, and the framework-owned lifecycle that runs it. lifecycle.py Tier 1, the kernel of trust: the child boundary that turns what a test method returns into one of the three terminal states. verdict.py The non-forgeable PASS sentinel and the Verdict a test method hands back. errors.py The failure taxonomy: which exception means Fail, which means Aborted, and who is being told. utils.py The per-node surface authored code is handed: exec, ctx, env, logging, measurements, hook registration. evidence.py @evidence : the readings a test method promises to carry with its PASS . measurement.py Parametric measurements: a number with a unit and limits, recorded beside the verdict ( measurements.md ). run_data.py The JSON-safe view of ctx and verdict evidence that reaches the run record. results.py The immutable evidence of a run and its JSON boundary to the Inspector ( inspector-json.md ). timeline.py The temporal backbone: the durable per-node records that are a run's authoritative chronology. artifacts.py Point-in-time captures and their framework-owned persistence. hooks.py The integration hooks (surveys, audits, before_each / after_each ) and the deliberately narrow contexts they see. executor.py The host-side execution choke point every blocking call passes through. routing.py Topology-aware exec routing: which hop a node's utils.exec travels through. remote.py The remote transport contract the concrete transports implement. ssh.py The SSH transport. mock.py The in-process transport for self-tests: no hardware, no SSH. arp.py MAC-to-IP resolution over the node's current exec route. device_api.py The Device API (CoAP/HTTP) contract: resource requests, not an exec subclass ( hil/device-api.md ). junit.py The JUnit XML reporter over the run record, for CI systems that read that format ( junit-xml.md ). cli.py The hilt command line: run , new , inspect ( hilt-run.md , hilt-new.md , inspector.md ). scaffold.py Writes a gated- PASS suite and its self-test from a class name, so a new suite starts inside the pit of success. inspector_*.py (ten modules) The Floor Technician's Inspector, split reader / model / view. Readers ( inspector_json , inspector_run , inspector_timeline , inspector_artifacts ) load saved evidence and execute nothing; models ( inspector_tree , inspector_selection , inspector_artifact_navigation ) turn it into rows and cursors; views ( inspector_timeline_view , inspector_artifact_view , inspector_app ) render and forward keys, deciding nothing.

docs.text: Root causes the framework must make obvious: 1. DUT failed a check — TestFailure from a test method or from configure() → state Fail . A TestFailure from configure() means "the device did not reach a testable state"; whether hardware or infrastructure is the cause is not knowable from code — the human triager decides. 2. Hardware lying — survey artifacts expose mismatch (claimed success vs actual state) 3. Test method contract violation — plain exception from a test method or from configure() → violation signal 4. Integration failure — ExternalIntegrationFailure from before_each / after_each aborts the run. The test may be fine; the harness around it broke (e.g. shopfloor DB unreachable, network congestion). 5. Operator interrupt — OperatorInterrupt from SIGINT/SIGTERM during a live run. The Floor Technician reads that the operator stopped the rack, not that the harness or the DUT failed. A human must always make the final determination. The framework presents evidence clearly enough that the tech can make the call without a software engineer's help.
docs.title: Failure Taxonomy

docs.text: The log artifact is the authoritative chronological record of a test run. Two complementary views: - Structural (inspector tree): what ran, what passed, what failed, how tests compose - Temporal (log backbone): what happened, in what order, what state at each moment await utils.capture_artifact(artifact) stitches artifacts onto the timeline via structured pointer log entries. The public Artifact value has no file-writing method, so the framework cannot persist evidence without also recording that pointer. Every full run creates one timestamped directory beneath the configured artifact root. Logging nodes stream a human timeline.log and a versioned Inspector timeline.jsonl ; leaves roll into their nearest owning ancestor. Both views are flushed entry by entry, preserving the accepted chronology through interruption. When the root reaches Pass, Fail, or Aborted, the framework atomically writes its versioned RunResult to result.json at that run-directory root. The root timeline's final entry points to the file, so the structural and temporal views remain joined. Timestamp integrity is a system requirement. NTP sync on the test host is not optional. The log backbone is used as a legal instrument in customer disputes ("did failures start before your 2pm firmware push?").
docs.title: The Temporal Backbone

docs.text: before_each and after_each on the run params are how HILT composes with the world outside the test framework — shop-floor databases, lab coordinators, audit pipelines, any system that needs a "started" signal before each test and a "finished" signal after. Registered once at the root run() call, fire around every executed test in the tree (fractal dispatch) Throw from either hook → run halts → enclosing node transitions to Aborted Pair invariant : after_each fires even when before_each threw, so "started" and "finished" records stay balanced in the external system. No orphan rows. Hooks receive a narrow context (node name, ancestor chain, scoped logger, env snapshot) — NOT utils.exec or get_shell . The interface encodes "integration hooks don't touch the hardware." When a hook throws, the required end state is for the framework to close every in-flight transport across the whole tree immediately (SSH connections destroyed, subprocesses killed). A 30-minute firmware flash in flight when the integration layer halts must NOT continue to mutate the hardware. This is load-bearing for manufacturing test integrity.
docs.title: Integration Hooks: The External-World Contract

docs.text: The correct pattern must be the path of least resistance — enforced by API shape, not documentation. HILT is deliberately designed so that the right way to write a test is also the easiest way. The framework uses runtime enforcement, import-time structural checks, sensible defaults, and loud signals to guide developers toward honest, evidence-rich tests without requiring them to constantly consult the docs. Here are some of the ways HILT implements this: No pass by default — test methods must explicitly return PASS , or PASS(evidence) with the readings that prove it. Reaching the end of the method without doing so is a missing verdict (node-local Aborted); raising a plain exception is a developer contract violation. A method that declares its evidence with @evidence(...) cannot pass without carrying it. Even internal implementations like TestSequence explicitly model the passing condition as (all tests ran AND all tests passed) — it does not silently pass if nothing threw. Setup is constrained to configure() — All infrastructure wiring, readiness checks, and context creation must happen in configure() . The framework merges the return value into utils.ctx for the rest of the lifecycle and all descendants, and ctx is read-only from then on: inputs come in through configure, readings go out with the verdict. This prevents hidden state coupling and makes the data flow explicit. Unmodeled failure modes are loud — Raising anything other than a TestFailure (or subclass) from a test method produces a clear "CONTRACT VIOLATION" message. The framework refuses to let an unhandled error silently become a pass. use_shell() auto-wires execution routing — Calling utils.use_shell() in configure() automatically rebinds utils.exec to route through the SSH connection. Child tests and descendants inherit the routing with zero extra code. The SE never has to manually thread SSH interfaces. Composition takes bound methods directly — self.test("name", self._my_method) works with a plain bound method reference. No wrapping, no binding ceremony. Sensible defaults reduce boilerplate — self.test("name", self._my_method) defaults to discrete_log_file=False , so its logs automatically roll up into the parent. This gives you one log per logical abstraction instead of one log per screw . Survey and audit hooks belong in the constructor — Registering them only in __init__ makes them part of the test's stable identity (visible on the class and consistent across runs). wait_for() requires intent — The looking_for parameter is mandatory and becomes the primary diagnostic string when a timeout occurs. This nudges developers to write human-readable failure messages. Import-time structural enforcement — a tier the TypeScript original never had. __init_subclass__ on TestComponent verifies at class definition (import time, before any hardware is touched) that the subclass is structurally sound: required lifecycle methods present and async, sealed internals ( main , run , _run_lifecycle , the _safe_* family) not overridden. A malformed test refuses to import; it can never reach the floor. These constraints are not restrictions — they are guardrails that make it difficult to write ambiguous or incomplete tests while making the correct patterns feel natural.
docs.title: The Pit of Success Model

docs.text: Most test frameworks treat "the test reached the end without throwing an error" as a passing result. This is the default mental model the industry has used for decades. HILT rejects it outright.
docs.title: Why HILT Rejects "Pass by Default"

docs.text: When a test passes by default, it has only proven one thing: It did not encounter any of the failure modes the author happened to think of and write explicit checks for. That is not evidence that the system works. It is a quiet lie — one that accumulates silently until it causes a line stoppage. HILT provides the guardrails that make it difficult to accidentally ship a test that only appears complete. The same conviction governs what a pass carries: a pass without its declared evidence is not a pass.
docs.title: The Quiet Lie

docs.text: Here are the situations where forcing an explicit PASS can feel clunky if you are coming from a pass-by-default mentality. In every case below, the job is the same: make the pass condition a readable check the next developer can find and understand. return PASS on its own is syntax, not modeling — the conditional that gates it is where your intent lives, and where hilt-check (the static-analysis tier) will insist it goes. Situation Why It Feels Awkward How to Model the Pass Condition Long-running / soak tests Success = "it didn't crash for 8 hours" Track error count or health samples across the run. if errors == 0 and samples_collected >= expected: return PASS — the conditional names what "healthy for 8 hours" actually means. Event-driven / callback tests Success depends on receiving a callback within time if await wait_for(lambda: callback_fired, looking_for=...): return PASS — the wait returning truthy IS the success condition, gated explicitly. Performance / load tests Success = "p99 latency < 50ms and throughput > 10k req/s" Collect metrics, then: if metrics.p99 < 50 and metrics.throughput > 10_000: return PASS — both thresholds named in code, not just in your head. Fuzzing / property-based tests Success is probabilistic ("no counterexample found in 10,000 runs") if iterations_completed == 10_000 and not counterexamples: return PASS — both halves matter : you ran the full budget AND found nothing. Best-effort / smoke tests "It's okay if some optional checks fail" Define the threshold as a variable then if critical_checks_passed: return PASS . The next reader sees the threshold immediately. Non-deterministic external systems Success depends on flaky third-party behavior After retries: if last_attempt_succeeded: return PASS . The retry loop models the flake tolerance; the final conditional models the verdict.
docs.title: Cases Where Explicit Pass Modeling Feels Awkward

docs.text: Floor Technicians are the primary consumers of everything you produce. They are the ones who will open the Inspector at 2am when a station is down. They need to answer three questions in under 60 seconds: What actually happened? Is this a hardware problem, a test problem, or an infrastructure problem? What should I do next? Pass-by-default tests make all three questions harder. The tech is left guessing at your intent, debugging ambiguous results, and sometimes having to escalate because the evidence is unclear. HILT is built so that the evidence a tech needs is produced automatically and presented clearly — without requiring them to read your source code or understand your design intent.
docs.title: Why This Matters to Floor Technicians

docs.text: HILT does not merely prefer explicit passes — it rejects implicit ones at every tier of the enforcement stack: Tier Mechanism Enforces 1 Runtime IoC wrapping (the child-boundary in lifecycle.py ) Verdict contract, failure taxonomy, lifecycle order — can never be bypassed 2 Import-time structural checks ( __init_subclass__ ) Subclass shape, sealed internals — fires before hardware is touched 3 Static analysis ( hilt-check ) Declarative syntax: pure build_suite , gated PASS , immutable-self idiom Rule: nothing that protects hardware or verdict integrity may live only in tier 3. In the runtime contract: test methods must return the PASS sentinel explicitly. Reaching the end without doing so produces no verdict — the node renders Aborted, never Pass. In internal implementations: even when all conditions are met (as in TestSequence ), the framework still performs an explicit check and refuses to silently pass. At the static-analysis level: returning PASS outside of an if condition is surfaced as a lint error — the framework wants you to model your success condition deliberately. This is more work up front. It forces you to think about what "success" actually looks like with the same rigor you apply to failure modes. In return, you get tests that mean what they say, clear failure categorization, and automatic structured evidence that a floor technician can trust.
docs.title: The three-tier enforcement stack

docs.text: The concepts above are carried by the modules under src/hilt . Each line says what the module is for, not what it contains; the contracts themselves are stated once, in contracts.md and the pages linked from it. Module What it is for __init__.py The public surface: hilt.__all__ is the documented API ( api.md ); every other name in the package is internal. base.py The atom: TestComponent , the one node every suite is composed from, and the framework-owned lifecycle that runs it. lifecycle.py Tier 1, the kernel of trust: the child boundary that turns what a test method returns into one of the three terminal states. verdict.py The non-forgeable PASS sentinel and the Verdict a test method hands back. errors.py The failure taxonomy: which exception means Fail, which means Aborted, and who is being told. utils.py The per-node surface authored code is handed: exec, ctx, env, logging, measurements, hook registration. evidence.py @evidence : the readings a test method promises to carry with its PASS . measurement.py Parametric measurements: a number with a unit and limits, recorded beside the verdict ( measurements.md ). run_data.py The JSON-safe view of ctx and verdict evidence that reaches the run record. results.py The immutable evidence of a run and its JSON boundary to the Inspector ( inspector-json.md ). timeline.py The temporal backbone: the durable per-node records that are a run's authoritative chronology. artifacts.py Point-in-time captures and their framework-owned persistence. hooks.py The integration hooks (surveys, audits, before_each / after_each ) and the deliberately narrow contexts they see. executor.py The host-side execution choke point every blocking call passes through. routing.py Topology-aware exec routing: which hop a node's utils.exec travels through. remote.py The remote transport contract the concrete transports implement. ssh.py The SSH transport. mock.py The in-process transport for self-tests: no hardware, no SSH. arp.py MAC-to-IP resolution over the node's current exec route. device_api.py The Device API (CoAP/HTTP) contract: resource requests, not an exec subclass ( hil/device-api.md ). junit.py The JUnit XML reporter over the run record, for CI systems that read that format ( junit-xml.md ). cli.py The hilt command line: run , new , inspect ( hilt-run.md , hilt-new.md , inspector.md ). scaffold.py Writes a gated- PASS suite and its self-test from a class name, so a new suite starts inside the pit of success. inspector_*.py (ten modules) The Floor Technician's Inspector, split reader / model / view. Readers ( inspector_json , inspector_run , inspector_timeline , inspector_artifacts ) load saved evidence and execute nothing; models ( inspector_tree , inspector_selection , inspector_artifact_navigation ) turn it into rows and cursors; views ( inspector_timeline_view , inspector_artifact_view , inspector_app ) render and forward keys, deciding nothing.
docs.title: Where things live

docs.text: Utilities ¶ Logging and the timeline ¶ utils.logger is scoped per node. Every entry is captured in artifacts. discrete_log_file=True (the default on class-based tests) gives the node its own log file; False rolls entries into the parent logger. Inline self.test() bodies default to False . Every full run creates a timestamped directory under the configured artifact root. A logging owner streams both timeline.log for humans and versioned timeline.jsonl for the Inspector, flushing both on every entry. Treat TestComponent.log_path as the authoritative path; directory names are not an API. While a durable timeline is attached, utils.logger.isEnabledFor(...) is true at every level so developer-side guards cannot suppress the chronology. Process logging handlers still apply their own level policy. Point-in-time artifacts ¶ Construct an immutable Artifact and pass it to utils.capture_artifact() . The method persists the JSON artifact under HILT_ARTIFACT_ROOT , then emits a structured pointer through the same scoped logger that records the surrounding test events. Artifact deliberately has no write() method: a file without its pointer would be absent from the chronology. from hilt import Artifact snapshot = Artifact( name="pre-flash", type="hardware-survey", data={"firmware": "2.4.1", "healthy": True} ) artifact_path = await utils.capture_artifact(snapshot) Names and types accept letters, numbers, dashes, and underscores. Payloads must be JSON serializable. Capture is async, never overwrites, and returns the absolute path recorded in the pointer entry. RunResult navigation ¶ Every RunResult carries the node's position in the tree: ancestor_names: list[str] , root-to-this inclusive. Use for programmatic aggregation (DB keys, leaf identity). bread_crumbs: str , "/".join(ancestor_names) precomputed. Use for display, log lines, error messages. summary_tree: SummaryTreeNode , a snapshot of this node's subtree at completion, so an integrator can reconstruct the full Inspector tree from the root's RunResult alone. The versioned payload is defined in inspector-json.md . A full run() also persists the root payload as result.json in the run's artifact directory. Suites consume the returned RunResult when they need the live value; they never write the canonical Inspector file themselves. ArpResolver: MAC to IP ¶ Create one via utils.get_arp_resolver() in configure() , call resolve() , and return both the resolved data and the resolver into ctx. Test methods read the IP and the resolver from utils.ctx . arp.ping(utils) checks reachability. arp.reacquire(utils) after anything that may change the IP (reboot, flash, DHCP churn) returns the new address and the resolver remembers it, so a later ping dials the address it last resolved while ctx stays as configure() left it. Carry the new address as evidence on the verdict if the Floor Technician should see it. ArpResolutionFailure is not a TestFailure . Catch it in configure and re-raise as TestFailure so a missing ARP entry is a verdict. Uncaught, it is a developer bug: the suite did not model the failure mode. arp = utils.get_arp_resolver(mac=self._mac) try: resolved = await arp.resolve() except ArpResolutionFailure as error: raise TestFailure( f"{error.mac} did not appear on the network", error.mac, error.host ) from error return {**resolved, "arp": arp} The resolver is scoped to the node's current exec route and its cache is keyed by the routing label, so a device composed under a gateway resolves through the hop with no change to the device's code. hilt run ...::DutDevice reads the test host's ARP table; hilt run ...::Gateway runs the same class through the hop. See examples/networked_device.py . SSH: use_shell and get_shell ¶ use_shell answers "where does utils.exec go": it rebinds the routing for this node and its descendants. get_shell hands you an additional interface without touching the routing. Both are framework-managed; no cleanup() override is needed, and the shell is disconnected after the post-cleanup survey. Open the device's shell in configure() with use_shell when one connection must be shared across all of the device's leaves. See examples/remote_device_ssh.py . The pi-hole dogfood suite ( examples/pi_hole_server.py ) is the same class-owned hop plus phase-boundary surveys that tail service logs for the Floor Technician. Tunneling ¶ Pass the Shell an earlier get_shell() returned as the via argument to the next one to tunnel the new connection through it. jump = await utils.get_shell(host=jump_host, username=jump_user) target = await utils.get_shell(host=target_host, username=target_user, via=jump) See examples/ssh_tunneling.py . Serial console: use_serial and get_serial ¶ use_serial(device=...) is use_shell(host=...) for a console reached by its device path: it opens the port, binds utils.exec to it for this node and its descendants, and the framework closes the port after the post-cleanup survey and from the abort sweep. get_serial(device=...) hands you an additional console without touching the routing. Both return a Shell ; use_serial() with no arguments reads the active route from any slot, and the declaring form is admitted only in configure() , under the same ContractViolation as use_shell . No cleanup() override is needed and no transport is imported. async def configure(self, utils: TestUtils) -> dict[str, Any]: await utils.use_serial( device=utils.env.require("SERIAL_DEVICE"), baud=utils.env.int("SERIAL_BAUD", default=115200), ) return {} The line settings are the transport's: prompt (a regex; None is a bare POSIX prompt), login_prompt / password_prompt with username / password for a console that logs in, login_timeout for connect, prompt_timeout for how long one exec waits for the prompt before settling exit_code == -1 with the text so far as evidence. A console's stderr is transport-generated only ( "prompt timeout" , "transport closed" ); everything the DUT writes lands in stdout . The contract is docs/hil/serial.md . A console behind a hop (a console server, a Pi with a USB-UART) is the same call: pass an SSH Shell as via , or declare use_shell(host=...) on the parent and let the console inherit the route. The device path then names a node on the hop box and the bytes bridge through it ( bridge_command overrides the default stty + cat bridge). A serial console accepts no other kind of hop; passing one is a TypeError naming the call. The policy-only shapes ( inherit=False , propagate=False ) belong to use_shell . pyserial-asyncio is the hilt-core[serial] extra; a local open without it raises ModuleNotFoundError naming the install. Device API: CoAP and HTTP ¶ A device API is not exec with a URL. Open a session from configure() with utils.get_http or utils.get_coap , then request a typed DeviceRequest . The response's status is data; HTTP 4xx/5xx is not an exception. Catch DeviceApiOperationFailure when the transfer itself did not complete (timeout, refused connection) and model it as a TestFailure . Retries default to zero and each declared attempt is logged. POST refuses retry unless retry_non_idempotent=True . Attempt logs keep header names and withhold every value unless the author lists that name in evidence_headers . Abort closes the session; it does not invent a shutdown PUT. api = await utils.get_http(base_url="https://dut.local") response = await api.request(DeviceRequest(method="GET", path="/whoami")) if response.status != 200: raise TestFailure("whoami rejected", 200, response.status) return PASS({"status": response.status}) The backends stay off the public surface, the way SshInterface does. wait_for ¶ looking_for is required and must be plain language: it is the Floor Technician's primary diagnostic string when a wait times out. Both placements raise TestFailure ; where the call sits decides what the timeout means, and that is a lifecycle question answered on the idioms page. The call returns the predicate's truthy value ( True stays True ), so a claim that needs the observation returns it from the predicate instead of writing into a closure. The runnable examples/wait_for_patterns.py shows both placements and how polling observations flow through scoped logs, surveys, artifacts, run_data , and the root summary_tree without another evidence API. utils.exec ¶ Never throws. Returns stdout , stderr , and exit_code ; output is bounded and truncation is recorded as evidence. Where it lands is the parent's decision (idioms, root 4).

docs.text: HIL interface design notes ¶ Phase 9 gives each hardware-in-the-loop interface its own contract, written to the same diligence as docs/contracts.md , and signed by Ty before any implementation begins. This page states the three standing rulings that govern every note below once, so each note can cite them instead of repeating them. The three rulings ¶ New contracts, not exec subclasses. exec is a command contract: a string goes in, an ExecResult comes out, and a non-zero exit is data for the test method to judge. A GPIO pin level, a PWM duty cycle, a CAN frame, an I2C/SPI transaction, and a CoAP/HTTP resource are not commands — none of them fit the shape of "run this string and collect stdout/stderr/exit_code." Coercing one into exec would either lose information (a frame is not text) or invite the test author to shell out to a protocol library instead of calling a typed method. Each interface below gets its own contract, in the same shape as docs/contracts.md : a named contract, the framework's obligation, the developer's obligation, and the consequence of getting it wrong. The framework owns lifecycle and hooks, unforked. Connected-flag ownership, the idempotent cancel_in_flight halt, before_each / after_each dispatch and the pair invariant, use_survey / use_audit asymmetry (survey swallows, audit does not), and the In-Flight Termination Contract belong to src/hilt/lifecycle.py , src/hilt/hooks.py , and the transport base in src/hilt/remote.py . A new interface contract governs transfer, error taxonomy, timing, and safe-state for its own protocol — it does not reopen how the framework sequences configure → build_suite → cleanup , how a hook pair fires, or how a hard abort reaches a resource. docs.text: Design note: CAN bus interface contract ¶ Status: SIGNED — Ty approved this note in !128 on 2026-09-09; recorded on #95 A CAN frame is not a command string. This note states the transfer, filter, bus-off, timing, and silent-bus obligations that make a controller fit HILT's existing lifecycle. The three HIL rulings govern it. Ty's approval of the actual note signs the obligations below. Implementation requires its own approved issue and Zavala's review under API stability . All names below ( CanInterface , CanFrame , CanFilter , CanBusOff , CanOperationFailure , MockCan , and the method names) are provisional. This note adds no public Python name and changes no stored record. The legacy framework and language server supply no CAN behavior to carry forward; the migration context is the preserved lifecycle and evidence contracts, with a new hardware contract for Ty to judge. Why not an exec subclass ¶ A CAN frame has an arbitration identifier, an extended-id flag, a remote flag, and a payload of bytes. None of that is a shell command. Forcing frames through exec would mean either shelling out to cansend / candump (lossy, racy, and blind to bus-off) or smuggling a controller inside a RemoteInterface subclass that answers _exec with a fake dialect — exactly the parallel-lifecycle-in-disguise ruling 1 forbids. A frame that has been stringified has already lost the identifier width, the ACK, and the error counters. CanInterface is its own ABC, structurally parallel to RemoteInterface ( src/hilt/remote.py ) and to the signed GpioInterface : it owns connect / disconnect / cancel_in_flight in the same shape, and adds frame-shaped operations in place of exec . The CAN Frame Transfer Contract ¶ Framework obligation: Present CAN as its own typed interface under HIL ruling 1. CanInterface is not an exec subclass and does not change where utils.exec routes. A handle is bound to one controller, one bitrate (or bitrate pair, for a backend that also speaks CAN FD), and a declared payload ceiling before it can send or receive. A provisional CanFrame carries arbitration_id (non-negative int), extended (11-bit vs 29-bit), rtr (remote transmission request), and data ( bytes ). Classic CAN admits 0–8 data bytes. A CAN-FD backend declares a larger ceiling (up to 64) and a bitrate switch; it does not earn a second interface or a second lifecycle. Reject a negative id, an id that does not fit the declared width, a payload longer than the ceiling, a non- bytes payload, and a remote frame that also carries data, at the call site, before the controller is touched. send(frame) places one data or remote frame on the wire and waits for the on-bus ACK bit. That ACK is evidence that a receiver on the bus acknowledged the frame. It is not evidence that the DUT parsed it, acted on it, or is even the node that ACKed. A send that the controller cannot represent is refused; a send the bus does not ACK within the backend's declared transmit ceiling is an operational failure, not a forged success. The interface does not retry. receive(deadline=...) returns the next frame that passes this handle's declared filters, or fails if none arrives before the deadline. The deadline is positive and finite seconds; booleans and non-finite values are refused. There is no GPIO-style stability window: a CAN frame is atomic. A timeout does not invent a frame, does not return empty data with a sentinel id, and does not raise TestFailure — see the failure vocabulary. Software matching on top of hardware filters is allowed; dropping a frame the hardware already accepted is not a protocol error. One in-flight send and one in-flight receive per handle. A second send or receive is refused while one is active; it is not queued to surprise the next lifecycle phase. Framework termination takes precedence over this admission rule. Each operation records the requested frame (id, flags, payload length; payload bytes when they are JSON-safe and within evidence bounds) and whether the controller confirmed the outcome. An unconfirmed send never becomes the last-successful frame in a cache the next test method reads as truth. Developer obligation: Declare the controller, bitrate, payload ceiling, and filters in configure() . Obtain the framework-managed handle through a provisional utils.get_can(...) ; return the handle and static inputs through configure's ctx. Keep self immutable, build_suite() pure, and later ctx reads read-only. Judge the DUT with frames actually received (or with an independent observation), never by treating a successful send ACK as a passing device. Consequence: The Floor Technician can tell the frame the suite asked to put on the wire, whether the bus ACKed it, and what the DUT sent back. A missing ACK cannot quietly become a delivered command in a record that claims otherwise. The CAN Filter Contract ¶ Framework obligation: Acceptance filters are part of the handle's identity, declared before the first receive , not discovered by dumping the bus into the test method. A provisional CanFilter names an arbitration-id base, a mask, and whether it matches standard, extended, or both. Hardware filters are programmed at bring-up. A backend that cannot install the declared set refuses the handle before any traffic is observed, naming the filters it cannot honour. Filters are immutable for the handle's lifetime. Changing the mask mid-run is the CAN instance of flipping a GPIO pin's direction live: TypeError at the call site. A suite that needs a different window opens a different declared handle. An open handle whose filters would accept every frame on a production bus is legal but must be explicit — a wildcard filter is a declaration, not a default. The default with no filters declared is "receive nothing," so an author who forgot to say what they are listening for does not silently subscribe to the whole network. Developer obligation: State the filters that belong to this node. Do not compensate for a missing filter by busy-looping receive and discarding ids in suite code; that turns the test method into a sniffer and hides the contract from the Floor Technician. Consequence: The record shows which ids this node was allowed to see. A pass that depended on a frame the handle was not declared to accept is not reconstructable from the artifacts. The CAN Bus-Off and Recovery Contract ¶ Framework obligation: Bus-off is a controller state, not a DUT verdict. When the transmit error counter crosses the bus-off threshold the controller stops driving the bus. That event is reported as an operational failure ( CanBusOff , a HiltError ) naming the handle and the last confirmed error counters if the backend can read them. Automatic recovery that resumes transmitting during the same run is refused. A controller whose driver auto-recovers in the background would put frames on the wire after the suite, or the abort path, has stopped sending — the CAN instance of a detached PWM ramp. Bring-up may enable a backend's recovery into silent/stopped , never into active TX, unless the suite calls a provisional recover() deliberately. recover() is a new operation, not an implicit retry of the failed send . It is refused while a send or receive is in flight, refused after cancel_in_flight has started, and records whether the controller re-entered the declared active state. Failure to recover is the same operational class, not a TestFailure . Error-passive and warning thresholds, when the backend exposes them, are logged as evidence of controller health. They do not change control flow. Only bus-off (unable to transmit) is a failure of send . Developer obligation: Catch CanBusOff and decide what it means. A DUT that storms the bus, a terminator that fell off, and a second tester fighting this node all produce the same controller state. The framework must not choose among those. Do not treat recover-and-retry inside the test method as a substitute for naming the failure. Consequence: Bus-off cannot masquerade as a green run, and it cannot masquerade as a DUT Fail the author never wrote. The Floor Technician sees a controller that stopped, not a verdict someone else invented. The CAN Safe-State and Timing Contract ¶ Framework obligation: The safe state is silence — no further frames originating from this handle — enforced at the resource by the existing termination sweep. This specializes the signed GPIO ownership and cut rules and the signed PWM disabled-output termination . It introduces no CAN halt signal, event loop, lifecycle runner, or integration hook, and it does not invent a shutdown frame. Register ownership as soon as acquisition can put a frame on the wire, so partial configure() failure cannot orphan a transmitter. Bring-up establishes and confirms the declared silent/stopped state before admitting the first send . An integration-hook failure or operator interrupt silences every open CAN handle. A node deadline silences only resources opened by the bounded subtree, under both fail_after (Fail) and abort_after (node-local Aborted). An inherited controller or borrowed hop remains its owner's resource; unrelated siblings are untouched. cancel_in_flight() is idempotent. It aborts a pending send or receive at the controller, attempts to enter the declared silent state under the backend's latency ceiling, and records whether silence was confirmed. A repeated call cannot resume TX or replay the last frame. A closed handle remains closed; there is no automatic reconnect. The framework does not transmit a "safe" or "shutdown" frame on abort. A DUT that needs a specific last frame gets it from authored cleanup() , which the hard cut does not wait for. Inventing a frame at abort would be a stimulus the suite never declared, written into a record the technician might trust. Transmit ACK ceiling, receive deadline, and bring-up/silence ceiling are each positive finite backend-declared bounds, separate from the node's fail_after / abort_after . An operation timeout names that operation and its ceiling. It does not manufacture the timeout evidence reserved for the winning node clock in the Time Budget Contract . A longer receive wait cannot extend the node clock. A backend whose shared adapter would let one node's silence or filter change starve another owner's handle must refuse the conflicting acquisition before either owner sends. It cannot sacrifice Group Isolation to offer more nodes on one stick. Developer obligation: Select a fixture for which "this node stops transmitting" is the intended safe state. Declare shared adapters honestly. Keep any required shutdown frame in cleanup() ; rely on framework ownership for termination. Never manually sequence another node's configure or cleanup. Consequence: Ending the test stops this node's frames and records what could be confirmed. A technician is never asked to infer bus safety from a disconnected handle, from Pass/Fail/Aborted alone, or from a shutdown frame nobody authored. Lifecycle and hook ownership: unchanged ¶ The HIL lifecycle ruling applies unchanged. Concretely: Bring-up happens the same way use_shell brings up SSH: a configure() call obtains a CanInterface handle (provisionally utils.get_can(...) , mirroring get_shell / get_gpio / get_pwm ), and the framework's existing bookkeeping tracks what this node opened versus what it inherited. Teardown order is the framework's: cancel_in_flight on every opened CanInterface fires as part of the same In-Flight Termination Contract sweep that already closes RemoteInterface transports and silences signed GPIO/PWM resources when RunAbort fires. use_survey / use_audit remain the only hooks a suite registers to observe the bus; a periodic audit that receives a watchdog frame and raises TestFailure on an unexpected payload is the existing audit contract, not a new hook kind. before_each / after_each remain the integrator's narrow context and still cannot touch hardware — a CAN controller is exactly the kind of thing those hooks are barred from reaching. Hardware that needs the controller to run its own concurrent RX loop outside survey/audit, or that cannot honor a hard cancel_in_flight , is a finding for Ty — not a reason to give CAN its own lifecycle. Failure vocabulary ¶ No new terminal state is introduced, and no new exception root. CanOperationFailure and CanBusOff derive from HiltError , not TestFailure , for the same reason GPIO's PinSettleFailure and PWM's PwmOperationFailure do: failure to put a frame on the wire, or a controller that has gone bus-off, does not identify the DUT as the cause. Situation Raised as Terminal state Invalid frame, filter, deadline, or conflicting in-flight use TypeError / ValueError at the call site ContractViolation (Fail, bug: true ) if it escapes Bus does not ACK a send within the transmit ceiling; receive deadline expires with no matching frame; silence cannot be confirmed at bring-up CanOperationFailure (provisional HiltError ) naming the handle, operation, requested frame or filter, and ceiling Fail when the author catches it and states the verdict; a ContractViolation Fail ( bug: true ) when it escapes Controller enters bus-off CanBusOff (provisional HiltError ) As above. Never an automatic DUT Fail Backend cannot reach the adapter at bring-up ConnectionError from the interface's own connect Absorbed the way RemoteInterface connect failures are absorbed today Silence cannot be confirmed during the safe-state sweep No exception; the run is already ending Terminal state unchanged; timeline records the unconfirmed silence, naming the handle. Never a success line Integration hook throws while frames are in flight Framework raises ExternalIntegrationFailure Aborted; run-level halt silences every open CanInterface Operator SIGINT/SIGTERM mid-run Framework raises OperatorInterrupt Aborted; same run-level sweep A node's time budget expires while it holds a handle Framework settles the node per its declared budget fail_after → Fail, abort_after → node-local Aborted; either way only that subtree's handles are silenced Test returns without a verdict Existing MissingVerdict Node-local Aborted. A completed send cannot supply the missing verdict Unknown is represented explicitly. A timed-out receive is not an empty frame. An unconfirmed silence is not a quiet bus. Mock and real backends: one contract, two implementations ¶ The pattern is the one RemoteInterface / MockTransport / SshInterface already proves, and that signed GPIO/PWM reuse: CanInterface is the ABC; a real backend (SocketCAN, a USB-CAN adapter, a vendor SDK) and a MockCan test double both implement the same connect / _send / _receive / _cancel_in_flight methods. Self-tests exercise both against a shared contract suite so a bug in either backend is caught by the same assertions. Required proofs: refuse unrepresentable frames before TX; exclusive in-flight send/receive; immutable filters; wildcard-vs-declared receive; ACK timeout; receive deadline with no invented frame; bus-off stops TX and does not auto-resume; recover() is explicit; partial configure() cannot orphan a transmitter; node cuts leave an independent sibling transmitting; repeated cancel_in_flight cannot replay a frame; unconfirmed silence produces only unconfirmed evidence. MockCan schedules park -style holds analogous to MockTransport.park , so lifecycle tests can abort mid-ACK without hardware. A suite author never constructs either backend directly: utils.get_can(...) resolves to whichever backend the run was configured with. Real-backend tests must verify frames through independent observation (a second SocketCAN interface, a logger); mock ACKs cannot establish that a DUT saw the payload. Evidence ¶ Frames that matter to the verdict travel with it exactly as the Evidence Contract already requires: PASS({"response_id": frame.arbitration_id}) or TestFailure(..., evidence={"response_id": ...}) , declared up front with @evidence(...) when the method promises to carry it. Commanded frames are stimulus, not measurements. A payload that is numeric in the problem domain (RPM on a J1939 PGN, a voltage packed in two bytes) follows whatever protocol issue #85 settled in docs/measurements.md , referenced there rather than restated here. This note neither fills the reserved measurements slot nor decodes anyone's application protocol. Every handle declaration — bitrate, payload ceiling, filters, silent-state — is logged through utils.logger at configuration time, the same way ExecRouting logs a connection's provenance. Sends, receives, bus-off, recover, and silence attempts use that scoped logger to distinguish requested, ACKed, received, interrupted, and unconfirmed outcomes. What the Floor Technician sees ¶ When a handle is silenced, the node's timeline.jsonl (and its timeline.log twin) carries a log entry at the scope of the node that owned it, naming the handle and whether silence was confirmed, immediately before that node's terminal entry — the same temporal-backbone placement the In-Flight Termination Contract already gives a hard-closed SSH transport and that signed GPIO/PWM reuse for idle/disable. The terminal entry is not always Aborted: a run-level halt and an abort_after expiry both settle Aborted, a fail_after expiry settles Fail, and the silence sweep is owed under every one of them. result.json 's summary_tree shows whichever state applies; there is no CAN-specific field, because a safe-state action is evidence of what the framework did to protect the bus, not a verdict of its own. A technician reading the timeline sees why the run ended and — from the log line — that this node stopped transmitting. Where the sweep could not confirm silence, the timeline says exactly that, naming the handle. An unconfirmed silence never leaves a success line behind. Signed decisions recorded on #95 ¶ The draft asks for a ruling on these concrete obligations before implementation: Frames as a typed value (id, extended, rtr, payload bytes), not an exec string; Classic CAN 0–8 bytes, CAN-FD as a backend-declared ceiling under the same contract, not a fork. send confirms the on-bus ACK bit only; a DUT response is a later receive . No silent retry. Filters declared in configure() , immutable for the handle's lifetime; the no-filter default is receive-nothing, not subscribe-everything. Bus-off is a HiltError operational condition; no automatic TX resume during the run; recover() is an explicit later operation. Abort safe-state is silence, not a framework-invented shutdown frame. Authored cleanup() may send a last frame; the hard cut does not wait for it and does not replace it. Shared adapters refuse conflicting ownership when one node's silence would starve another, same Group Isolation posture as signed PWM. The lifecycle, verdict, and evidence contracts above are constraints on that decision. If a required backend cannot satisfy them, the finding belongs on #95 with the affected guarantee named. It does not earn an alternate lifecycle or an exception enforced only by a linter.
