They do not change control flow. Only bus-off (unable to transmit) is a failure of send . Developer obligation: Catch CanBusOff and decide what it means. A DUT that storms the bus, a terminator that fell off, and a second tester fighting this node all produce the same controller state. The framework must not choose among those. Do not treat recover-and-retry inside the test method as a substitute for naming the failure. Consequence: Bus-off cannot masquerade as a green run, and it cannot masquerade as a DUT Fail the author never wrote. The Floor Technician sees a controller that stopped, not a verdict someone else invented.
docs.title: The CAN Bus-Off and Recovery Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: The safe state is silence — no further frames originating from this handle — enforced at the resource by the existing termination sweep. This specializes the signed GPIO ownership and cut rules and the signed PWM disabled-output termination . It introduces no CAN halt signal, event loop, lifecycle runner, or integration hook, and it does not invent a shutdown frame. Register ownership as soon as acquisition can put a frame on the wire, so partial configure() failure cannot orphan a transmitter. Bring-up establishes and confirms the declared silent/stopped state before admitting the first send . An integration-hook failure or operator interrupt silences every open CAN handle. A node deadline silences only resources opened by the bounded subtree, under both fail_after (Fail) and abort_after (node-local Aborted). An inherited controller or borrowed hop remains its owner's resource; unrelated siblings are untouched. cancel_in_flight() is idempotent. It aborts a pending send or receive at the controller, attempts to enter the declared silent state under the backend's latency ceiling, and records whether silence was confirmed. A repeated call cannot resume TX or replay the last frame. A closed handle remains closed; there is no automatic reconnect. The framework does not transmit a "safe" or "shutdown" frame on abort. A DUT that needs a specific last frame gets it from authored cleanup() , which the hard cut does not wait for. Inventing a frame at abort would be a stimulus the suite never declared, written into a record the technician might trust. Transmit ACK ceiling, receive deadline, and bring-up/silence ceiling are each positive finite backend-declared bounds, separate from the node's fail_after / abort_after . An operation timeout names that operation and its ceiling. It does not manufacture the timeout evidence reserved for the winning node clock in the Time Budget Contract . A longer receive wait cannot extend the node clock. A backend whose shared adapter would let one node's silence or filter change starve another owner's handle must refuse the conflicting acquisition before either owner sends. It cannot sacrifice Group Isolation to offer more nodes on one stick. Developer obligation: Select a fixture for which "this node stops transmitting" is the intended safe state. Declare shared adapters honestly. Keep any required shutdown frame in cleanup() ; rely on framework ownership for termination. Never manually sequence another node's configure or cleanup. Consequence: Ending the test stops this node's frames and records what could be confirmed. A technician is never asked to infer bus safety from a disconnected handle, from Pass/Fail/Aborted alone, or from a shutdown frame nobody authored.
docs.title: The CAN Safe-State and Timing Contract

docs.text: The HIL lifecycle ruling applies unchanged. Concretely: Bring-up happens the same way use_shell brings up SSH: a configure() call obtains a CanInterface handle (provisionally utils.get_can(...) , mirroring get_shell / get_gpio / get_pwm ), and the framework's existing bookkeeping tracks what this node opened versus what it inherited. Teardown order is the framework's: cancel_in_flight on every opened CanInterface fires as part of the same In-Flight Termination Contract sweep that already closes RemoteInterface transports and silences signed GPIO/PWM resources when RunAbort fires. use_survey / use_audit remain the only hooks a suite registers to observe the bus; a periodic audit that receives a watchdog frame and raises TestFailure on an unexpected payload is the existing audit contract, not a new hook kind. before_each / after_each remain the integrator's narrow context and still cannot touch hardware — a CAN controller is exactly the kind of thing those hooks are barred from reaching. Hardware that needs the controller to run its own concurrent RX loop outside survey/audit, or that cannot honor a hard cancel_in_flight , is a finding for Ty — not a reason to give CAN its own lifecycle.
docs.title: Lifecycle and hook ownership: unchanged

docs.text: No new terminal state is introduced, and no new exception root. CanOperationFailure and CanBusOff derive from HiltError , not TestFailure , for the same reason GPIO's PinSettleFailure and PWM's PwmOperationFailure do: failure to put a frame on the wire, or a controller that has gone bus-off, does not identify the DUT as the cause. Situation Raised as Terminal state Invalid frame, filter, deadline, or conflicting in-flight use TypeError / ValueError at the call site ContractViolation (Fail, bug: true ) if it escapes Bus does not ACK a send within the transmit ceiling; receive deadline expires with no matching frame; silence cannot be confirmed at bring-up CanOperationFailure (provisional HiltError ) naming the handle, operation, requested frame or filter, and ceiling Fail when the author catches it and states the verdict; a ContractViolation Fail ( bug: true ) when it escapes Controller enters bus-off CanBusOff (provisional HiltError ) As above. Never an automatic DUT Fail Backend cannot reach the adapter at bring-up ConnectionError from the interface's own connect Absorbed the way RemoteInterface connect failures are absorbed today Silence cannot be confirmed during the safe-state sweep No exception; the run is already ending Terminal state unchanged; timeline records the unconfirmed silence, naming the handle. Never a success line Integration hook throws while frames are in flight Framework raises ExternalIntegrationFailure Aborted; run-level halt silences every open CanInterface Operator SIGINT/SIGTERM mid-run Framework raises OperatorInterrupt Aborted; same run-level sweep A node's time budget expires while it holds a handle Framework settles the node per its declared budget fail_after → Fail, abort_after → node-local Aborted; either way only that subtree's handles are silenced Test returns without a verdict Existing MissingVerdict Node-local Aborted. A completed send cannot supply the missing verdict Unknown is represented explicitly. A timed-out receive is not an empty frame. An unconfirmed silence is not a quiet bus.
docs.title: Failure vocabulary

docs.text: The pattern is the one RemoteInterface / MockTransport / SshInterface already proves, and that signed GPIO/PWM reuse: CanInterface is the ABC; a real backend (SocketCAN, a USB-CAN adapter, a vendor SDK) and a MockCan test double both implement the same connect / _send / _receive / _cancel_in_flight methods. Self-tests exercise both against a shared contract suite so a bug in either backend is caught by the same assertions. Required proofs: refuse unrepresentable frames before TX; exclusive in-flight send/receive; immutable filters; wildcard-vs-declared receive; ACK timeout; receive deadline with no invented frame; bus-off stops TX and does not auto-resume; recover() is explicit; partial configure() cannot orphan a transmitter; node cuts leave an independent sibling transmitting; repeated cancel_in_flight cannot replay a frame; unconfirmed silence produces only unconfirmed evidence. MockCan schedules park -style holds analogous to MockTransport.park , so lifecycle tests can abort mid-ACK without hardware. A suite author never constructs either backend directly: utils.get_can(...) resolves to whichever backend the run was configured with. Real-backend tests must verify frames through independent observation (a second SocketCAN interface, a logger); mock ACKs cannot establish that a DUT saw the payload.
docs.title: Mock and real backends: one contract, two implementations

docs.text: Frames that matter to the verdict travel with it exactly as the Evidence Contract already requires: PASS({"response_id": frame.arbitration_id}) or TestFailure(..., evidence={"response_id": ...}) , declared up front with @evidence(...) when the method promises to carry it. Commanded frames are stimulus, not measurements. A payload that is numeric in the problem domain (RPM on a J1939 PGN, a voltage packed in two bytes) follows whatever protocol issue #85 settled in docs/measurements.md , referenced there rather than restated here. This note neither fills the reserved measurements slot nor decodes anyone's application protocol. Every handle declaration — bitrate, payload ceiling, filters, silent-state — is logged through utils.logger at configuration time, the same way ExecRouting logs a connection's provenance. Sends, receives, bus-off, recover, and silence attempts use that scoped logger to distinguish requested, ACKed, received, interrupted, and unconfirmed outcomes.
docs.title: Evidence

docs.text: When a handle is silenced, the node's timeline.jsonl (and its timeline.log twin) carries a log entry at the scope of the node that owned it, naming the handle and whether silence was confirmed, immediately before that node's terminal entry — the same temporal-backbone placement the In-Flight Termination Contract already gives a hard-closed SSH transport and that signed GPIO/PWM reuse for idle/disable. The terminal entry is not always Aborted: a run-level halt and an abort_after expiry both settle Aborted, a fail_after expiry settles Fail, and the silence sweep is owed under every one of them. result.json 's summary_tree shows whichever state applies; there is no CAN-specific field, because a safe-state action is evidence of what the framework did to protect the bus, not a verdict of its own. A technician reading the timeline sees why the run ended and — from the log line — that this node stopped transmitting. Where the sweep could not confirm silence, the timeline says exactly that, naming the handle. An unconfirmed silence never leaves a success line behind.
docs.title: What the Floor Technician sees

docs.text: The draft asks for a ruling on these concrete obligations before implementation: Frames as a typed value (id, extended, rtr, payload bytes), not an exec string; Classic CAN 0–8 bytes, CAN-FD as a backend-declared ceiling under the same contract, not a fork. send confirms the on-bus ACK bit only; a DUT response is a later receive . No silent retry. Filters declared in configure() , immutable for the handle's lifetime; the no-filter default is receive-nothing, not subscribe-everything. Bus-off is a HiltError operational condition; no automatic TX resume during the run; recover() is an explicit later operation. Abort safe-state is silence, not a framework-invented shutdown frame. Authored cleanup() may send a last frame; the hard cut does not wait for it and does not replace it. Shared adapters refuse conflicting ownership when one node's silence would starve another, same Group Isolation posture as signed PWM. The lifecycle, verdict, and evidence contracts above are constraints on that decision. If a required backend cannot satisfy them, the finding belongs on #95 with the affected guarantee named. It does not earn an alternate lifecycle or an exception enforced only by a linter.
docs.title: Signed decisions recorded on #95

docs.text: Design note: Device API (CoAP/HTTP) interface contract ¶ Status: SIGNED — Ty approved this note in !130 on 2026-09-09; recorded on #97 A CoAP or HTTP resource is not a command string. This note states the request and response shape, retry-as-evidence, timing, error taxonomy, and closed-session obligations that make a device API fit HILT's existing lifecycle. The three HIL rulings govern it. Ty's approval of the actual note signs the obligations below. Implementation requires its own approved issue and Zavala's review under API stability . This is the interface most likely to be waved through as "just exec with a URL." It is not. An HTTP call needs its own contract, error taxonomy, and safe-state, same as a pin or a bus. All names below ( DeviceApiInterface , HttpInterface , CoapInterface , DeviceRequest , DeviceResponse , DeviceApiOperationFailure , MockDeviceApi , and the method names) are provisional. This note adds no public Python name and changes no stored record. The legacy CoapInterface is a design reference only — see below. The migration context is the preserved lifecycle and evidence contracts, with a new hardware contract for Ty to judge. Why not an exec subclass ¶ exec is a command contract: a string goes in, an ExecResult comes out, and a non-zero exit is data for the test method to judge. A device-API call is a typed resource operation: method, path, payload bytes, status, headers or CoAP options, and a body. None of that is a shell command. Forcing it through exec would mean either shelling out to curl / wget / the coap CLI (lossy, racy, and blind to in-flight cancellation) or smuggling an HTTP client inside a RemoteInterface subclass that answers _exec with a fake dialect — exactly the parallel-lifecycle-in-disguise ruling 1 forbids. A URL that has been stringified into curl -X POST ... has already lost the status as a first-class value, the header set, whether the body was truncated, and whether the client retried. DeviceApiInterface is its own ABC, structurally parallel to RemoteInterface ( src/hilt/remote.py ) and to the signed GpioInterface / PwmInterface : it owns connect / disconnect / cancel_in_flight in the same shape, and adds request-shaped operations in place of exec . The legacy TypeScript CoapInterface wrapped the coap CLI through utils.exec because the UDP-only node-coap package could not speak coaps+tcp:// (RFC 8323). That was a toolchain constraint, not a contract. This port does not carry the CLI wrapper forward. A backend that can only shell out to curl or coap is a finding for Ty, not the shape of the interface. The Device Request Contract ¶ Framework obligation: Present CoAP and HTTP as one resource-request contract under HIL ruling 1. DeviceApiInterface is not an exec subclass and does not change where utils.exec routes. A handle is bound to one scheme, one base URL, and a declared timing envelope before it can request. HTTP and CoAP share the request/response shape (method, path, payload, status, body). They are not one handle type. An HttpInterface cannot speak CoAP; a CoapInterface cannot follow HTTP redirects. Scheme is identity, fixed for the handle's lifetime: http / https for HTTP, coap / coaps / coaps+tcp for CoAP. Flipping the scheme live is the Device API instance of flipping a GPIO pin's direction. A provisional DeviceRequest carries method (GET, PUT, POST, DELETE; CoAP may add the methods its backend declares), path (appended to the declared base URL, never a second origin), payload ( bytes or absent), protocol options (HTTP headers, CoAP options), and evidence_headers (the set of request header or option names whose values may appear in the attempt log; default empty). For HTTP the name is the field name, matched case-insensitively. For CoAP the name is the registered option name ( Uri-Path , Content-Format ); an option number is not a name and is refused at the call site. PATCH is not in that method set; whether the first backend declares it as a non-idempotent sibling of POST is a decision for Ty below, not a silent widening. Reject a non- bytes payload, a path that is an absolute URL, a method the backend did not declare, and a header or option name that is not a string, at the call site, before the adapter is touched. Booleans are not integers; a dict passed as payload is not a JSON body. The approved convenience on #155 adds keyword-only json=value : serialize once to UTF-8 bytes and default the HTTP Content-Type to application/json , preserving an explicitly supplied content type case-insensitively. Omission sends no JSON; json=None sends null. Combining it with a non- None payload (including empty bytes) is refused, as are unserializable values and non-finite numbers. The wire payload remains bytes, and logs still record lengths, never body contents. A provisional DeviceResponse carries status (an HTTP status integer, or a CoAP code as the dotted string 2.05 — see CoapCode ), protocol options (headers / CoAP options), and body ( bytes ). The wire integer ( class << 5 | detail , so Content is 69 ) stays inside the transport. Issue #156. JSON parsing is a convenience on top of those bytes, not the contract: a body that is not JSON is still a successful transfer of bytes. The interface does not invent an empty body, a 200, or a CoAP 2.05 to stand in for a missing response. Issue #155 adds json() and parse(response_type="json") to decode those bytes explicitly; parse(response_type="yaml") uses yaml.safe_load and requires the optional hilt-core[yaml] extra. Parser errors propagate unchanged, unsupported formats raise ValueError , and a missing YAML extra raises ImportError . Neither method changes status or bytes or interprets a status as a verdict. A malformed body remains a completed transfer. Status is data. HTTP 4xx / 5xx and CoAP 4.xx / 5.xx are fields on the response, the way a non-zero exit_code is a field on ExecResult . The interface does not raise TestFailure because a resource returned 404, and it does not raise because a resource returned 500. The test method judges the status. Transport failure, protocol violation, and timeout are the operational exceptions; a well-formed error response is not one of them. request(req) -> DeviceResponse performs one application-level attempt (see retries below). One handle carries one request at a time, in call order. A request that arrives while another is on the wire waits its turn; it does not collide, and it does not fail. A handle shared by the leaves of a parallel therefore serialises them: the claims stay independent, their requests do not, and a latency measured around request on that handle includes the wait for siblings. A leaf that must measure the DUT alone takes its own handle. The wait is bounded by the node clock, not by the request ceiling, because a sibling ahead in the queue is not the DUT being slow. Framework termination takes precedence over the queue: a handle cancelled or closed while a request waited its turn never sends it (see the closed-session contract below). The only refusal left is re-entrancy — a backend's _exchange calling request on the handle it is already mid-attempt on — and that is a ValueError at the call site, a developer bug, not a queue. Each operation records the requested method, path, payload length, request-header names , whether the adapter confirmed a response, the status if one arrived, and the body length. Request-header values stay out of that record unless the author listed the name in evidence_headers . Response protocol options — HTTP response headers, CoAP response options — are not in that list. Their values are never recorded by the framework; carrying one into evidence is the author's act, the same as a body. evidence_headers does not govern them. An unconfirmed request never becomes the last-successful response in a cache the next test method reads as truth. Unknown is explicit. Developer obligation: Declare the scheme, base URL, and protocol parameters in configure() . Obtain the framework-managed handle through a provisional utils.get_http(...) or utils.get_coap(...) ; return the handle and static inputs through configure's ctx. Keep self immutable, build_suite() pure, and later ctx reads read-only. Judge the DUT with the status and body actually returned (or with an independent observation), never by treating a 2xx as a passing device. Consequence: The Floor Technician can tell which resource was addressed, what was sent, what status came back, and whether the transfer completed. A 404 cannot quietly become a missing payload in a record that claims the call succeeded, and a 200 cannot quietly become a verdict. The Retry-as-Evidence Contract ¶ Framework obligation: A retry is stimulus the DUT saw. Hiding it lies to the Floor Technician. Application-level retries default to zero . A handle that retries without a declaration is refused at the call site. Each declared attempt — including the first — is logged through the scoped logger with attempt index, outcome (response status, operational failure, or cancelled), and delay before the next attempt when one is scheduled. The retry budget is a count of application-level attempts, not a duration. Delay between attempts is positive finite seconds, declared with the count. Booleans and non-finite values are refused. The node's fail_after / abort_after still bounds the whole sequence; a retry loop cannot extend the node clock. Non-idempotent methods (POST, and any other method the backend declares non-idempotent) refuse application retry unless the author sets an explicit retry_non_idempotent=True on that call. GET / PUT / DELETE may retry when a count is declared. The interface does not guess idempotency from the path. Protocol-level reliability is not an application retry. HTTP/TCP retransmits and CoAP CON retransmits belong to the backend's declared request ceiling. CON retransmits that actually go on the wire are counted in the attempt's evidence (the DUT saw them) but they do not consume the application retry budget. A backend whose CON loop cannot be bounded by the request ceiling, or cannot be cut by cancel_in_flight , is a finding for Ty. cancel_in_flight stops the in-flight attempt and the retry loop. A cancelled retry does not start the next attempt. The record names how many attempts ran and that the remainder were not started. One logical request holds the handle's turn from its first attempt to its last. A retry never interleaves with a sibling's request, so the attempt log for one request reads as one request. Developer obligation: Leave retries at zero unless this bench has a named reason to repeat a request. When retries are declared, treat the attempt log as part of the evidence that will be read after a Fail — especially for POST. Do not wrap request() in a suite-owned retry loop to dodge the declaration; that is the same lie with worse artifacts. Consequence: The timeline shows every request the DUT actually received from this handle. A pass that depended on the third try cannot be reconstructed as a single clean GET. The Closed-Session and Timing Contract ¶ Framework obligation: The safe state is a closed session — no further requests originating from this handle — enforced at the resource by the existing termination sweep. This specializes the signed GPIO ownership and cut rules and the signed PWM disabled-output termination . It introduces no Device API halt signal, event loop, lifecycle runner, or integration hook, and it does not invent a shutdown request. Register ownership as soon as acquisition can put a request on the wire, so partial configure() failure cannot orphan a session. Bring-up establishes and confirms the session (TLS handshake, CoAP identity) before admitting the first request . An integration-hook failure or operator interrupt closes every open Device API handle. A node deadline closes only resources opened by the bounded subtree, under both fail_after (Fail) and abort_after (node-local Aborted). An inherited adapter or borrowed hop remains its owner's resource; unrelated siblings are untouched. cancel_in_flight() is idempotent. It aborts the in-flight request at the socket (HTTP: cancel the stream and close the connection; CoAP: stop CON retransmits; a RST or connection-close is the protocol cancel, analogous to I2C STOP, not a resource write), attempts the closed state under the backend's latency ceiling, and records whether close was confirmed. A repeated call cannot start a new request or replay the last one. A closed handle remains closed; there is no automatic reconnect. A request waiting its turn behind the aborted one is not sent. When its turn comes on a cancelled or closed handle it fails with DeviceApiOperationFailure naming that the handle was cancelled or closed while the request was queued — an operational failure the author catches and models as a verdict, never a ValueError and never a silent request on a dead session. disconnect() treats waiters the same way. The framework does not transmit a "safe" PUT, DELETE, or CoAP action on abort. A DUT that needs a specific last request gets it from authored cleanup() , which the hard cut does not wait for. Inventing a /shutdown write at abort would be a stimulus the suite never declared, written into a record the technician might trust. Request ceiling (including protocol-level CON/TCP reliability), retry delay, bring-up/close ceiling, and the node's fail_after / abort_after are separate clocks. An operation timeout names that operation and its ceiling. It does not manufacture the timeout evidence reserved for the winning node clock in the Time Budget Contract . A long poll cannot extend the node clock. The request ceiling starts when the request takes its turn on the handle, not when it was queued: the wait behind a sibling is bounded by the node clock alone. A backend whose shared session would let one node's close starve another owner's in-flight request must refuse the conflicting acquisition before either owner requests. It cannot sacrifice Group Isolation to offer more nodes on one socket. Serialising requests on one handle is not that: the handle has one owner, the node whose configure() opened it, and the leaves queuing on it are that owner's subtree, closed together when that owner's clock expires. Developer obligation: Select a fixture for which "this node stops talking" is the intended safe state. Declare shared sessions honestly. Keep any required shutdown request in cleanup() ; rely on framework ownership for termination. Never manually sequence another node's configure or cleanup. Consequence: Ending the test stops this node's requests and records what could be confirmed. A technician is never asked to infer that a session is idle from Pass/Fail/Aborted alone, or from a DELETE nobody authored. Redirects, credentials, and the legacy action helper ¶ Framework obligation: HTTP redirects are a declared policy, default do not follow . Same-origin follow is an opt-in on the handle. Cross-host follow is refused: a 302 to a second origin is data on the response, not a silent second request, and it must not carry the original credentials. A backend that auto-follows across hosts is refused at bring-up. Authentication material (Bearer tokens, basic passwords, client certificates, CoAP DTLS PSKs) is declared in configure() and never reaches evidence. Provenance names the credential path or slot, never the value — the same containment SSH already proves. URL userinfo in the declared base URL is withheld the same way. Attempt logs keep every request-header name and withhold every value unless the author lists that name in evidence_headers on the DeviceRequest . Default is empty: the safe case costs the author no thought. A secret-name allowlist cannot deliver "never" — X-Device-Token , Api-Key , and the next DUT's favorite all miss it. Matching is case-insensitive for HTTP field names. For CoAP, the name is the registered option name; an option number is not a name and is refused at the call site — a guess that silently matches nothing would look like a working redaction. Opting Authorization in is the author's leak to stop, not a framework rewrite. Response protocol option values are never recorded by the framework. evidence_headers is a request-side opt-in; it does not cover Set-Cookie , WWW-Authenticate , or a CoAP response option. Carrying a response option into evidence is the author's act, the same as a body. Response bodies still go to evidence when the author puts them there; secrets in a body are the author's leak to stop, not a framework rewrite of the payload. TLS / DTLS verification is on by default. Skipping it is a lab-only declaration analogous to SSH skip_host_verification , logged as such at bring-up. The legacy performAction helper (PUT an action id, poll until a K2-specific status set) is application protocol . It is not part of this contract. Authors who need a long-running device action compose request() with the existing wait_for . Porting that helper into DeviceApiInterface would bake one vendor's action DSL into the framework the way decoding a J1939 PGN would bake an application protocol into CAN. Developer obligation: Do not follow redirects in suite code to dodge the handle policy. Do not log tokens. Do not opt a secret request header into evidence_headers unless the Floor Technician is meant to read that value. Do not treat evidence_headers as covering response headers or CoAP response options; those values never enter the attempt log, and putting one in a verdict is the author's act. Do not ask the framework for a perform_action sugar that hides the poll. Consequence: A redirect cannot launder a second origin into a record that still names the declared base URL. An attempt log cannot carry a bearer token off the bench unless the author opted that header in. A Set-Cookie or WWW-Authenticate cannot walk into the attempt log because evidence_headers was assumed to cover the response. A K2 action poll is visible as the requests it actually made. Lifecycle and hook ownership: unchanged ¶ The HIL lifecycle ruling applies unchanged. Concretely: Bring-up happens the same way use_shell brings up SSH: configure() obtains a handle (provisionally utils.get_http(...) / utils.get_coap(...) , mirroring get_shell / get_gpio / get_pwm ), and the framework's bookkeeping tracks what this node opened versus what it inherited. Teardown order is the framework's: cancel_in_flight fires as part of the same In-Flight Termination Contract sweep that already closes RemoteInterface transports and silences signed GPIO/PWM resources. use_survey / use_audit remain the observation hooks. A periodic audit that GETs a health resource and raises TestFailure on an unexpected status or body is the existing audit contract. before_each / after_each remain the integrator's narrow context and still cannot touch hardware. Hardware that needs the client to run its own concurrent receive loop outside survey/audit, that cannot honor a hard cancel_in_flight (a request that keeps running on the device after the socket is cut is the device's problem; a client that cannot cut the socket is a finding), or that requires the CLI-wrapper shape the legacy CoapInterface used, is a finding for Ty — not a reason to give Device API its own lifecycle. Failure vocabulary ¶ No new terminal state is introduced, and no new exception root. DeviceApiOperationFailure derives from HiltError , not TestFailure , for the same reason GPIO's PinSettleFailure and PWM's PwmOperationFailure do: failure to complete a transfer does not identify the DUT as the cause. Situation Raised as Terminal state Invalid method, path, payload, or retry declaration; request re-entered from inside the handle's own in-flight request TypeError / ValueError at the call site ContractViolation (Fail, bug: true ) naming the exception if it escapes A second request while one is on the wire No exception: it waits its turn, logged as queued Whatever verdict the author writes; the measured latency includes the wait Handle cancelled or closed while a request waited its turn DeviceApiOperationFailure naming the handle, method, path, and that it was queued, never sent Fail when the author catches it and states the verdict; a ContractViolation Fail ( bug: true ) when it escapes HTTP 4xx / 5xx or CoAP 4.xx / 5.xx on a well-formed response No exception: status and body are the result Whatever verdict the author writes. The interface does not guess Fail Connection refused, TLS/DTLS handshake failure, protocol violation, request exceeds its ceiling, close cannot be confirmed at bring-up DeviceApiOperationFailure (provisional HiltError ) naming the handle, operation, method, path, and ceiling Fail when the author catches it and states the verdict; a ContractViolation Fail ( bug: true ) when it escapes Backend cannot reach the adapter at bring-up ConnectionError from the interface's own connect Absorbed the way RemoteInterface connect failures are absorbed today Close cannot be confirmed during the safe-state sweep No exception; the run is already ending Terminal state unchanged; timeline records the unconfirmed close, naming the handle. Never a success line Integration hook throws mid-request Framework raises ExternalIntegrationFailure Aborted; run-level halt closes every open handle Operator SIGINT/SIGTERM mid-run Framework raises OperatorInterrupt Aborted; same run-level sweep A node's time budget expires while it holds a handle Framework settles the node per its declared budget fail_after → Fail, abort_after → node-local Aborted; either way only that subtree's handles are closed Test returns without a verdict Existing MissingVerdict Node-local Aborted. A completed request cannot supply the missing verdict Unknown is represented explicitly. A timed-out request is not a 200 with an empty body. An unconfirmed close is not an idle session. Mock and real backends: one contract, two implementations ¶ The pattern is the one RemoteInterface / MockTransport / SshInterface already proves, and that signed GPIO/PWM reuse: DeviceApiInterface is the ABC; HttpInterface and CoapInterface are real backends; MockDeviceApi is the test double. Self-tests exercise mock and real against a shared contract suite so a bug in either backend is caught by the same assertions. Required proofs: refuse a non- bytes payload and an absolute-URL path before the adapter is touched; concurrent requests on one handle run one at a time in call order, and a cancel or close mid-queue fails the waiters as DeviceApiOperationFailure without sending them; a re-entered request is refused rather than deadlocked; status-as-data (4xx is a response, not an exception); retries default to zero and each declared attempt is evidenced; non-idempotent retry refused unless opted in; cancel_in_flight stops the retry loop; redirects do not follow cross-host; request-header values never appear in evidence unless the author opted that name into evidence_headers ; a CoAP option number is refused as an evidence_headers name; response option values never appear in the attempt log; partial configure() cannot orphan a session; node cuts leave a sibling's in-flight request untouched; repeated cancel_in_flight cannot replay a POST; unconfirmed close produces only unconfirmed evidence. MockDeviceApi schedules park -style holds analogous to MockTransport.park , so lifecycle tests can abort mid-request without a server. A suite author never constructs either backend directly: utils.get_http / utils.get_coap resolve to whichever backend the run was configured with. Real-backend tests must verify transfers through independent observation (a second client, a capturing proxy); mock statuses cannot establish that a DUT saw the body. Core install stays dependency-light. HTTP and CoAP clients land as optional extras on the implementation issue; this note does not pick the library. Evidence ¶ Responses that matter to the verdict travel with it exactly as the Evidence Contract already requires: PASS({"status": 200, "whoami": ...}) or TestFailure(..., evidence={"status": 404}) , declared with @evidence(...) when the method promises to carry it. Commanded requests are stimulus, not measurements. A body field that is parametric in the problem domain (a temperature in a JSON object, a firmware version) follows whatever protocol issue #85 settled in docs/measurements.md , referenced there rather than restated here. This note neither fills the reserved measurements slot nor decodes anyone's application protocol. Every handle declaration — scheme, base URL, retry policy, redirect policy, verification posture, ceilings — is logged through utils.logger at configuration time. Requests, retries, operational failures, and close attempts use that scoped logger to distinguish requested, responded, interrupted, and unconfirmed outcomes. Attempt index and status belong in that log even when the body does not. Request-header names belong there too; their values do not, unless the author listed that name in evidence_headers . Response option values do not belong there at all. The terminal entry is not always Aborted: a run-level halt and an abort_after expiry both settle Aborted, a fail_after expiry settles Fail, and the close sweep is owed under every one of them. result.json 's summary_tree shows whichever state applies; there is no Device API-specific field, because a safe-state action is evidence of what the framework did to protect the session, not a verdict of its own. A technician reading the timeline sees why the run ended and — from the log line — that this node stopped requesting. Where the sweep could not confirm close, the timeline says exactly that, naming the handle. An unconfirmed close never leaves a success line behind. Retry lines, when present, sit with the request that produced them, so a Fail that landed on the third attempt cannot be read as a single call. They are not one handle type, and they are not exec with a URL. Status (including 4xx/5xx) is data. Typed DeviceRequest / DeviceResponse . Payload is bytes . Path is relative to the declared base URL. JSON parsing is convenience, not the contract. Retries are evidence. Default is zero. Each attempt is logged. Non-idempotent retry is refused unless opted in. Abort cancels the in-flight attempt and the remainder of the loop. CoAP CON retransmits are protocol-level, bounded by the request ceiling, and counted in that attempt's evidence. Legacy CoapInterface is reference only. The CLI-through- exec wrapper is the trap this note closes. Legacy performAction is application protocol and stays out of the framework; authors compose request() with wait_for . Abort safe-state is a closed session (socket cancel / CON stop / connection-close), not a framework-invented shutdown request. Authored cleanup() may send a last request; the hard cut does not wait for it and does not replace it. Redirects default to do-not-follow; cross-host follow is refused. Shared sessions refuse conflicting ownership, same Group Isolation posture as signed PWM. Attempt logs keep request-header names and withhold every value unless the author lists that name in evidence_headers (default empty). A secret-name allowlist cannot keep X-Device-Token out of an artifact. Opting Authorization in is the author's leak. For CoAP the name is the registered option name, not an option number. Response option values are never recorded by the framework; carrying one into evidence is the author's act, the same as a body. PATCH stays undeclared. The declared HTTP methods are GET, PUT, POST, DELETE. POST refuses application retry unless opted in. PATCH is the same double-stimulus, and the signature of 2026-09-09 did not choose between the two branches this decision offered, so it takes the branch that adds nothing to the public surface: PATCH is refused at the call site as an undeclared method. Declaring it is a later note against this contract, not a widening of the first backend. The lifecycle, verdict, and evidence contracts above are constraints on that decision. If a required backend cannot satisfy them, the finding belongs on #97 with the affected guarantee named. It does not earn an alternate lifecycle or an exception enforced only by a linter.

docs.text: Status: SIGNED — Ty approved this note in !130 on 2026-09-09; recorded on #97 A CoAP or HTTP resource is not a command string. This note states the request and response shape, retry-as-evidence, timing, error taxonomy, and closed-session obligations that make a device API fit HILT's existing lifecycle. The three HIL rulings govern it. Ty's approval of the actual note signs the obligations below. Implementation requires its own approved issue and Zavala's review under API stability . This is the interface most likely to be waved through as "just exec with a URL." It is not. An HTTP call needs its own contract, error taxonomy, and safe-state, same as a pin or a bus. All names below ( DeviceApiInterface , HttpInterface , CoapInterface , DeviceRequest , DeviceResponse , DeviceApiOperationFailure , MockDeviceApi , and the method names) are provisional. This note adds no public Python name and changes no stored record. The legacy CoapInterface is a design reference only — see below. The migration context is the preserved lifecycle and evidence contracts, with a new hardware contract for Ty to judge.
docs.title: Design note: Device API (CoAP/HTTP) interface contract

docs.text: exec is a command contract: a string goes in, an ExecResult comes out, and a non-zero exit is data for the test method to judge. A device-API call is a typed resource operation: method, path, payload bytes, status, headers or CoAP options, and a body. None of that is a shell command. Forcing it through exec would mean either shelling out to curl / wget / the coap CLI (lossy, racy, and blind to in-flight cancellation) or smuggling an HTTP client inside a RemoteInterface subclass that answers _exec with a fake dialect — exactly the parallel-lifecycle-in-disguise ruling 1 forbids. A URL that has been stringified into curl -X POST ... has already lost the status as a first-class value, the header set, whether the body was truncated, and whether the client retried. DeviceApiInterface is its own ABC, structurally parallel to RemoteInterface ( src/hilt/remote.py ) and to the signed GpioInterface / PwmInterface : it owns connect / disconnect / cancel_in_flight in the same shape, and adds request-shaped operations in place of exec . The legacy TypeScript CoapInterface wrapped the coap CLI through utils.exec because the UDP-only node-coap package could not speak coaps+tcp:// (RFC 8323). That was a toolchain constraint, not a contract. This port does not carry the CLI wrapper forward. A backend that can only shell out to curl or coap is a finding for Ty, not the shape of the interface.
docs.title: Why not an exec subclass

docs.text: Framework obligation: Present CoAP and HTTP as one resource-request contract under HIL ruling 1. DeviceApiInterface is not an exec subclass and does not change where utils.exec routes. A handle is bound to one scheme, one base URL, and a declared timing envelope before it can request. HTTP and CoAP share the request/response shape (method, path, payload, status, body). They are not one handle type. An HttpInterface cannot speak CoAP; a CoapInterface cannot follow HTTP redirects. Scheme is identity, fixed for the handle's lifetime: http / https for HTTP, coap / coaps / coaps+tcp for CoAP. Flipping the scheme live is the Device API instance of flipping a GPIO pin's direction. A provisional DeviceRequest carries method (GET, PUT, POST, DELETE; CoAP may add the methods its backend declares), path (appended to the declared base URL, never a second origin), payload ( bytes or absent), protocol options (HTTP headers, CoAP options), and evidence_headers (the set of request header or option names whose values may appear in the attempt log; default empty). For HTTP the name is the field name, matched case-insensitively. For CoAP the name is the registered option name ( Uri-Path , Content-Format ); an option number is not a name and is refused at the call site. PATCH is not in that method set; whether the first backend declares it as a non-idempotent sibling of POST is a decision for Ty below, not a silent widening. Reject a non- bytes payload, a path that is an absolute URL, a method the backend did not declare, and a header or option name that is not a string, at the call site, before the adapter is touched. Booleans are not integers; a dict passed as payload is not a JSON body. The approved convenience on #155 adds keyword-only json=value : serialize once to UTF-8 bytes and default the HTTP Content-Type to application/json , preserving an explicitly supplied content type case-insensitively. Omission sends no JSON; json=None sends null. Combining it with a non- None payload (including empty bytes) is refused, as are unserializable values and non-finite numbers. The wire payload remains bytes, and logs still record lengths, never body contents. A provisional DeviceResponse carries status (an HTTP status integer, or a CoAP code as the dotted string 2.05 — see CoapCode ), protocol options (headers / CoAP options), and body ( bytes ). The wire integer ( class << 5 | detail , so Content is 69 ) stays inside the transport. Issue #156. JSON parsing is a convenience on top of those bytes, not the contract: a body that is not JSON is still a successful transfer of bytes. The interface does not invent an empty body, a 200, or a CoAP 2.05 to stand in for a missing response. Issue #155 adds json() and parse(response_type="json") to decode those bytes explicitly; parse(response_type="yaml") uses yaml.safe_load and requires the optional hilt-core[yaml] extra. Parser errors propagate unchanged, unsupported formats raise ValueError , and a missing YAML extra raises ImportError . Neither method changes status or bytes or interprets a status as a verdict. A malformed body remains a completed transfer. Status is data. HTTP 4xx / 5xx and CoAP 4.xx / 5.xx are fields on the response, the way a non-zero exit_code is a field on ExecResult . The interface does not raise TestFailure because a resource returned 404, and it does not raise because a resource returned 500. The test method judges the status. Transport failure, protocol violation, and timeout are the operational exceptions; a well-formed error response is not one of them. request(req) -> DeviceResponse performs one application-level attempt (see retries below). One handle carries one request at a time, in call order. A request that arrives while another is on the wire waits its turn; it does not collide, and it does not fail. A handle shared by the leaves of a parallel therefore serialises them: the claims stay independent, their requests do not, and a latency measured around request on that handle includes the wait for siblings. A leaf that must measure the DUT alone takes its own handle. The wait is bounded by the node clock, not by the request ceiling, because a sibling ahead in the queue is not the DUT being slow. Framework termination takes precedence over the queue: a handle cancelled or closed while a request waited its turn never sends it (see the closed-session contract below). The only refusal left is re-entrancy — a backend's _exchange calling request on the handle it is already mid-attempt on — and that is a ValueError at the call site, a developer bug, not a queue. Each operation records the requested method, path, payload length, request-header names , whether the adapter confirmed a response, the status if one arrived, and the body length. Request-header values stay out of that record unless the author listed the name in evidence_headers . Response protocol options — HTTP response headers, CoAP response options — are not in that list. Their values are never recorded by the framework; carrying one into evidence is the author's act, the same as a body. evidence_headers does not govern them. An unconfirmed request never becomes the last-successful response in a cache the next test method reads as truth. Unknown is explicit. Developer obligation: Declare the scheme, base URL, and protocol parameters in configure() . Obtain the framework-managed handle through a provisional utils.get_http(...) or utils.get_coap(...) ; return the handle and static inputs through configure's ctx. Keep self immutable, build_suite() pure, and later ctx reads read-only. Judge the DUT with the status and body actually returned (or with an independent observation), never by treating a 2xx as a passing device. Consequence: The Floor Technician can tell which resource was addressed, what was sent, what status came back, and whether the transfer completed. A 404 cannot quietly become a missing payload in a record that claims the call succeeded, and a 200 cannot quietly become a verdict.
docs.title: The Device Request Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: A retry is stimulus the DUT saw. Hiding it lies to the Floor Technician. Application-level retries default to zero . A handle that retries without a declaration is refused at the call site. Each declared attempt — including the first — is logged through the scoped logger with attempt index, outcome (response status, operational failure, or cancelled), and delay before the next attempt when one is scheduled. The retry budget is a count of application-level attempts, not a duration. Delay between attempts is positive finite seconds, declared with the count. Booleans and non-finite values are refused. The node's fail_after / abort_after still bounds the whole sequence; a retry loop cannot extend the node clock. Non-idempotent methods (POST, and any other method the backend declares non-idempotent) refuse application retry unless the author sets an explicit retry_non_idempotent=True on that call. GET / PUT / DELETE may retry when a count is declared. The interface does not guess idempotency from the path. Protocol-level reliability is not an application retry. HTTP/TCP retransmits and CoAP CON retransmits belong to the backend's declared request ceiling. CON retransmits that actually go on the wire are counted in the attempt's evidence (the DUT saw them) but they do not consume the application retry budget. A backend whose CON loop cannot be bounded by the request ceiling, or cannot be cut by cancel_in_flight , is a finding for Ty. cancel_in_flight stops the in-flight attempt and the retry loop. A cancelled retry does not start the next attempt. The record names how many attempts ran and that the remainder were not started. One logical request holds the handle's turn from its first attempt to its last. A retry never interleaves with a sibling's request, so the attempt log for one request reads as one request. Developer obligation: Leave retries at zero unless this bench has a named reason to repeat a request. When retries are declared, treat the attempt log as part of the evidence that will be read after a Fail — especially for POST. Do not wrap request() in a suite-owned retry loop to dodge the declaration; that is the same lie with worse artifacts. Consequence: The timeline shows every request the DUT actually received from this handle. A pass that depended on the third try cannot be reconstructed as a single clean GET.
docs.title: The Retry-as-Evidence Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: The safe state is a closed session — no further requests originating from this handle — enforced at the resource by the existing termination sweep. This specializes the signed GPIO ownership and cut rules and the signed PWM disabled-output termination . It introduces no Device API halt signal, event loop, lifecycle runner, or integration hook, and it does not invent a shutdown request. Register ownership as soon as acquisition can put a request on the wire, so partial configure() failure cannot orphan a session. Bring-up establishes and confirms the session (TLS handshake, CoAP identity) before admitting the first request . An integration-hook failure or operator interrupt closes every open Device API handle. A node deadline closes only resources opened by the bounded subtree, under both fail_after (Fail) and abort_after (node-local Aborted). An inherited adapter or borrowed hop remains its owner's resource; unrelated siblings are untouched. cancel_in_flight() is idempotent. It aborts the in-flight request at the socket (HTTP: cancel the stream and close the connection; CoAP: stop CON retransmits; a RST or connection-close is the protocol cancel, analogous to I2C STOP, not a resource write), attempts the closed state under the backend's latency ceiling, and records whether close was confirmed. A repeated call cannot start a new request or replay the last one. A closed handle remains closed; there is no automatic reconnect. A request waiting its turn behind the aborted one is not sent. When its turn comes on a cancelled or closed handle it fails with DeviceApiOperationFailure naming that the handle was cancelled or closed while the request was queued — an operational failure the author catches and models as a verdict, never a ValueError and never a silent request on a dead session. disconnect() treats waiters the same way. The framework does not transmit a "safe" PUT, DELETE, or CoAP action on abort. A DUT that needs a specific last request gets it from authored cleanup() , which the hard cut does not wait for. Inventing a /shutdown write at abort would be a stimulus the suite never declared, written into a record the technician might trust. Request ceiling (including protocol-level CON/TCP reliability), retry delay, bring-up/close ceiling, and the node's fail_after / abort_after are separate clocks. An operation timeout names that operation and its ceiling. It does not manufacture the timeout evidence reserved for the winning node clock in the Time Budget Contract . A long poll cannot extend the node clock. The request ceiling starts when the request takes its turn on the handle, not when it was queued: the wait behind a sibling is bounded by the node clock alone. A backend whose shared session would let one node's close starve another owner's in-flight request must refuse the conflicting acquisition before either owner requests. It cannot sacrifice Group Isolation to offer more nodes on one socket. Serialising requests on one handle is not that: the handle has one owner, the node whose configure() opened it, and the leaves queuing on it are that owner's subtree, closed together when that owner's clock expires. Developer obligation: Select a fixture for which "this node stops talking" is the intended safe state. Declare shared sessions honestly. Keep any required shutdown request in cleanup() ; rely on framework ownership for termination. Never manually sequence another node's configure or cleanup. Consequence: Ending the test stops this node's requests and records what could be confirmed. A technician is never asked to infer that a session is idle from Pass/Fail/Aborted alone, or from a DELETE nobody authored.
docs.title: The Closed-Session and Timing Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: HTTP redirects are a declared policy, default do not follow . Same-origin follow is an opt-in on the handle. Cross-host follow is refused: a 302 to a second origin is data on the response, not a silent second request, and it must not carry the original credentials. A backend that auto-follows across hosts is refused at bring-up. Authentication material (Bearer tokens, basic passwords, client certificates, CoAP DTLS PSKs) is declared in configure() and never reaches evidence. Provenance names the credential path or slot, never the value — the same containment SSH already proves. URL userinfo in the declared base URL is withheld the same way. Attempt logs keep every request-header name and withhold every value unless the author lists that name in evidence_headers on the DeviceRequest . Default is empty: the safe case costs the author no thought. A secret-name allowlist cannot deliver "never" — X-Device-Token , Api-Key , and the next DUT's favorite all miss it. Matching is case-insensitive for HTTP field names. For CoAP, the name is the registered option name; an option number is not a name and is refused at the call site — a guess that silently matches nothing would look like a working redaction. Opting Authorization in is the author's leak to stop, not a framework rewrite. Response protocol option values are never recorded by the framework. evidence_headers is a request-side opt-in; it does not cover Set-Cookie , WWW-Authenticate , or a CoAP response option. Carrying a response option into evidence is the author's act, the same as a body. Response bodies still go to evidence when the author puts them there; secrets in a body are the author's leak to stop, not a framework rewrite of the payload. TLS / DTLS verification is on by default. Skipping it is a lab-only declaration analogous to SSH skip_host_verification , logged as such at bring-up. The legacy performAction helper (PUT an action id, poll until a K2-specific status set) is application protocol . It is not part of this contract. Authors who need a long-running device action compose request() with the existing wait_for . Porting that helper into DeviceApiInterface would bake one vendor's action DSL into the framework the way decoding a J1939 PGN would bake an application protocol into CAN. Developer obligation: Do not follow redirects in suite code to dodge the handle policy. Do not log tokens. Do not opt a secret request header into evidence_headers unless the Floor Technician is meant to read that value. Do not treat evidence_headers as covering response headers or CoAP response options; those values never enter the attempt log, and putting one in a verdict is the author's act. Do not ask the framework for a perform_action sugar that hides the poll. Consequence: A redirect cannot launder a second origin into a record that still names the declared base URL. An attempt log cannot carry a bearer token off the bench unless the author opted that header in. A Set-Cookie or WWW-Authenticate cannot walk into the attempt log because evidence_headers was assumed to cover the response. A K2 action poll is visible as the requests it actually made.
docs.title: Redirects, credentials, and the legacy action helper

docs.text: The HIL lifecycle ruling applies unchanged. Concretely: Bring-up happens the same way use_shell brings up SSH: configure() obtains a handle (provisionally utils.get_http(...) / utils.get_coap(...) , mirroring get_shell / get_gpio / get_pwm ), and the framework's bookkeeping tracks what this node opened versus what it inherited. Teardown order is the framework's: cancel_in_flight fires as part of the same In-Flight Termination Contract sweep that already closes RemoteInterface transports and silences signed GPIO/PWM resources. use_survey / use_audit remain the observation hooks. A periodic audit that GETs a health resource and raises TestFailure on an unexpected status or body is the existing audit contract. before_each / after_each remain the integrator's narrow context and still cannot touch hardware. Hardware that needs the client to run its own concurrent receive loop outside survey/audit, that cannot honor a hard cancel_in_flight (a request that keeps running on the device after the socket is cut is the device's problem; a client that cannot cut the socket is a finding), or that requires the CLI-wrapper shape the legacy CoapInterface used, is a finding for Ty — not a reason to give Device API its own lifecycle.
docs.title: Lifecycle and hook ownership: unchanged

docs.text: No new terminal state is introduced, and no new exception root. DeviceApiOperationFailure derives from HiltError , not TestFailure , for the same reason GPIO's PinSettleFailure and PWM's PwmOperationFailure do: failure to complete a transfer does not identify the DUT as the cause. Situation Raised as Terminal state Invalid method, path, payload, or retry declaration; request re-entered from inside the handle's own in-flight request TypeError / ValueError at the call site ContractViolation (Fail, bug: true ) naming the exception if it escapes A second request while one is on the wire No exception: it waits its turn, logged as queued Whatever verdict the author writes; the measured latency includes the wait Handle cancelled or closed while a request waited its turn DeviceApiOperationFailure naming the handle, method, path, and that it was queued, never sent Fail when the author catches it and states the verdict; a ContractViolation Fail ( bug: true ) when it escapes HTTP 4xx / 5xx or CoAP 4.xx / 5.xx on a well-formed response No exception: status and body are the result Whatever verdict the author writes. The interface does not guess Fail Connection refused, TLS/DTLS handshake failure, protocol violation, request exceeds its ceiling, close cannot be confirmed at bring-up DeviceApiOperationFailure (provisional HiltError ) naming the handle, operation, method, path, and ceiling Fail when the author catches it and states the verdict; a ContractViolation Fail ( bug: true ) when it escapes Backend cannot reach the adapter at bring-up ConnectionError from the interface's own connect Absorbed the way RemoteInterface connect failures are absorbed today Close cannot be confirmed during the safe-state sweep No exception; the run is already ending Terminal state unchanged; timeline records the unconfirmed close, naming the handle. Never a success line Integration hook throws mid-request Framework raises ExternalIntegrationFailure Aborted; run-level halt closes every open handle Operator SIGINT/SIGTERM mid-run Framework raises OperatorInterrupt Aborted; same run-level sweep A node's time budget expires while it holds a handle Framework settles the node per its declared budget fail_after → Fail, abort_after → node-local Aborted; either way only that subtree's handles are closed Test returns without a verdict Existing MissingVerdict Node-local Aborted. A completed request cannot supply the missing verdict Unknown is represented explicitly. A timed-out request is not a 200 with an empty body. An unconfirmed close is not an idle session.
docs.title: Failure vocabulary

docs.text: The pattern is the one RemoteInterface / MockTransport / SshInterface already proves, and that signed GPIO/PWM reuse: DeviceApiInterface is the ABC; HttpInterface and CoapInterface are real backends; MockDeviceApi is the test double. Self-tests exercise mock and real against a shared contract suite so a bug in either backend is caught by the same assertions. Required proofs: refuse a non- bytes payload and an absolute-URL path before the adapter is touched; concurrent requests on one handle run one at a time in call order, and a cancel or close mid-queue fails the waiters as DeviceApiOperationFailure without sending them; a re-entered request is refused rather than deadlocked; status-as-data (4xx is a response, not an exception); retries default to zero and each declared attempt is evidenced; non-idempotent retry refused unless opted in; cancel_in_flight stops the retry loop; redirects do not follow cross-host; request-header values never appear in evidence unless the author opted that name into evidence_headers ; a CoAP option number is refused as an evidence_headers name; response option values never appear in the attempt log; partial configure() cannot orphan a session; node cuts leave a sibling's in-flight request untouched; repeated cancel_in_flight cannot replay a POST; unconfirmed close produces only unconfirmed evidence. MockDeviceApi schedules park -style holds analogous to MockTransport.park , so lifecycle tests can abort mid-request without a server. A suite author never constructs either backend directly: utils.get_http / utils.get_coap resolve to whichever backend the run was configured with. Real-backend tests must verify transfers through independent observation (a second client, a capturing proxy); mock statuses cannot establish that a DUT saw the body. Core install stays dependency-light. HTTP and CoAP clients land as optional extras on the implementation issue; this note does not pick the library.

docs.text: Design note: GPIO interface contract ¶ Status: SIGNED — Ty ruled the open questions on #93 on 2026-09-07 This note states the developer-framework contract for digital I/O pins — direction, level, debounce, safe-state on abort, the error taxonomy for a pin that will not settle, and timing guarantees. It is written to the diligence of docs/contracts.md and governed by the three rulings in docs/hil/index.md . All names below ( GpioInterface , GpioPin , PinDirection , PinLevel , PinSettleFailure ) are provisional: they name the shape Ty signed off, not a promised spelling. Why not an exec subclass ¶ A GPIO pin does not run commands. "Set this pin high" and "read this pin's level" are typed operations on a fixed set of physical lines, not strings handed to a shell. Forcing pin control through exec would mean either shelling out to sysfs / libgpiod command-line tools per call (slow, racy, and impossible to debounce cleanly) or smuggling a pin controller inside a RemoteInterface subclass that answers _exec with a fake shell dialect — exactly the parallel-lifecycle-in-disguise ruling 1 forbids. GpioInterface is its own ABC, structurally parallel to RemoteInterface ( src/hilt/remote.py ) but not a subclass of it: it owns connect / disconnect / cancel_in_flight in the same shape, and adds pin-shaped operations in place of exec . The GPIO Interface Contract ¶ Framework obligation: GpioInterface presents a fixed set of named pins, each with a declared direction and idle level, and guarantees the following regardless of backend: Direction and level. Every pin is declared PinDirection.OUT or PinDirection.IN before first use; direction is fixed for the pin's lifetime — a suite that needs the other direction opens a different declared pin, it does not flip one live. set_level(pin, PinLevel.HIGH | PinLevel.LOW) and read_level(pin) -> PinLevel are the only level operations. PinLevel carries three members, not two: HIGH , LOW , and UNAVAILABLE — the last meaning the controller could not be reached for this read. A two-valued return would have to answer that case with a level nobody measured, and there is no honest choice between them. Setting an input pin or reading an output-only pin (on hardware that cannot read back its own output) is a TypeError at the call site, not a silent no-op — the same posture RemoteInterface.exec takes toward a disconnected transport, caught before it can be mistaken for a hardware reading. Debounce. A read on an input pin names two quantities, never one: a stability window — how long the level must hold unchanged for the reading to count — and an acquisition deadline — how long the framework keeps looking for such a stretch. Both are seconds, both validated positive and finite, and the deadline must exceed the window. One number cannot carry both jobs: a transition halfway through a window leaves no complete stable stretch before that same instant, so a single settle can demand an outcome it has also made unreachable. Given the two, the framework samples at an interval no coarser than a tenth of the window and returns the first level that holds for a full window. A pin still chattering when the deadline passes does not return a guessed value — it raises (see the failure vocabulary below). Both defaults are per-backend but always explicit in the resolved call. Debounce is symmetric: it is not a filter for "the level I expected," it is a filter for "the level that stopped moving." Safe-state on abort. Every declared output pin carries a required idle level, given at declaration time, not inferred from its first set_level call. Two different events drive pins to idle, and this note keeps them apart because the contracts do: The run-level halt — an integration hook throw, or an operator SIGINT/SIGTERM — drives every output pin that every open GpioInterface holds to its declared idle level before any interface reports cancel_in_flight complete. The whole bench is coming down. A node's time budget expiring is not that halt. Deadline Aborted is node-local: it never fires the shared run halt and never cascades past the bounded subtree ( docs/contracts.md , Time Budget Contract). It drives only the pins the cut subtree itself opened; an inherited controller or an inherited hop is never in that owned set, and a sibling outside the subtree is untouched under the Group Isolation Contract. On a rack of thirty units, one node overrunning its clock must not idle the other twenty-nine. The sweep is owed under both budget names. fail_after renders Fail and abort_after renders node-local Aborted; the verdict differs, the safe state does not. This is the GPIO-specific instance of the In-Flight Termination Contract's "cancel the resource, not just the coroutine": for a relay driving mains power or a reset line holding a DUT in a known state, leaving the last-written level in place across an abort is the failure mode this contract exists to prevent. Input pins have no safe-state action; they carry no risk from being read after abort, and cancel_in_flight stops accepting reads immediately. Timing guarantees. set_level and read_level (after debounce settles) complete within a bounded, backend-declared latency ceiling — the interface states its worst-case pin-toggle latency so a suite author can reason about whether a protocol timing requirement (a reset pulse width, a chip-select setup time) is achievable at all through this backend before writing the test. A call that cannot complete within that ceiling is a backend-operation timeout — the controller gave up — and it is reported as the operational failure below. It is not the node's clock expiring, and the record must never conflate the two: a suite that declared a generous fail_after has not thereby reclassified a controller that timed out in milliseconds, and a node deadline firing during a pin call has not made the controller at fault. Developer obligation: Declare every pin's direction and, for outputs, its idle level at configuration time — in configure() , the same place use_shell is called. A pin whose idle level is not knowable ("depends on what the last test left it at") is a design defect in the test, not something the framework can paper over. State both debounce quantities deliberately. The defaults are not "right for every signal" — a mechanical relay and a solid-state one settle on different timescales, and a noisy line often needs a strict window with a generous deadline. The author who knows the hardware states both numbers. Catch PinSettleFailure and decide what it means. It is a HiltError , not a TestFailure , and that ancestry is the whole point: a pin that will not stop moving does not by itself say whether the DUT is faulty, the harness is noisy, or the probe is loose. The author models it into a verdict or the child boundary classifies the escape as the bug it is — a mode the suite never handled. Handle PinLevel.UNAVAILABLE at every read. It is a real state of the bench, not defensive padding: the controller was unreachable and no measurement exists. Compare against the member you mean ( if level is PinLevel.LOW: ), never against its negation — if level != PinLevel.HIGH: quietly reads an unreachable controller as a low line, and a technician acting on that verdict believes a wire is dead when nothing confirmed it. Consequence: A relay left energized, a reset line left asserted, or a power-enable pin left high across an aborted run is a safety and equipment- damage risk, not merely a test artifact. Declaring idle levels up front and enforcing them on every abort path — not just a clean cleanup() — is what makes GPIO safe to use on live hardware under this framework. Lifecycle and hook ownership: unchanged ¶ GpioInterface does not run its own event loop, does not register its own before_each / after_each , and does not own a competing halt signal. Concretely: Bring-up happens the same way use_shell brings up SSH: a configure() call obtains a GpioInterface handle (provisionally utils.get_gpio(...) , mirroring get_shell ), and the framework's existing ExecRouting -style bookkeeping tracks what this node opened versus what it inherited. Teardown order is the framework's, not the interface's: cancel_in_flight on every opened GpioInterface fires as part of the same In-Flight Termination Contract sweep that already closes RemoteInterface transports when RunAbort fires, not on a separate GPIO-specific abort path. use_survey / use_audit are the only hooks a suite registers to observe pin state; a periodic audit that reads a watchdog pin and raises TestFailure on an unexpected level is exactly the audit contract's existing shape (thermal-runaway-style monitoring), not a new hook kind. before_each / after_each remain the integrator's narrow context ( BeforeEachContext / AfterEachContext ) and still cannot touch hardware — a GPIO pin is exactly the kind of thing those hooks are barred from reaching, same as exec and get_shell today. Hardware that needs a GPIO controller to run its own concurrent polling loop outside the audit/survey pattern, or that cannot honor a hard cancel_in_flight , is a finding for Ty — not a reason to give GPIO its own lifecycle. Failure vocabulary ¶ Situation Raised as Terminal state A pin never settles within its acquisition deadline PinSettleFailure (provisional; a HiltError , deliberately not a TestFailure — the exact posture ArpResolutionFailure holds, src/hilt/errors.py ) Fail when the author catches it and states the verdict; a ContractViolation -wrapped Fail ( bug: true ) when it escapes, because the suite never modeled the mode A pin call exceeds the backend's declared latency ceiling PinSettleFailure , naming the backend operation As above. Never recorded as a node time-budget expiry Direction/level operation misused (write to an input, read an output-only pin) TypeError at the call site ContractViolation (Fail, bug: true ) — same posture as ExecRouting 's connection-pair TypeError s Backend cannot reach the controller during a read No exception: read_level returns PinLevel.UNAVAILABLE Whatever verdict the author writes for that state. An unhandled third member is not a framework error — it is a reading the suite declined to judge Backend cannot reach the controller at bring-up ConnectionError from the interface's own connect Absorbed the way RemoteInterface 's connect failures are absorbed today — not a bug, a hardware-unreachable condition for the test method to judge An idle drive cannot be confirmed during the safe-state sweep No exception; the run is already ending The node's terminal state is unchanged, and the timeline records the failure to confirm, naming the pin. A sweep that could not verify idle never leaves a success line behind Integration hook throws while pins are held mid-toggle Framework raises ExternalIntegrationFailure Aborted; the run-level halt drives every open GpioInterface to idle, per the In-Flight Termination Contract Operator SIGINT/SIGTERM mid-run Framework raises OperatorInterrupt Aborted; same run-level sweep A node's time budget expires while it holds pins Framework settles the node per its declared budget fail_after → Fail, abort_after → node-local Aborted; either way only the pins that subtree opened are driven to idle No new terminal state is introduced, and no new exception root. PinSettleFailure is an operational condition rather than a verdict, which is why it takes HiltError and not TestFailure : "this pin will not stop moving" does not tell anyone whether the DUT is faulty, the harness is noisy, or the probe is loose, and the framework must not choose among those on the author's behalf. That is the epistemic position ArpResolutionFailure already occupies. PinLevel.UNAVAILABLE is likewise data and never control flow — a reading the author judges, exactly as a non-zero exit code from exec is. Mock and real backends: one contract, two implementations ¶ The pattern is the one RemoteInterface / MockTransport / SshInterface already proves for exec : GpioInterface is the ABC; a real backend (provisionally targeting libgpiod or a vendor SDK) and a MockGpio test double both implement the same connect / _set_level / _read_level / _cancel_in_flight methods, and self-tests exercise both against a shared contract-suite of assertions (declare pin, set level, read level, abort mid- toggle, verify idle drive) so a bug in either backend is caught by the same tests. MockGpio schedules park -style holds analogous to MockTransport.park , so lifecycle tests can assert that an abort arriving mid-debounce still drives idle levels without a real controller on the bench. A suite author never constructs either backend directly, mirroring use_shell / get_shell : a provisional utils.get_gpio(...) call resolves to whichever backend the run was configured with. Evidence ¶ A pin read that matters to the verdict travels with it exactly as the Evidence Contract already requires: PASS({"reset_pin_level": level}) or TestFailure(..., evidence={"reset_pin_level": level}) , declared up front with @evidence(...) when the method promises to carry it. A GPIO level itself is not a parametric measurement (there is no unit, limit, or continuous scale to it — it is boolean-shaped evidence), so it is recorded as a plain evidence entry, not through the #85 measurements protocol. Where a GPIO-adjacent reading is parametric — a pulse-width or duty-cycle-like timing measured off a pin transition — that measurement follows whatever protocol issue #85 settles on, referenced there rather than re-specified here. Every pin declaration, direction, and idle-level assignment is logged through utils.logger at configuration time, the same way ExecRouting logs a connection's provenance lines — so the Floor Technician can see what idle state was promised without opening the suite source. What the Floor Technician sees ¶ When a pin is driven to its idle level, the node's timeline.jsonl (and its human-readable timeline.log twin) carries a log entry at the scope of the node that owned the pin, naming which pin was driven and to what level, immediately before that node's terminal entry — the same temporal-backbone placement the In-Flight Termination Contract already gives a hard-closed SSH transport. The terminal entry is not always Aborted: a run-level halt and an abort_after expiry both settle the node Aborted, a fail_after expiry settles it Fail, and the idle sweep is owed under every one of them. result.json 's summary_tree shows whichever state applies; there is no separate GPIO-specific field, because a safe-state action is evidence of what the framework did to protect the hardware, not a verdict of its own. A technician reading the timeline sees why the run ended (from failure , naming the operator, the integration hook that threw, or the clock that fired) and — from the log line — that the reset/enable/relay pin the suite declared was left in its documented idle state, not in whatever level the test last happened to set. Where the sweep could not confirm a pin reached its idle level, the timeline says exactly that, naming the pin. This is the most load-bearing line in the note. A technician reaching into a rack trusts a record that says a relay was de-energized, and a success line written for a drive nobody confirmed is how someone puts a hand on a line believing it dead. An unconfirmed idle is recorded as unconfirmed.
