docs.text: Design note: I2C/SPI interface contract ¶ Status: SIGNED — Ty approved this note in !129 on 2026-09-09; recorded on #96 I2C and SPI carry register transactions, not command strings. This note states the transfer, addressing, arbitration, timing, and released-bus obligations that make both buses fit HILT's existing lifecycle. They are two interfaces under one contract shape, not one type with a protocol flag. The three HIL rulings govern both. Ty's approval of the actual note signs the obligations below. Implementation requires its own approved issue and Zavala's review under API stability . All names below ( I2cInterface , SpiInterface , I2cAddress , SpiMode , BusArbitrationFailure , BusOperationFailure , MockI2c , MockSpi , and the method names) are provisional. This note adds no public Python name and changes no stored record. The legacy framework and language server supply no I2C/SPI behavior to carry forward; the migration context is the preserved lifecycle and evidence contracts, with a new hardware contract for Ty to judge. Why not an exec subclass ¶ A register read is an addressed transaction: a 7- or 10-bit I2C address and a register pointer, or a SPI chip-select plus a command byte, then a bounded payload. None of that is a shell command. Forcing it through exec would mean shelling out to i2cget / spidev tools (lossy, racy, and blind to a stuck-low SDA) or smuggling a controller inside a RemoteInterface subclass that answers _exec with a fake dialect — exactly the parallel-lifecycle-in-disguise ruling 1 forbids. I2cInterface and SpiInterface are their own ABCs, structurally parallel to RemoteInterface ( src/hilt/remote.py ) and to the signed GpioInterface / PwmInterface : each owns connect / disconnect / cancel_in_flight in the same shape, and adds transaction-shaped operations in place of exec . They are not subclasses of each other. An I2C NACK is not a SPI 0xFF. A shared "bus transfer" ABC that pretended otherwise would lose the arbitration and chip-select contracts this note exists to name. The Bus Transaction Contract ¶ Framework obligation: Present each bus as its own typed interface under HIL ruling 1. Neither is an exec subclass; neither changes where utils.exec routes. A handle is bound to one adapter, one protocol, and a declared timing envelope before it can transfer. A transaction is atomic at the wire: I2C from START through STOP; SPI for the whole time chip-select is asserted. The interface does not expose a pile of unbound read() / write() calls that another node, or an abort, can interleave mid-address. One in-flight transaction per handle. A second transfer is refused while one is active; it is not queued to surprise the next lifecycle phase. Framework termination takes precedence over this admission rule. Each operation records the requested address or chip-select, the direction, the payload length, and whether the controller confirmed the outcome. An unconfirmed transfer never becomes the last-successful value in a cache the next test method reads as truth. Unknown is explicit. Payload is bytes . Reject a non- bytes payload, a negative length, and a length above the backend-declared ceiling, at the call site, before the adapter is touched. Booleans are not integers. Developer obligation: Declare the adapter, protocol parameters, and every device this node will address in configure() . Obtain the framework-managed handle through a provisional utils.get_i2c(...) or utils.get_spi(...) ; return the handle and static inputs through configure's ctx. Keep self immutable, build_suite() pure, and later ctx reads read-only. Judge the DUT with bytes actually returned (or with an independent observation), never by treating a successful ACK or a full-duplex clock-out as a passing device. Consequence: The Floor Technician can tell which device was addressed, what was written, what came back, and whether the transaction completed. A NACK or a short read cannot quietly become a register value in a record that claims otherwise. The I2C Addressing and Arbitration Contract ¶ Framework obligation: I2C identity is an address, not a path. A provisional I2cAddress carries the 7-bit or 10-bit address and the width. Reject an address that does not fit the declared width. 8-bit "address plus R/W" encodings are refused: the R/W bit is the transfer's, not the handle's. Provisional write(address, data) , read(address, n) , and write_read(address, tx, n) each emit one START–STOP transaction. write_read is a repeated-START, not two transactions the abort path could split. There is no "hold the bus across calls" mode. NACK on address (no device ACKed) and NACK on data (device ACKed the address then rejected a byte) are distinct operational failures, named in the error. Neither is a TestFailure . The interface does not retry, does not clock out dummy bytes after a NACK, and does not return a truncated payload as success. Do not busy-loop a NACK into existence of a device. Consequence: A missing part, a device that refused a register, and a bus fight are three records, not one "I2C failed" blob. docs.text: A register read is an addressed transaction: a 7- or 10-bit I2C address and a register pointer, or a SPI chip-select plus a command byte, then a bounded payload. None of that is a shell command. Forcing it through exec would mean shelling out to i2cget / spidev tools (lossy, racy, and blind to a stuck-low SDA) or smuggling a controller inside a RemoteInterface subclass that answers _exec with a fake dialect — exactly the parallel-lifecycle-in-disguise ruling 1 forbids. They are not subclasses of each other. An I2C NACK is not a SPI 0xFF. A shared "bus transfer" ABC that pretended otherwise would lose the arbitration and chip-select contracts this note exists to name.

docs.text: Design note: PWM interface contract ¶ Status: SIGNED — Ty approved this note in !125 on 2026-09-08; recorded on #94 PWM controls a repeating output through its frequency and duty cycle. This note states the transfer, ramp, timing, and disabled-output obligations that make that control fit HILT's existing lifecycle. The three HIL rulings govern it. Ty's approval of the actual note signs the obligations below. Implementation requires its own approved issue and Zavala's review under API stability . All names below ( PwmInterface , PwmChannel , PwmOperationFailure , MockPwm , and the method names) are provisional. This note adds no public Python name and changes no stored record. The legacy framework and language server supply no PWM behavior to carry forward; the migration context is the preserved lifecycle and evidence contracts, with a signed hardware contract for a later implementation. The PWM Transfer Contract ¶ Framework obligation: Present PWM as its own typed interface under HIL ruling 1. PwmInterface is not an exec subclass and does not change where utils.exec routes. Each named channel has a declared output polarity, frequency range, duty-cycle resolution, and disabled-output behavior before it can be enabled. Frequency is in hertz, positive and finite. Duty cycle is the fraction of the period spent in the declared active polarity, from 0.0 through 1.0 inclusive. Reject booleans, non-numbers, non-finite values, out-of-range values, and unsupported frequency/duty pairs at runtime before any write. A fraction and a percentage are not interchangeable: 50 is invalid. A provisional set_output(channel, frequency_hz=..., duty_cycle=...) deliberately enables or updates the output. It validates the complete pair before applying either member. The backend must describe its supported pairs and update behavior, including shared timing resources; it cannot silently clamp, round, or momentarily apply an undeclared combination. A value the hardware cannot represent is refused, with the supported resolution named, so the author can request a different value deliberately. disable(channel) stops output generation. Neither a zero duty cycle nor a lost controller connection counts as confirmation that output is disabled. The inactive electrical behavior of a disabled channel is part of its declaration; disabled does not claim that an attached load has lost power. Each operation records the requested setting and whether the controller confirmed applying it. An acknowledgement is evidence of controller state, not an independent measurement of the waveform at the DUT. A failure or timeout leaves the unconfirmed setting explicitly unknown, never cached as the last successful setting. One operation owns a channel at a time. A second write or ramp is refused while one is active; it is not queued to surprise the next lifecycle phase. Framework termination takes precedence over this admission rule. A backend whose shared timer would let one channel's update or disable alter another owner's channel must refuse the conflicting acquisition before touching either owner's output. It cannot sacrifice Group Isolation to offer more channels. Developer obligation: Declare the channel, polarity, supported settings, and disabled behavior in configure() . Obtain its framework-managed handle through a provisional utils.get_pwm(...) ; return the handle and static inputs through configure's ctx. Keep self immutable, build_suite() pure, and later ctx reads read-only. Judge the DUT with actual observations, rather than treating a successful output request as a passing test. Consequence: The Floor Technician can distinguish the stimulus requested, the controller's acknowledgement, and the DUT's response. A rejected request cannot quietly become a different stimulus in a record that claims otherwise. The PWM Ramp and Timing Contract ¶ Framework obligation: A provisional ramp(channel, target_duty_cycle=..., duration=...) changes duty at a fixed frequency. The channel must already be enabled with a confirmed starting setting. Duration is positive finite seconds, with booleans refused by the same numeric rule as transfer; target duty follows the transfer validation above. A frequency ramp is outside this proposal. The requested trajectory is linear from the confirmed starting duty to the target over the declared duration. The backend states its update interval, duty resolution, and worst-case scheduling deviation. Quantized intermediate steps must remain within those declared bounds, progress monotonically, and reach the representable target; they must not overshoot. Before starting, refuse a trajectory that cannot meet the backend's declared envelope. Ramp duration and backend-operation deadline are separate quantities. The former describes the requested change; the latter bounds how long the controller may take to confirm it. As in the signed GPIO stability-window/acquisition-deadline distinction , one number cannot describe both the work and the allowance to finish it. The resolved ramp completion deadline must exceed its duration and include the backend's declared scheduling and acknowledgement allowances. Both values appear in evidence before the ramp starts. Ordinary output updates, disable operations, and bring-up also have positive finite backend-declared latency ceilings. An operation timeout names that operation and its ceiling. It does not manufacture the timeout evidence reserved for the winning node clock in the Time Budget Contract . The node's fail_after or abort_after bounds an awaited ramp like any other work. A longer ramp or backend deadline cannot extend that clock. Cancellation interrupts the resource's ramp; it does not wait for the target duty or a graceful ramp-down before disabling output. A ramp settles only when its completion is confirmed or a failure/cut has been recorded. An operational failure stops further ramp writes and attempts bounded disable of that channel before settlement; failed confirmation stays explicit. It cannot leave a detached task changing the output after it settles. Blocking SDK work uses the existing framework executor boundary. A late native completion must not re-enable or rewrite an output after the framework has disabled it. Developer obligation: Choose a supported trajectory and name the node budget for what expiry means to this test. Do not create a suite-owned timing loop, suppress CancelledError , or use an output ramp as a substitute for measuring the DUT's response. Catch operational failures and model their meaning at the test boundary. Consequence: A completed ramp means the declared controller trajectory completed within its stated envelope. An interrupted ramp carries the point last confirmed and an explicit interruption, not a fabricated endpoint. The record keeps a slow controller distinct from a node that spent its budget. The PWM Safe-State Contract ¶ Framework obligation: The safe state is output disabled, enforced at the resource by the existing termination sweep. This specializes the signed GPIO ownership and cut rules ; it introduces no PWM halt signal, event loop, lifecycle runner, or integration hook. Register ownership as soon as acquisition can affect a channel, so partial configure() failure cannot orphan an output. Bring-up establishes and confirms disabled state before admitting the first enable operation. Failure to establish it refuses use and records the unconfirmed state. An integration-hook failure or operator interrupt disables every output owned by every open PWM interface. A node deadline disables only resources opened by the bounded subtree, under both fail_after (Fail) and abort_after (node-local Aborted). An inherited controller or borrowed hop remains its owner's resource; unrelated siblings are untouched. Normal teardown disables owned outputs as well. The framework retains its existing order: bounded authored cleanup and post-cleanup survey, then release of owned resources before their borrowed transport. On a hard cut, disable starts immediately through resource termination; it never waits for authored cleanup to remember the channel. cancel_in_flight() is idempotent and refuses further output work when the cut begins. It cancels pending ramps at the controller, attempts the disable under the declared backend bound, and records whether disable was confirmed. A repeated call cannot restart a ramp or perform an enable. A closed handle remains closed; there is no automatic reconnect or replay of its last duty. Loss of access can prevent confirmation. As the signed GPIO note requires, the scoped timeline records that fact with the channel and operation named. An unconfirmed disable never leaves a success line behind or rewrites the original terminal state. A backend unable to stop autonomous output through the existing resource-termination boundary is a finding for Ty before it can be admitted; closing its control socket alone does not satisfy this note. Developer obligation: Select a fixture for which the declared disabled output is the intended safe state. Declare shared controller resources honestly. Keep restoration in cleanup() but rely on framework ownership for termination; never manually sequence another node's configure or cleanup. Consequence: Ending the test stops its output work and records what could be confirmed. A technician is never asked to infer electrical safety from a disconnected handle or from Pass, Fail, or Aborted alone. Lifecycle, hooks, and failure vocabulary ¶ The HIL lifecycle ruling applies unchanged. Framework bookkeeping owns connection flags, acquisition, release, and halt dispatch. before_each / after_each keep their pair invariant and their narrow context without hardware access. Constructor-registered surveys and audits remain the observation hooks: survey errors are logged and swallowed, audit errors fail their own scope, and ExternalIntegrationFailure is never swallowed. PWM transfer methods return operational results, never PASS . The proposed PwmOperationFailure derives from HiltError , not TestFailure , for the same reason GPIO's PinSettleFailure does: failure to apply a stimulus does not identify the DUT as the cause. It names the channel, operation, requested setting, last confirmed setting if known, and any backend ceiling that expired. Unknown is represented explicitly, never as zero duty or disabled output. Situation Signal and existing classification Invalid setting, unsupported trajectory, or conflicting channel use TypeError for a wrong type, ValueError for an invalid value or unsupported request; rejected before writes. Escaping configure/test code becomes a ContractViolation : Fail with the CONTRACT VIOLATION banner and bug: true . Controller unavailable during bring-up or an output request; backend operation exceeds its ceiling PwmOperationFailure ; the author handles the condition and may raise a modeled TestFailure . An unmodeled escape through configure/test code is a ContractViolation Fail, not an automatic hardware verdict. No silent retry or assumed setting. Independent observation shows the DUT missed its declared requirement Author raises TestFailure(..., evidence=...) ; Fail under the existing verdict contract. Disable cannot be confirmed during finalization Scoped evidence names the unconfirmed channel; the established terminal state is preserved, as in GPIO's safe-state sweep. Integration hook throws or the operator interrupts Framework-owned ExternalIntegrationFailure or OperatorInterrupt ; run-level Aborted and the full resource sweep. Node budget expires during transfer or ramp The winning clock supplies its existing structured evidence: fail_after produces Fail, abort_after node-local Aborted. Only the owned resources within the cut are disabled. Test returns without a verdict Existing MissingVerdict , node-local Aborted. A completed PWM operation cannot supply the missing verdict. This is one proposed operational exception under the existing root, not a new terminal state. Cancellation still propagates and outranks an attempted late return or substituted error at the child boundary. Evidence and backend acceptance ¶ Configuration logs name the channel, owner, polarity, disabled behavior, supported resolution, and timing envelope. Transfers and ramps use the same scoped logger to distinguish requested, confirmed, interrupted, and unconfirmed outcomes. The safe-state entry names its cause and confirmation before evidence closes. timeline.log and timeline.jsonl remain the owning node's two views; result.json retains the existing state and failure shape. Readings that establish a verdict travel as JSON-safe PASS(evidence) or TestFailure(..., evidence=...) , with @evidence(...) when a pass owes those keys. Commanded frequency and duty are stimulus settings, not measured frequency and duty. Actual parametric observations follow the signed #85 measurement design , whose implementation remains 86; this note neither fills the reserved measurements slot nor redefines ¶ units, limits, or verdict evaluation. In-flight observations use the scoped log or capture_artifact , since a cancelled leaf has no verdict evidence. MockPwm and a real backend must face the same contract suite, following the RemoteInterface / MockTransport precedent without inheriting command semantics. Required proofs include boundary/unsupported values before writes, atomic pair updates, exclusive channel ownership and shared-timer refusal, representable ramps within declared bounds, partial acquisition failure, normal teardown, and interruption at every ramp boundary. Parked operations must prove repeated cancellation cannot allow a late enable, node cuts leave an independent sibling unchanged, and unavailable disable produces only unconfirmed evidence. Real-backend tests must verify output behavior through independent observation; mock acknowledgements cannot establish it. Signed decisions recorded on #94 ¶ Ty approved these obligations with the note in !125 on 2026-09-08. The signature is also recorded on #94 : Explicit frequency/duty pairs with refusal of unrepresentable requests, rather than implicit rounding; fixed polarity and declared disabled behavior. Linear duty-only ramps at fixed frequency, with a backend-declared timing envelope and a separate completion deadline; no detached ramp after settlement. Exclusive channel operations and refusal of independent ownership when shared hardware cannot preserve node-local isolation and disable semantics. Operational write/bring-up failures as a modeled HiltError condition, with unconfirmed finalization recorded under the signed GPIO rule. GPIO's typed UNAVAILABLE read is not silently extended into a PWM write result. The lifecycle, verdict, and evidence contracts above are constraints on that decision. If a required backend cannot satisfy them, the finding belongs on 94 with the affected guarantee named. It does not earn an alternate lifecycle ¶ or an exception enforced only by a linter.

docs.text: Framework obligation: Present PWM as its own typed interface under HIL ruling 1. PwmInterface is not an exec subclass and does not change where utils.exec routes. Each named channel has a declared output polarity, frequency range, duty-cycle resolution, and disabled-output behavior before it can be enabled. Frequency is in hertz, positive and finite. Duty cycle is the fraction of the period spent in the declared active polarity, from 0.0 through 1.0 inclusive. Serial/UART console transport ¶ Status: SIGNED — Ty, 2026-09-10 ("all approved", recorded on #91). Implementation lands with the MR that carries this status change. Amendment SIGNED — Ty, 2026-10-18 (#150, merged as !184): the Serial Turn Contract below changes the transport's concurrency contract (one command on the wire at a time, queued in call order). Ty ruled "queue", not "refuse". Ty ruled both placements on 2026-09-05: SerialInterface as a local peer of SshInterface (console header on the HILT host), and the same transport reached through the existing via hop (a console server, or a Pi with a USB-UART, driven over SSH). One transport, two placements. This note specifies the transport's contract once — prompt detection, timeouts, line discipline, exit-status recovery, output bounding, safe-state on abort — and gives via composition its own section, per Ty's scoping note on the issue. Serial is a transport, not a new HIL contract: it slots in beside SshInterface behind RemoteInterface , matching remote.py 's own framing ("SSH, and later serial/UART, are peers behind this class"). Blocked on #90 (closed): the shared transport-contract suite this design must pass before any implementation MR opens. SerialInterface(RemoteInterface) opens a local device node ( /dev/ttyUSB0 , a Windows COM port) via pyserial-asyncio ; it never dials a socket. address is None — matching RemoteInterface 's own note that "a UART on a local device node has no address" — so connect() rejects host / port with TypeError , same as any unaddressed transport. endpoint is the device basename. A suite reaches it the way it reaches SSH: utils.use_serial(device=...) in configure() declares the console as the node's exec route, utils.get_serial opens one as an auxiliary endpoint, both hand back a Shell , and the framework owns the close (see "Routing" below). The transport itself is constructed only by the router and the self-tests. await utils.use_serial(device="/dev/ttyUSB0", baud=115200) Serial Prompt Contract ¶ Framework obligation: A console is a byte stream, not a request/response protocol — exec recognizes a command's end by the shell's prompt reappearing, never by an EOF or a status arriving on the wire. prompt (a regex, default a bare POSIX prompt) is matched against the tail of decoded output; login_prompt / password_prompt , when configured, are answered during connect() before the transport reads until prompt matches — a console already at a shell is unaffected. login_timeout (default 10s, connect-time only) bounds that resolution; expiry raises ConnectionError naming the last bytes seen, connect() raising whatever _connect raises, matching RemoteInterface . prompt_timeout (default 30s, fixed at construction) bounds how long exec waits for the prompt after sending a command — the transport's own safety net, not a substitute for fail_after / abort_after : a wedged console is a resource the transport cannot leave parked forever even with no ancestor budget declared. prompt_timeout and an ancestor's fail_after / abort_after are independent clocks racing the same await; whichever fires first decides the state, exactly as the Time Budget Contract already specifies. An echoed line unchanged across two read cycles is named in the eventual timeout's message, distinguishing "wedged, frozen" from "slow, still producing bytes" without the Floor Technician opening the suite. Developer obligation: Supply prompt (and login_prompt / password_prompt where the console logs in) at construction for anything but a bare POSIX shell — guessing a prompt at runtime is how a stuck read gets misread as a fast command. Set prompt_timeout shorter than any fail_after wrapping this node's exec calls when a wedge should surface on its own evidence line rather than only as an ancestor's TimeoutEvidence . Consequence: exec never raises for a command's own completion. Expiry settles like a killed command — ExecResult.settled(partial_output, "prompt timeout", None) , exit_code == -1 , partial output kept as evidence — never an exception the suite must catch. If the harness's own clock wins the race instead, the coroutine is cancelled ( CancelledError propagates, never swallowed) and cancel_in_flight runs the Serial Abort Contract below. Serial Line Discipline Contract ¶ Framework obligation: The wire is raw bytes with none of an SSH channel's structure (separate stdout/stderr, a real exit status). _exec normalizes before matching the prompt or handing bytes to ExecResult.settled : input is written as bare  (real-terminal Enter , since some bootloader shells ignore 
 alone), output CRLF is normalized to 
 ; exactly one leading echoed line matching the command just sent is stripped before that normalization (strip-if-present — a console with echo already off is unaffected); ANSI/VT100 escapes are stripped on the accumulated decoded buffer, so an escape split across two reads still resolves and a colorized prompt cannot defeat the prompt regex; decoding is UTF-8 with errors="replace" , matching ExecResult.settled 's existing path for every transport. Developer obligation: Read ExecResult.stdout with 
 line endings and no local echo, the same as any other transport's result — do not special-case serial output in suite code for line endings or echo. Consequence: A suite calling result.stdout.splitlines() does not need to know the transport was serial. A DUT's binary or non-UTF-8 output is evidence, not a dead channel. Serial Exit-Status Contract ¶ Framework obligation: A raw console has no exit-status side-channel — no equivalent of asyncssh's process.exit_status . The transport appends a sentinel to what it sends and parses it back out of the reply: <command>; echo "__HILT_RC__=$?" Once the prompt reappears, the transport scans for __HILT_RC__=<digits> , strips that one line from ExecResult.stdout , and parses the digits as exit_code . A sentinel that never appears — echo suppression failed, the shell died mid-command — settles as exit_code == -1 via ExecResult.settled(..., None) , the same "no real status exists" path every transport shares, with the raw captured text kept as evidence rather than discarded: the documented -1 case ("killed by a signal, or aborted before an exit status existed") with a lost sentinel standing in for the signal-kill. Stdout and the sentinel-bearing reply together are bounded by hilt.executor.BoundedCapture and DEFAULT_EXEC_OUTPUT_BUDGET unmodified — the same named ceiling LocalExec and SshInterface already share. Hitting the budget sets truncated=True , stops accepting bytes, and triggers the Serial Abort Contract below (there is no process to SIGTERM on the other end of a UART, only a wire to interrupt); the port stays open afterward, matching "the SSH session stays up" for the equivalent case. Developer obligation: Read ExecResult.stderr as transport-generated messages only ( "prompt timeout" , "transport closed" ) — never a slice of the DUT's own output. A console has one combined byte stream, not separate stdout/stderr descriptors; everything the DUT writes settles into stdout . A suite ported from an SSH-backed console that greps stderr for DUT error text needs to read stdout instead — the one place the two transports are not drop-in interchangeable. Consequence: Every ExecResult this transport produces is a real, bounded value a suite can treat exactly like any other transport's result — a missing or truncated status is evidence, never a raised exception. Serial Abort Contract ¶ Framework obligation: cancel_in_flight is the load-bearing halt ("kill every in-flight operation as hard as the protocol allows... a later exec rejects"). A serial line has no socket to destroy the way SshInterface._abort_client does, so the sequence is protocol-shaped: send a BREAK condition (a real UART primitive) to interrupt whatever runs in the foreground on most bootloader and kernel consoles; send Ctrl-C ( \x03 ) for a foreground shell command a BREAK alone misses; close the port unconditionally, whether or not the prompt reappeared after those two — no graceful wait, matching SSH's "graceful hangup is not used on either path" and the In-Flight Termination Contract's "closed HARD immediately... not at the next polling boundary." This contract does not fork that one; it names what "closed hard" means on a protocol with no socket to abort. The connected flag clears even if the BREAK/Ctrl-C sends themselves raise, same try / finally pattern as RemoteInterface.cancel_in_flight . Developer obligation: None beyond the existing RemoteInterface contract — abort is framework-owned and idempotent; suite code never calls cancel_in_flight itself. Consequence: Any exec still parked when the sequence runs settles with stderr naming "transport closed" — the same cause string _name_transport_death gives SSH, so a Floor Technician's grep for a dead resource does not need to know which transport produced it. An exec still queued behind it settles the same way without ever reaching the wire (Serial Turn Contract below). A 30-minute console session in progress when the run aborts does not keep mutating hardware after the sequence completes. Serial Turn Contract ¶ Framework obligation: exec on one SerialInterface runs one command at a time, in call order. A console carries one byte stream and no channel per caller — unlike an SSH session, which opens a channel per exec — so two callers writing back to back would both read the same reply. The transport holds an asyncio.Lock around each command's write-and-read; a caller that arrives while another is on the wire waits its turn, and waiters are served in the order they called. This is the turn a shared DeviceApi handle takes per request (bench finding F13), applied to the console, and it is what makes a use_serial route safe under self.parallel() : the leaves run concurrently, their commands go out one at a time. prompt_timeout bounds only the command's own wait for the prompt once it is on the wire, never its time in the queue — a sibling ahead in the queue is not the DUT being slow, and the node clock bounds the whole wait. A command still queued when cancel_in_flight or disconnect lands never reaches the wire: it settles exit_code == -1 with stderr "transport closed" , the same evidence an in-flight command gets from the Serial Abort Contract. The halt itself takes no turn — BREAK, Ctrl-C, and the close go out past whatever holds the lock, so the halt never waits. Developer obligation: Know what the leaves share. Queued leaves share one shell, so its state travels between them: a cd , an exported variable, or a background job started in one leaf is visible to the next. That is the cost particular to a console — a DeviceApi handle shares a session, not a shell. Claims that need isolation want one console each ( get_serial(device=...) per leaf, or one use_serial per child suite), and a latency measured around utils.exec on a shared console includes the wait for siblings. docs.text: Status: SIGNED — Ty, 2026-09-10 ("all approved", recorded on #91). Implementation lands with the MR that carries this status change. Amendment SIGNED — Ty, 2026-10-18 (#150, merged as !184): the Serial Turn Contract below changes the transport's concurrency contract (one command on the wire at a time, queued in call order). Ty ruled "queue", not "refuse". Ty ruled both placements on 2026-09-05: SerialInterface as a local peer of SshInterface (console header on the HILT host), and the same transport reached through the existing via hop (a console server, or a Pi with a USB-UART, driven over SSH). One transport, two placements. This note specifies the transport's contract once — prompt detection, timeouts, line discipline, exit-status recovery, output bounding, safe-state on abort — and gives via composition its own section, per Ty's scoping note on the issue. Serial is a transport, not a new HIL contract: it slots in beside SshInterface behind RemoteInterface , matching remote.py 's own framing ("SSH, and later serial/UART, are peers behind this class"). Blocked on #90 (closed): the shared transport-contract suite this design must pass before any implementation MR opens. SerialInterface(RemoteInterface) opens a local device node ( /dev/ttyUSB0 , a Windows COM port) via pyserial-asyncio ; it never dials a socket. address is None — matching RemoteInterface 's own note that "a UART on a local device node has no address" — so connect() rejects host / port with TypeError , same as any unaddressed transport. endpoint is the device basename. A suite reaches it the way it reaches SSH: utils.use_serial(device=...) in configure() declares the console as the node's exec route, utils.get_serial opens one as an auxiliary endpoint, both hand back a Shell , and the framework owns the close (see "Routing" below). The transport itself is constructed only by the router and the self-tests. await utils.use_serial(device="/dev/ttyUSB0", baud=115200)

docs.text: Framework obligation: A console is a byte stream, not a request/response protocol — exec recognizes a command's end by the shell's prompt reappearing, never by an EOF or a status arriving on the wire. prompt (a regex, default a bare POSIX prompt) is matched against the tail of decoded output; login_prompt / password_prompt , when configured, are answered during connect() before the transport reads until prompt matches — a console already at a shell is unaffected. login_timeout (default 10s, connect-time only) bounds that resolution; expiry raises ConnectionError naming the last bytes seen, connect() raising whatever _connect raises, matching RemoteInterface . prompt_timeout (default 30s, fixed at construction) bounds how long exec waits for the prompt after sending a command — the transport's own safety net, not a substitute for fail_after / abort_after : a wedged console is a resource the transport cannot leave parked forever even with no ancestor budget declared. prompt_timeout and an ancestor's fail_after / abort_after are independent clocks racing the same await; whichever fires first decides the state, exactly as the Time Budget Contract already specifies. An echoed line unchanged across two read cycles is named in the eventual timeout's message, distinguishing "wedged, frozen" from "slow, still producing bytes" without the Floor Technician opening the suite. Developer obligation: Supply prompt (and login_prompt / password_prompt where the console logs in) at construction for anything but a bare POSIX shell — guessing a prompt at runtime is how a stuck read gets misread as a fast command. Set prompt_timeout shorter than any fail_after wrapping this node's exec calls when a wedge should surface on its own evidence line rather than only as an ancestor's TimeoutEvidence . Consequence: exec never raises for a command's own completion. Expiry settles like a killed command — ExecResult.settled(partial_output, "prompt timeout", None) , exit_code == -1 , partial output kept as evidence — never an exception the suite must catch. If the harness's own clock wins the race instead, the coroutine is cancelled ( CancelledError propagates, never swallowed) and cancel_in_flight runs the Serial Abort Contract below.
docs.title: Serial Prompt Contract

docs.text:
Framework obligation: The wire is raw bytes with none of an SSH channel's structure (separate stdout/stderr, a real exit status). _exec normalizes before matching the prompt or handing bytes to ExecResult.settled : input is written as bare  (real-terminal Enter , since some bootloader shells ignore 
 alone), output CRLF is normalized to 
 ; exactly one leading echoed line matching the command just sent is stripped before that normalization (strip-if-present — a console with echo already off is unaffected); ANSI/VT100 escapes are stripped on the accumulated decoded buffer, so an escape split across two reads still resolves and a colorized prompt cannot defeat the prompt regex; decoding is UTF-8 with errors="replace" , matching ExecResult.settled 's existing path for every transport. Developer obligation: Read ExecResult.stdout with 
 line endings and no local echo, the same as any other transport's result — do not special-case serial output in suite code for line endings or echo. Consequence: A suite calling result.stdout.splitlines() does not need to know the transport was serial. A DUT's binary or non-UTF-8 output is evidence, not a dead channel.
docs.title: Serial Line Discipline Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: A raw console has no exit-status side-channel — no equivalent of asyncssh's process.exit_status . The transport appends a sentinel to what it sends and parses it back out of the reply: <command>; echo "__HILT_RC__=$?" Once the prompt reappears, the transport scans for __HILT_RC__=<digits> , strips that one line from ExecResult.stdout , and parses the digits as exit_code . A sentinel that never appears — echo suppression failed, the shell died mid-command — settles as exit_code == -1 via ExecResult.settled(..., None) , the same "no real status exists" path every transport shares, with the raw captured text kept as evidence rather than discarded: the documented -1 case ("killed by a signal, or aborted before an exit status existed") with a lost sentinel standing in for the signal-kill. Stdout and the sentinel-bearing reply together are bounded by hilt.executor.BoundedCapture and DEFAULT_EXEC_OUTPUT_BUDGET unmodified — the same named ceiling LocalExec and SshInterface already share. Hitting the budget sets truncated=True , stops accepting bytes, and triggers the Serial Abort Contract below (there is no process to SIGTERM on the other end of a UART, only a wire to interrupt); the port stays open afterward, matching "the SSH session stays up" for the equivalent case. Developer obligation: Read ExecResult.stderr as transport-generated messages only ( "prompt timeout" , "transport closed" ) — never a slice of the DUT's own output. A console has one combined byte stream, not separate stdout/stderr descriptors; everything the DUT writes settles into stdout . A suite ported from an SSH-backed console that greps stderr for DUT error text needs to read stdout instead — the one place the two transports are not drop-in interchangeable. Consequence: Every ExecResult this transport produces is a real, bounded value a suite can treat exactly like any other transport's result — a missing or truncated status is evidence, never a raised exception.
docs.title: Serial Exit-Status Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: cancel_in_flight is the load-bearing halt ("kill every in-flight operation as hard as the protocol allows... a later exec rejects"). A serial line has no socket to destroy the way SshInterface._abort_client does, so the sequence is protocol-shaped: send a BREAK condition (a real UART primitive) to interrupt whatever runs in the foreground on most bootloader and kernel consoles; send Ctrl-C ( \x03 ) for a foreground shell command a BREAK alone misses; close the port unconditionally, whether or not the prompt reappeared after those two — no graceful wait, matching SSH's "graceful hangup is not used on either path" and the In-Flight Termination Contract's "closed HARD immediately... not at the next polling boundary." This contract does not fork that one; it names what "closed hard" means on a protocol with no socket to abort. The connected flag clears even if the BREAK/Ctrl-C sends themselves raise, same try / finally pattern as RemoteInterface.cancel_in_flight . Developer obligation: None beyond the existing RemoteInterface contract — abort is framework-owned and idempotent; suite code never calls cancel_in_flight itself. Consequence: Any exec still parked when the sequence runs settles with stderr naming "transport closed" — the same cause string _name_transport_death gives SSH, so a Floor Technician's grep for a dead resource does not need to know which transport produced it. An exec still queued behind it settles the same way without ever reaching the wire (Serial Turn Contract below). A 30-minute console session in progress when the run aborts does not keep mutating hardware after the sequence completes.
docs.title: Serial Abort Contract

docs.text: Framework obligation: exec on one SerialInterface runs one command at a time, in call order. A console carries one byte stream and no channel per caller — unlike an SSH session, which opens a channel per exec — so two callers writing back to back would both read the same reply. The transport holds an asyncio.Lock around each command's write-and-read; a caller that arrives while another is on the wire waits its turn, and waiters are served in the order they called. This is the turn a shared DeviceApi handle takes per request (bench finding F13), applied to the console, and it is what makes a use_serial route safe under self.parallel() : the leaves run concurrently, their commands go out one at a time. prompt_timeout bounds only the command's own wait for the prompt once it is on the wire, never its time in the queue — a sibling ahead in the queue is not the DUT being slow, and the node clock bounds the whole wait. A command still queued when cancel_in_flight or disconnect lands never reaches the wire: it settles exit_code == -1 with stderr "transport closed" , the same evidence an in-flight command gets from the Serial Abort Contract. The halt itself takes no turn — BREAK, Ctrl-C, and the close go out past whatever holds the lock, so the halt never waits. Developer obligation: Know what the leaves share. Queued leaves share one shell, so its state travels between them: a cd , an exported variable, or a background job started in one leaf is visible to the next. That is the cost particular to a console — a DeviceApi handle shares a session, not a shell.
